Title: Nommas — Autonomous Operations for Every Factory
Subtitle: Edge-native industrial AI that understands the plant, reasons across systems, and acts under human governance — deployed by local partners in weeks, not months.
Problem Statement: Industry automated the work but never automated the decisions. Sensing, control and execution have been automated since the 1980s; the decisions still run through monitors, reports and dashboards until a human intervenes — manually, on historical data, not in real time. Nothing in the plant understands the operation, thinks, and acts under governance. The result is decisions made on yesterday’s reports and manual readings: late, incomplete and often wrong. This gap is widest in the small and mid-sized factories that make up most of industry in the Gulf, MENA and the Global South — plants that large-enterprise vendors cannot serve economically, that lack clean data and cloud connectivity, and that have been through pilots but never reached production.
Solution Overview: Nommas is a modular platform that gives a factory the ability to Understand, Think and Act. Understand — the Nommas Edge Stack runs on standard off-the-shelf hardware on-site; AI Capabilities (quality, safety, predictive maintenance, energy) see the machine, the line and the camera; Orbii AI Infra connects what the factory already has (PLCs, sensors, CCTV, existing systems) into one unified, real-time context. Think — Cortexa, the agentic brain, reasons across systems, finds root cause, recommends and explains. Act — Cortexa AI agents carry out the decision within a governance harness: each agent acts only within set permissions (observe, recommend, act), decisions beyond set limits wait for human approval, and every decision is logged with its evidence, action and approver. Guardrails run on the edge, even offline. Technologies: private LLM and vision-language models trained on industrial data and fine-tuned per plant (patent pending); computer vision on existing cameras; edge inference — only approved events leave the plant. Delivery model: customers land with one AI capability on one edge node and expand to Orbii and Cortexa. Deployment is done by certified local system integrators using Nommas templates, playbooks and reusable models; deployment time has fallen from 4 weeks to 1.5 weeks. In production since 2021.
Solution Provider(s): Saudi Can Company (packaging manufacturer, Saudi Arabia — quality capability live since 2021), Modern National Chemicals (chemicals manufacturer, Saudi Arabia — safety capability), Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources, Saudi Arabia (Smart Manufacturing initiative; Nommas is a certified SIRI assessor), DISAI (industrial AI consortium with Saudi Aramco, Qualcomm, Humain and RDIA), Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, Saudi Arabia (national digital initiative — projects and PoCs across Saudi factories), World Economic Forum (Technology Pioneer 2026; Gulf energy working group), Saudi Made programme (registered Saudi Tech member), certified system-integrator network (20 trained integrators in Saudi Arabia).
Implementation location(s): Saudi Arabia — 20 client factories, across food & beverage, packaging, chemicals, plastics and FMCG.
Implementation timeline(s): 2021 – present (Saudi Can Company quality deployment live since 2021; ongoing deployments through 2026).
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 1.5–4 weeks per site
Desired impact: Saudi Can Company — closed-loop quality inspection of can lids, 4 years in production: USD 2.7M annual savings, ROI in 8 months, inspection consistency raised from ~70% to 98% (reduced scrap and rework). Overall Winner, MIMA Middle East 2025. Modern National Chemicals — safety capability on existing CCTV: 100+ potential fire risks detected early, real-time alerts instead of after-the-fact review, one FTE of manual monitoring per shift redeployed, MODON compliance strengthened. Platform: 20 client factories, 7 edge nodes live, 15 paid AI capabilities; deployment time cut from 4 weeks to 1.5 weeks.
Key technologies: Agentic AI (Cortexa: cross-domain reasoning, AI agents, governance harness, decision log); private industrial LLM and vision-language models, fine-tuned per plant (patent pending); computer vision on existing cameras; edge computing on standard hardware with local inference and offline operation; industrial IoT and OT integration via Orbii AI Infra (PLCs, sensors, existing systems into one real-time context); predictive maintenance and energy analytics.
Unique Characteristics: Perceives, decides and acts across domains — not one sensor, one model, or a dashboard. Governed autonomy: observe/recommend/act permissions, human approval beyond limits, full decision audit log — autonomy you can audit, not a black box. Edge-native and offline: data stays in the plant; only approved events leave. Own models trained on industrial data, not just open source. Business model: modular, one SKU per capability, priced per unit of physical coverage (from USD 320 per unit per year) — affordable for small and mid factories. Partner-deployed: certified local integrators deploy with templates and playbooks; Nommas builds the platform and models. Built in Saudi Arabia for the industrial Global South.
Sustainable Change: Industrial AI today is concentrated in the few hundred largest plants that can afford custom projects, clean data and cloud infrastructure. The other 10,000+ factories — the small and mid-sized manufacturers that employ most industrial workers in the Gulf, MENA and the Global South — are stuck in pilots. Nommas was built to close this execution gap, and it is already doing so in production. The model is designed to replicate without us. Every deployment leaves behind three things: a certified local integrator, a reusable industrial model, and a plant that can add agents and coverage without a new project. Capability compounds inside the country rather than flowing back to a foreign vendor. The same playbook — certify local integrators, they deploy, Nommas provides the platform and models — scales from 20 integrators in Saudi Arabia today to 100 partners across the GCC, North Africa, Asia and Europe, and 2,000 industrial sites within five years. Because it runs on standard hardware, offline, with data staying on-site, the solution works where connectivity, data quality and budgets are limited — the conditions of most developing-country industry. Because autonomy is governed, logged and human-supervised, it gives regulators and plant owners an auditable path to adopting AI safely, a practical contribution to AI readiness and trust frameworks. Linked to national programmes — SIRI assessments that unlock government grants, ministry smart-manufacturing initiatives — it turns policy targets into measured outcomes on real factory floors: less scrap, fewer incidents, lower energy use, higher productivity. Built in Saudi Arabia and proven with Saudi manufacturers, it is a South-to-South model that other industrialising economies can adopt directly: local integrators, local data, local ownership, with the next era of industrial autonomy available to every factory, not only the largest.
Funding Sources: Nommas has been funded through customer revenue and a USD 1M deep-tech grant from the NextEra initiative of the National Technology Development Program (NTDP), a Saudi government programme under the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, delivered in partnership with KAUST. Deployments are paid by the customers themselves through capability subscriptions and one-time deployment fees, with project capital covered by customer advances, supplier terms and project financing. Nommas is also a certified SIRI assessor under the Ministry of Industry’s Smart Manufacturing initiative, where each assessment can unlock a ~USD 100K government grant for the factory. The company is now raising a USD 5M growth round to scale its partner network to the first 100 sites.

Title: Lumenn: AI Control Tower and Digital Twin for Resilient Supply Chains
Subtitle: AI demand forecasting and real-time KPIs on top of existing WMS, TMS and ERP systems, already in paid production with a logistics operator in Peru
Problem Statement: Mid-sized manufacturers, distributors and logistics operators in emerging economies run their operations on disconnected systems: a warehouse system, a transport system, an ERP and many spreadsheets. Managers lack a single, real-time view of stock, orders and shipments, and plan demand by intuition. The result is costly: stockouts and excess inventory at the same time, idle capital, wasted products, late deliveries and supply chains that break easily under disruption. Enterprise-grade planning and digital twin tools exist, but they are expensive, require replacing existing systems and are designed for large multinationals, leaving SMEs in developing and middle-income economies behind.
Solution Overview: Lumenn is an AI decision layer that sits on top of a company’s existing systems. It does not replace them and requires no new hardware. How it works: 1. Data ingestion. Connectors pull data from the client’s WMS, TMS and ERP into one unified data model. 2. AI demand forecasting. Gradient-boosting models (LightGBM) forecast demand per product and location and recommend optimal stock levels. 3. Control Tower. Real-time KPIs and rules flag stockouts, overstock and delivery risks, and send alerts to the people who must act. 4. What-if simulation. Managers test decisions (reorder points, routes, capacity) before applying them. 5. Operational digital twin. Lumenn extends the Control Tower into a digital twin of operations, built on open standards (OPC-UA, MQTT, Modbus, NGSI-LD) to connect plant and logistics data over time. Collaboration model: Building Blocks deploys the solution with each client’s operations team, adapting the models to their data. The commercial model combines an implementation fee with a recurring licence, and can be delivered through local integrators or technology centres.
Solution Provider(s): Logistics operator in Peru
Implementation location(s): Peru: Piura, Tumbes, Trujillo, Chimbote, Chiclayo, Cajamarca and Huamachuc
Implementation timeline(s): June 2026 – present (in paid production)
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3–4 months (cloud-based software connected to the client’s existing systems. No hardware installation)
Desired impact: Objectives: • Give operations managers one real-time view of stock, orders and shipments across their existing systems. • Replace intuition-based planning with AI demand forecasts and stock recommendations. • Make supply chains more resilient and less wasteful, at a cost that mid-sized companies in emerging economies can afford. Demonstrated impact: • In paid production since June 2026 with a logistics operator in Peru, across seven cities (Piura, Tumbes, Trujillo, Chimbote, Chiclayo, Cajamarca and Huamachuco), integrated with its WMS and TMS. • Demand forecasting error (MAPE) of around 5–6.6 %. • Share of products at optimal stock level raised from 68.5 % to 82 %.
Key technologies: • Machine learning demand forecasting (LightGBM gradient boosting) with stock-level optimisation. • Data ingestion connectors for WMS, TMS and ERP systems into a unified data model. • Control Tower with real-time KPIs, rules engine and alerts. • What-if simulation for operational decisions. • Operational digital twin (Lumenn) built on open standards: OPC-UA, MQTT, Modbus and NGSI-LD. • Cloud deployment. Platform code, data model and training pipelines fully owned by Building Blocks.
Unique Characteristics: • A layer, not a replacement. Lumenn works on top of the systems a company already uses, so adoption does not require new hardware or an ERP migration. • Proven in an emerging market. The solution runs in paid production in Peru, not only as a lab prototype. • AI that drives decisions. Forecasts feed directly into stock recommendations, alerts and what-if scenarios, so managers act on them every day. • Open standards, no lock-in. The data model uses open industrial standards, so clients and local integrators can extend it. • Affordable for SMEs. An implementation fee plus a recurring licence keeps the entry cost low for mid-sized companies.
Sustainable Change: Supply chain disruptions hit companies in developing and middle-income economies hardest, because they lack the planning tools large multinationals use. Lumenn brings AI forecasting and digital twin capabilities to these firms without requiring them to replace their systems. Because it connects to existing software and runs in the cloud, the same solution can be replicated across manufacturers, distributors and logistics operators in Latin America, Africa and Asia, and delivered through local integrators, industrial clusters or AIM Global Centres of Excellence. Better forecasts mean less waste, less idle capital and more reliable supply, while local teams gain practical skills in data and AI.
Funding Sources: Development was funded by Building Blocks’ own resources and by commercial revenue from client contracts. The Peru deployment is a paid commercial implementation.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: Lumenn is a decision layer that sits on a client's existing warehouse, transport and ERP systems, forecasting demand with gradient boosting and flagging stock and delivery risk through a control tower. It has been in paid production with a Peruvian logistics operator since June 2026 across seven cities.

Title: PCITC AI Platform for Petrochemical Industry
Subtitle: A technical platform for AI application development in the petrochemical industry, covering computing resource management, data processing, model training and inference, agent development and other technical capabilities.
Problem Statement: The petrochemical refining process features strong physical-chemical coupling and strict safety constraints. AI decisions cannot be fully autonomous, and clear boundaries for human-AI collaboration are required. There is a shortage of high-quality mechanism-data fusion datasets, lacking unified industry standards and labeling specifications. The intelligent-native transformation demands synchronous changes to organization, talent and business workflows. Besides, it is challenging to achieve closed-loop implementation of industrial agents with DCS/MES control systems, with no mature norms for interfaces, permissions and safety accountability.
Solution Overview: We develop an intelligent-native AI platform tailored for petrochemical refining scenarios. 1. How it works: The platform unifies computing resource management, data processing, high-quality mechanism-data fusion dataset development, LLM training & inference, and industrial agent development. It combines large-model generation with mechanism model verification; all outputs are validated by material balance, energy balance and equipment constraints to define clear human-AI collaboration boundaries and avoid risky autonomous decisions. It enables closed-loop interconnection with DCS/MES systems for safety monitoring and production optimization. 2. Methodologies and technologies used: We adopt large models, trusted data space, standardized dataset specifications, and industrial agent frameworks. Mechanism-data fusion and multi-dimensional constraint checking are core methodologies to guarantee the safety and reliability of AI outputs. 3. Partnerships and collaboration models: Co-creation with Sinopec Group. We jointly formulate industry standards, build datasets and pilot AI applications, aligning technical transformation with organizational, talent and business process upgrades.
Solution Provider(s): China Petroleum & Chemical Corporation‌(S‌inopec Corp.), Tsinghua University , Zhipu AI（Z AI）,China Electronics Standardization Institute
Implementation location(s): China, Beijing/Ningbo/Shanghai/Guangzhou/Jiujiang/Zhanjiang, etc.
Implementation timeline(s): 2023 – ongoing
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6-12 months
Desired impact: The throughput of the single-instance inference service of the large model is increased by 34% by tuning, and the throughput of the large-model cluster inference service is increased by 58%. The Great Wall Large Model achieves 5% improvement in industry-specific capabilities and 10% improvements in general capabilities. A high-quality petrochemical dataset of 570T has been established. And the skill pool contains 10,848 skills.
Key technologies: Large language model, multimodal model and its training & inference framework, model training and inference framework, trusted data space, high-quality mechanism-data fusion dataset technology, industrial agent, agent collaboration technology, computing resource management, mechanism model verification.
Unique Characteristics: 1. A specific intelligent inference scheduling engine dedicated to large models for the petrochemical industry, substantially cutting the cost of inference services. 2. An innovative closed-loop empowerment system is established as tool development – dataset production – AI scenario validation – iterative optimization of tools and datasets. Supported by an independently developed intelligent dataset toolchain, high-quality multimodal industrial datasets are accumulated. 3. Hybrid modeling is realized by integrating petrochemical process mechanism models and large models to ensure safe and trustworthy AI outputs, catering to highly constrained refining production scenarios.
Sustainable Change: This platform and standardized dataset assets have been replicated and deployed across multiple refining sites within Sinopec Group. The supporting standards, dataset specifications and human-AI collaboration paradigms can be further extended to the petrochemical sector, energy and chemical industry and other process industries. With localized process adaptation and safety & compliance customization, it can be applied in different regions and countries.

Title: Buy Good: AI market access for women-led small producers in Afghanistan
Subtitle: A live marketplace and payment network that takes women-led micro-enterprises to international buyers, adding an AI layer for listings, pricing signals and finance readiness.
Problem Statement: In Herat, women sort saffron that international tasting panels have ranked the best in the world year after year, most recently in January 2026. In Kandahar and Kabul, women embroider and weave pieces that buyers abroad prize. Yet most of them have nowhere to sell what they make. Since 2021, the de facto authorities have barred girls from secondary school and women from university, from most paid work, including with NGOs and the UN, and from much of public life. Restrictions on movement, including the requirement of a male guardian for travel, keep women out of markets and trade fairs, and few have a bank account. The International Labour Organization estimates that only 5.1 per cent of Afghan women were in the labour force in 2026, down from 16.5 per cent in 2020, the second-lowest rate in the world. For many women, what they make at home is now the only income they can earn. The skill and the product are already there: Afghan saffron, embroidery, carpets and dried fruit are known around the world. What is missing is the route to buyers. Product details exist only in Dari or Pashto, photographs are poor, connectivity is limited, and the banking system has been largely cut off since 2021. Value goes to intermediaries, and the women who make the goods stay invisible. Connecting them directly to buyers worldwide, and paying them directly, turns a craft they already master into a real and lasting income.
Solution Overview: Buy Good is Aseel's online marketplace for Afghan producers, selling to buyers worldwide with shipping, duties and taxes included. It runs on the same operating system as AidOS, Aseel's platform for verified identity, payments and delivery in low-connectivity settings. How it works today: Aseel's team onboards producers, photographs and lists their products, and opens each producer's shop on Buy Good. Buyers order online, Aseel fulfils the orders, and producers can receive their earnings directly in their HesabPay mobile wallet, so a woman without a bank account can still be paid. Every order is recorded on the platform. AidOS, which runs on the same system, already registers households without documents through Omid ID and verifies delivery with GPS and photo proof through 708 local agents. What we will add (the AI layer, at concept stage): (1) a listing assistant in the Atalan agent app that turns a producer's photos and Dari or Pashto description, captured offline, into a complete English product listing with structured attributes such as grade, weight and origin; (2) demand and pricing signals drawn from marketplace sales data, telling producers which products and markets are selling and at what price; and (3) a finance-readiness profile that, with the producer's consent, turns her sales and payment record into evidence that lenders, grant programmes and buyers can rely on. Partnership model: Aseel delivers through institutional programmes, with UN agencies, NGOs and foundations funding producer onboarding, and earns a service fee on programme value and a margin on marketplace sales.
Solution Provider(s): HesabPay (Afghan mobile wallet and payments provider, financial services; payment partner under an MOU signed September 2025, through which producers receive their earnings), UNDP Afghanistan (UN development agency; Aseel trained and onboarded 140 women-led SMEs in 15 provinces under its ABADEI programme, January-November 2025), Aga Khan Foundation and JICA (development agencies; digital marketing and e-commerce training under LITACA III in Kunduz and Takhar)
Implementation location(s): Afghanistan: producers across the country selling through Buy Good to buyers worldwide.
Implementation timeline(s): Aseel since 2018; Buy Good sales records 2022-present (ongoing). The AI layer is not yet implemented.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: About six months to build and test the AI listing assistant with producers in Afghanistan. The marketplace and payment rails can be extended to a partner country in about three months once a local payment partner is in place.
Desired impact: Objective: give women-led micro and small enterprises in fragile settings a direct route to international buyers and to finance. Demonstrated impact of the live platform: Buy Good producers earned USD 94,137 in sales in 2026 up to 28 October, and marketplace sales have grown by about 10% a year since 2022. Under UNDP's ABADEI programme in 2025, Aseel trained and onboarded 140 women-led SMEs in 15 provinces through 35 training sessions. More than 90 institutions use Aseel's platforms, and 708 verified local agents work through them. Expected impact of the AI layer: more producers listed with less staff time per listing, better prices and product choices based on what sells, and sales records that open finance to producers who have none today. We will set baselines and measure listings created, sales per producer, price realised, and the number of producers whose records support a loan or grant application.
Key technologies: Today: an online marketplace and storefront with international fulfilment; payouts to producers' HesabPay mobile wallets; order records and sales analytics; and, through AidOS on the same system, Omid ID digital identity and GPS, photo and time-stamped delivery verification. Planned: offline product capture in the Atalan agent app; multimodal AI (image and text) to generate structured English listings from photos and Dari/Pashto descriptions; machine-learning demand and price signals from marketplace sales data; and finance-readiness profiles built from producers' transaction histories, shared only with their consent. No AI is in production yet.
Unique Characteristics: Buy Good works where most e-commerce cannot: for women who cannot travel or open a bank account, and with poor connectivity. Aseel does the digital work on producers' behalf, from photography and listing to international fulfilment, and pays them to a mobile wallet. The planned AI layer is built on real sales and payment data from a fragile market, rather than on assumptions, and turns a producer's trading history into evidence of creditworthiness. The model is commercially sustained through service fees and marketplace margins, not only grants.
Sustainable Change: Once a producer's identity, sales and payments are recorded in one place, she becomes visible to buyers, lenders and support programmes that currently cannot reach her. The same rails can carry matching grants, payments and procurement from UN agencies and NGOs, so programmes can buy from and invest in women-led enterprises directly. The approach is built for settings with weak banking, limited connectivity and restrictions on women's mobility, and can be replicated in other fragile and least-developed economies through local payment partners. Aseel is also open-sourcing Omid ID, its identity layer, so other agencies can adopt it.
Funding Sources: Aseel has raised USD 737,500 in funding to date, alongside revenue from institutional service fees and marketplace sales. Foundations and agencies, including the Vitol Foundation (three programmes) and Humaniti, have funded programmes delivered through our platforms; UNDP and the Aga Khan Foundation/JICA funded producer training and onboarding.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access
Summary: Buy Good is Aseel's marketplace for women-led producers in Afghanistan, with mobile-wallet payouts and international fulfilment. Its strength is a working commercial platform with USD 94,137 of sales and named institutional funders; its weakness is that the AI layer is not yet built, which caps technical capability at band 2 and limits the case to market access rather than industrial AI.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access

Title: Guarding Green Mobility: An Intelligent Ultrasonic Testing Solution for Railway Wheelsets and Axles—Toward Safe, Sustainable, and Inclusive Rail Transit
Subtitle: The solution integrates AI-enabled defect recognition, mobile manipulators, and ultrasonic testing (UT) to provide efficient, standardized, and traceable intelligent operation and maintenance (O&M) inspection services for railway wheels and axles. Its core technology employs deep learning-based recognition algorithms to enable automated defect recognition (AutoDR) of internal defects in railway wheels and axles, achieving high defect recognition accuracy. Mobile manipulator–machine vision integration reduces inspection cycle time and provides end-to-end traceability of inspection results. While improving inspection efficiency and reliability, the solution leverages AI to drive the modernization of O&M inspection, enabling frontline workers to share in the benefits of industrial AI. It supports phased upgrades of existing equipment and adopts a localized delivery model featuring an “equipment + training + remote support” package. The solution was successfully deployed at the Tegalluar EMU Depot on the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway in 2023. It is intended for rollout in Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) partner countries, Southeast Asia, and other regions with rapidly growing demand for rail transport, contributing to the development of more inclusive, resilient, and sustainable transport infrastructure.
Problem Statement: 1.Public safety (1)The quality of critical rail vehicle components must be maintained to support safe, stable rail operations. (2)In some regions, rail operators lack standardized, traceable procedures for carrying out and managing O&M work. 2.Availability of low-carbon rail capacity (1)Technical bottlenecks in O&M limit the value of low-carbon rail assets. This constrains their ability to serve the public and limits the contribution of public transport to green mobility. 3.Affordable O&M in developing countries (1)Wheel and axle maintenance requires substantial investment in personnel, technology and equipment, and the benefits take time to materialize. (2)Ultrasonic inspection of railway wheels and axles requires specialized qualifications, and training personnel for these roles is time-consuming and expensive. 4.Human-centered automation (1)Current equipment has limited automation and intelligent capabilities and relies heavily on personnel. Workers generally have to move, attach and operate conventional equipment manually. Each unit requires both inspection and support personnel, making the work labor-intensive. (2)Working conditions are poor. Maintenance sheds are often semi-open, exposing personnel to seasonal temperature variation, noise and oil contamination. Prolonged on-site work under these conditions reduces efficiency and is detrimental to physical and mental health. 5.Inclusive industrial capability (1)In some developing countries and in least developed countries with suitable conditions for rail applications, local capabilities in equipment adaptation, inspection procedure development and quality management for ultrasonic testing of railway wheels and axles remain limited. Significant barriers to accessing advanced inspection technologies and deploying them in operational settings make it difficult to build sustainable local inspection capabilities. (2) Local technical personnel often lack systematic training and knowledge-transfer mechanisms for interpreting ultrasonic inspection results, maintaining equipment, and managing quality. After project implementation, they remain heavily dependent on external experts and suppliers, resulting in insufficient capacity for independent inspection and sustainable O&M. (3) Railway wheel and axle ultrasonic testing projects in China and overseas differ considerably in vehicle types, axle diameters, depot track layouts, applicable standards and maintenance work organization. Conventional equipment solutions cannot easily be adapted to local existing assets and O&M conditions through modular configuration and phased upgrades, nor can they readily integrate personnel training and ongoing technical support into project deployment.
Solution Overview: How the solution works The solution integrates intelligent ultrasonic testing robots for railway wheels and axles with a common management and control platform. It combines ultrasonic testing, AI-assisted analysis, robotic operation and digital quality management. Equipment can be configured for new or existing facilities and deployed in phases. 1. Task dispatch. The platform issues tasks from the maintenance schedule and links each vehicle, wheelset, inspection procedure and robot route to its quality record. 2. Self-check and verification. The system checks the mobile platform, robot, vision, UT, power and coupling systems, then verifies performance using a reference wheelset or axle. 3. Autonomous movement. An RGV moves the wheel robot along depot tracks, while a LiDAR-guided AGV moves the axle robot, plans paths, avoids obstacles and docks at the target vehicle. 4. Target localization. Laser, vision and position sensors identify the component and determine an initial docking position. 5. Precise alignment. The wheel system checks position and workspace, then supports, lifts and rotates the wheelset as required. For axles, 3D vision guides a 6-DOF parallel robot to center the probe lance in the bore. 6. Docking and coupling. Dual six-axis manipulators position wheel probes and supply water couplant. The axle robot inserts the probe lance without an external axle-end adapter, supplies oil couplant and checks oil conditions. 7. Parameter loading. UT settings are loaded automatically according to vehicle, wheelset and task. 8. Scanning and acquisition. The wheel robot performs conventional UT and PAUT on both wheels, with optional polygonization measurement. The axle robot performs helical bore scanning. Both generate images, waveforms and process records. 9. Process monitoring. The system monitors positioning, scanning, coupling, signal quality, power, couplant and safety status, uploads data and responds to anomalies. 10. AI-assisted analysis. The system flags suspected defects and, when required, uses FMC/TFM for high-resolution wheel imaging and confirmatory inspection. 11. Expert review. Qualified personnel remotely review raw data, images and AI findings before making the final determination. 12. Closeout. The platform archives all task, process, inspection and review data for traceability. Equipment retracts, returns to standby and recharges automatically. Methods and technologies: The solution integrates AI-assisted defect recognition, mobile robotics, IoT-based coordination and multimodal ultrasonic testing. AI analyzes ultrasonic images and waveforms to flag suspected defects and reduce false alarms, while labeled field data support iterative model improvement. AGVs, RGVs and multi-DOF manipulators enable autonomous movement, precise docking and controlled scanning. Cloud–edge collaboration supports task scheduling, equipment monitoring, remote analysis and multi-unit supervision. Conventional UT, PAUT and FMC/TFM combine rapid scanning with targeted confirmatory inspection, while automated reference-based verification, probe docking, couplant supply, parameter loading and process monitoring enable end-to-end inspection. Partnership and collaboration model: The solution is delivered through collaboration among Beijing Sheenline Group Co., Ltd., rail operators and maintenance organizations. The company provides the solution, equipment, algorithms, software and engineering services, while partners contribute procedures, site conditions and validation environments. The parties jointly adapt procedures, conduct trials and evaluate performance, using field feedback to refine products and algorithms. For new regions, local partners will adapt the solution to local standards, vehicles, networks and work organization. Joint pilots, O&M training, remote support and local service development will build sustainable capabilities beyond equipment delivery.
Solution Provider(s): 1.Guangdong Goworld Co., Ltd. The Guangdong Goworld Co., Ltd. Ultrasonic Instrument Branch was the first manufacturer in China to develop and produce ultrasonic instruments and transducers. The company now primarily develops, manufactures and sells products such as ultrasonic electronic instruments and printed circuit boards (PCBs). Its products can be used in applications such as millimeter-wave radar, LiDAR and “low-altitude satellites.” 2.Shantou Institute of Ultrasonic Instruments Co., Ltd. (SIUI). SIUI is an internationally known national key high-tech enterprise that develops, manufactures and sells industrial inspection equipment and other products. Its products are widely used in nondestructive testing (NDT) equipment and medical imaging systems. 3.Guangzhou Doppler Electronic Technologies Co., Ltd. The company specializes in the development, manufacture and sale of industrial ultrasonic testing equipment. It is a pioneer in high-performance phased array ultrasonic testing in China, and its technology is at an advanced international level. Its products are widely used in sectors such as rail transport and aerospace. 4.Instrumentation Technology and Economy Institute (ITEI). ITEI is a public institution at the central government level and a national intermediary organization for science and technology in instrumentation. It has developed into a multidisciplinary research institute grounded in standards science and soft science research and guided by advanced technologies such as smart manufacturing and the industrial Internet. It conducts research in measurement, control and automation, smart sensors, and intelligent instruments. 5. Nanjing EMU Depot, China Railway Shanghai Group Co., Ltd. Nanjing EMU Depot is a branch managed by China Railway Shanghai Group Co., Ltd. Its main activities are EMU operations and Level 1 and Level 2 maintenance in Jiangsu and Anhui provinces. It oversees five EMU workshops and provides maintenance for more than ten high-speed railway lines, including the Beijing–Shanghai High-Speed Railway. 6. PT Kereta Cepat Indonesia China (KCIC). KCIC is the joint venture responsible for building and operating the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway, the first high-speed railway in Indonesia and Southeast Asia. For this flagship Belt and Road Initiative project, KCIC is responsible for investment and financing, construction, and operations management. It is committed to advancing technology transfer and localizing operations.
Implementation location(s): International: Tegalluar EMU Depot Operations & Maintenance Division, Bandung, Indonesia (Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway Project). China: 80+ facilities under China State Railway Group Co., Ltd., including EMU depots, EMU servicing depots and locomotive depots in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Wuhan, Chengdu, Chongqing, Tianjin, Xi’an, Shenyang and other cities. The solution has also been implemented at rolling stock manufacturers under CRRC Group Co., Ltd., including CRRC Tangshan Co., Ltd., CRRC Dalian Co., Ltd. and CRRC Changchun Railway Vehicles Co., Ltd.
Implementation timeline(s): International — Indonesia (Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway Project): Solution design and planning began in June 2020. The solution officially entered service in September 2023.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: One to two years, subject to further assessment of local conditions.
Desired impact: By combining AI-assisted defect recognition, automated inspection by mobile manipulators and intelligent networked management, the solution aims to improve the safety, efficiency and traceability of railway wheel and axle inspection. It provides O&M technology to support safe, reliable and sustainable public transport in developing countries and middle-income economies. In response to transport service needs arising from population growth and urban development, the solution focuses on continuity of public infrastructure operations, protection of life, worker health and access to industrial technology. It also lays the groundwork for future rollout in LDCs with suitable conditions for adoption. 1.Strengthen inspection capability for critical components to protect public safety, life and health. Standardized ultrasonic scanning, AI-assisted identification of suspected defects, remote expert review and records covering the entire process reduce variability in manual operations and improve inspection consistency and quality traceability. These measures support the timely detection of wheelset defects and safe vehicle operations. 2.Improve maintenance efficiency and strengthen O&M capacity for public transport infrastructure. In one implementation, the intelligent ultrasonic testing system for wheelsets underwent field trials at Nantong EMU Depot from August 2023 to August 2024. During the trial, it inspected nearly 500 hollow axles and 1,000 wheelsets. Alongside improving the efficiency of the inspection procedure through automation and intelligent technologies, the solution streamlines equipment movement, positioning and docking, and preparatory work. This helps teams complete more work within limited maintenance windows and supports stable, continuous public transport operations. 3.Make better use of O&M resources and support affordable technology upgrading. The solution enables one inspector to supervise multiple units remotely and supports phased upgrades based on existing equipment and site conditions. Estimates from the field trial at Nantong EMU Depot indicated that ultrasonic testing efficiency increased by at least 40% compared with the conventional approach. For operators with limited funding and few specialists, the expected benefit is more efficient use of scarce resources and lower barriers to training, ongoing O&M and upgrades to intelligent systems. The solution offers a deployable option for strengthening rail maintenance capability in developing countries and LDCs with relatively few technical specialists. 4.Improve working conditions and support skills development. Automated equipment handling and probe docking reduce repetitive on-site work. For hollow-axle inspection, adapter-free docking removes the need for repeated manual installation and removal of external axle-end adapters. This reduces the time personnel spend working amid noise, oil contamination and temperature variations or in confined spaces, as well as physical workload and the risk of operator error. Together with operation and maintenance training and remote technical support, the solution can help personnel transition to duties such as equipment supervision, inspection data analysis and quality management. The benefits of automation and intelligent technologies can thus translate into safer working conditions and stronger professional skills. 5.Indirectly support inclusive development and green mobility. By strengthening railway O&M capability, the solution helps existing rail assets continue to serve the public. In future international rollouts, reliable transport services are expected to indirectly support access to employment and public services such as education and health care, with attention to the mobility needs of low-income groups.
Key technologies: 1.Artificial intelligence 1)AI-assisted defect recognition. The system combines deep learning, machine vision, multi-feature waveform discrimination and pattern recognition to analyze ultrasonic images and waveforms together. These methods primarily support the identification and classification of suspected defects and decision-support alerting, reducing the risk of false alarms associated with simple threshold alarms or purely manual interpretation. 2)Iterative model refinement. The defect sample database is expanded with samples from a range of operating conditions collected during field inspections. Labeled historical defect samples are used for model training, and the structure and parameters of the model are refined iteratively. This improves the model’s ability to handle complex operating conditions and different defect characteristics and improves its performance as an inspection aid. 2.Mobile manipulators (1)Autonomous mobility and safe navigation. The solution integrates LiDAR-based SLAM navigation for AGVs, rail guidance for RGVs, laser sensing, safe obstacle avoidance and path planning. The choice of mobility system depends on the site conditions for wheel and axle inspection. These technologies primarily support mapping, movement between workstations, target workstation location, safe obstacle avoidance and precision docking. They replace manual movement and power reconnections between workstations. (2)Flexible control and actuation of robots with multiple degrees of freedom, and automated docking. The solution uses a 6-DOF parallel robot for axles and dual six-axis serial manipulators for wheels. Techniques such as path optimization and adapter-free docking enable the inspection mechanisms to adapt their movements to the task. In axle ultrasonic testing, these technologies provide precise centering of the probe lance in the axle bore and controlled scanning. In wheel ultrasonic testing, they coordinate positioning and automated contact of the probe assemblies on both sides. 3.Internet of Things （1）Cloud–edge collaboration and intelligent robot fleet management and control. The system brings together task scheduling, data uploads, equipment condition monitoring and remote analysis. One inspector can supervise multiple units, reducing on-site staffing, centralizing data management and enabling cross-device coordination. 4.Ultrasonic testing （1）Multimodal ultrasonic testing and end-to-end inspection automation. The system combines conventional UT, PAUT and FMC/TFM with automated operations in a workflow that pairs rapid scanning with targeted confirmatory inspection of suspected defects. It also automates verification using reference test pieces, probe docking, couplant supply, loading of scanning parameters, process status monitoring and charging. This provides end-to-end process automation from pre-job preparation to inspection closeout.
Unique Characteristics: 1.An integrated system for intelligent ultrasonic testing of wheelsets. The solution moves beyond stand-alone equipment and fragmented inspections by bringing axle robots, wheel robots, proven ultrasonic testing equipment and a networked management and control platform into a single system. This integrates the management of inspection tasks, their execution, defect analysis and quality data. 2.Coordination of AGVs, RGVs and different types of robots. The solution uses autonomous AGV navigation, RGV rail guidance, and serial or parallel robots to suit different depot tracks and workstations. This coordinates mobility, sensing and manipulation—the system’s “feet, eyes and hands.” The modular design supports high-precision docking at axle bores and can be extended to other inspection targets such as wheels. 3.High-precision docking using combined 2D–3D vision and a 6-DOF parallel robot. Coordinated control of 2D coarse localization, 3D fine localization and the 6-DOF parallel platform addresses automatic centering difficulties caused by track irregularities, differences in vehicle body orientation and axle bore offsets. The parallel structure has a high load capacity, a compact design and no cumulative error, making it suitable for high-precision work over a small range of motion. 4.Streamlined operation with adapter-free docking. The hollow-axle ultrasonic testing robot uses a removable guide module integrated into the front end of the probe lance to perform the function of a conventional external adapter. Precise robotic positioning eliminates the need for personnel to frequently install and remove an axle-end adapter, reducing preparatory steps, staffing needs and the risk of operator error. 5.Multi-probe helical scanning and compatibility with multiple EMU and locomotive axle types. Different probe combinations, probe lance specifications and inspection parameter settings allow the system to detect transverse and longitudinal defects on the axle’s outer surface as well as internal material discontinuities. This approach accommodates hollow axles on multiple types of EMUs and locomotives. 6.Integration of advanced FMC/TFM ultrasonic imaging. The solution applies FMC/TFM to wheelset inspections to improve the imaging, localization and sizing of defects in complex structures. The project also contributes to the development of relevant national standards, supporting the practical adoption and standardization of advanced inspection methods. 7.Integrated waveform-rule and deep learning-based defect evaluation. The system combines multiple waveform features and waveform discrimination rules with deep learning and machine vision to overcome the high false alarm rate associated with simple gate-based alarm methods. It automatically flags suspected defects and issues alerts for expert review. 8.All-DC low-noise power supply and intelligent charging. Lithium batteries and an all-DC power supply reduce the need to disconnect and reconnect power between workstations, lower electromagnetic interference (EMI) and improve ultrasonic signal quality. The robots support automatic charging for continuous operation across multiple tasks. 9.Cloud–edge collaboration and intelligent robot fleet management and control. The system brings together task scheduling, data uploads, equipment condition monitoring and remote analysis. One inspector can supervise multiple units, reducing on-site staffing, centralizing data management and enabling cross-device coordination.
Sustainable Change: 1.Provide a technology upgrade path for different stages of development. The modular configuration supports phased deployment of proven inspection equipment, intelligent assistive functions, individual robots and the fleet management and control platform. It also supports upgrades to existing equipment and deployment at new maintenance facilities. Countries and operators can choose configurations based on their vehicle types, facilities, connectivity, staff capabilities and investment plans, then gradually expand inspection coverage and automation. This can ease the pressure of undertaking a comprehensive retrofit all at once and give resource-constrained developing countries and LDCs with suitable rail infrastructure or development needs more flexible options for industrial digitalization. 2.Build sustainable local capacity through technical cooperation and training. Existing hollow-axle ultrasonic testing equipment has been used on the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway Project in Indonesia, providing practical experience for overseas implementation. In new regions, the plan is to work with local rail operators, maintenance organizations and technology partners to adapt to local technical standards, vehicle types, languages, networks and work organization. Joint pilots, operation and maintenance training, remote expert support and development of local service capacity would gradually strengthen the ability of local personnel to operate, maintain and manage the equipment. In the long term, this can promote knowledge sharing and the adoption of technology so that partner regions can continue to benefit from industrial AI applications. 3.Support the transition to new skills and create opportunities for local technical services. Automation transfers some repetitive manual work to equipment, allowing specialists to spend more time on remote supervision, quality review and data analysis. As deployment expands, ongoing services such as installation and commissioning, maintenance and repair, software support and technical training could be provided locally. By combining staff training with deployment, the solution could help workers take on digital roles and improve occupational safety and health conditions. 4.Expand from maintenance into the industrial supply chain and more transport settings. The solution is already in use on multiple projects at sites in China and abroad. Within a defined scope, and following application-specific adaptation and validation, shared inspection procedures, software and modular equipment can support further expansion into areas such as wheelset manufacturing, assembly, higher-level maintenance and urban rail transit. This would enable the exchange of data and experience between manufacturing quality control and O&M. Replication in other countries would enable the exchange of data and experience between manufacturing quality control and O&M. Replication in other countries would depend on adapting to local standards, certification requirements and site conditions. The aim is to build sustainable delivery and service capacity over time. 5.Translate stronger industrial capability into long-term public service benefits. As populations grow, cities develop and demand for public infrastructure services increases, sustained and reliable O&M capability helps rail transport continue to serve the public over the long term. By supporting reliable mobility and connecting people to jobs and public services, the solution can potentially contribute to poverty reduction, public health and safety, and social inclusion. Combining equipment upgrades with local capacity building, quality management and ongoing services could extend the technical benefits of individual projects into longer-lasting support for public transport.
Funding Sources: This industrial AI solution has been implemented at scale. To meet nondestructive testing needs across different types of rolling stock, including EMUs, locomotives and metro trains, and for different wheel and axle models, the company continues to fund research and development from its own resources. It also earns contract revenue from equipment sales and project partnerships with customers in China, including EMU depots, rolling stock depots and rolling stock manufacturers. This provides ongoing funding for the development and refinement of the product line, including the intelligent ultrasonic testing robots for wheels and axles and the Intelligent Ultrasonic Testing Management and Control Platform for Wheelsets. It also supports manufacturing, custom development, on-site deployment and O&M services.
Testimonials and Endorsements: 1. Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway Operating Testimonial The equipment's overall performance fully meets all original design specifications and exhibits excellent environmental resilience along the Jakarta-Bandung line. Technical metrics comply with Chinese railway standards and Indonesian regulatory requirements for EMU Level 2 maintenance. The system achieves a seamless closed-loop workflow spanning work plan creation, automatic docking, automated scanning, AI flaw recognition, and automatic archiving—serving as a mature benchmark for intelligent rail depot O&M. Zero missed flaw detections were recorded throughout the 36-month evaluation period, achieving a 100% data integrity rate and providing a robust safety foundation for 350 km/h commercial operations. The standardized inspection methodology possesses direct application value for high-speed rail, intercity lines, and urban transit networks, making it highly suitable for deployment in international export projects. — PT Kereta Cepat Indonesia China (KCIC), Tegalluar EMU Depot Operations & Maintenance Division 2. Testimonial from Shanghai EMU Depot Intelligent capabilities: Both units integrate technologies such as vision-based recognition, robot control and AI-assisted defect evaluation. Both offer one-button automated flaw detection with a fully automated operating sequence. The units can be operated and controlled remotely, and one person can operate multiple units. This frees staff from having to accompany the train during inspection and improves working conditions. High operating efficiency: The axle ultrasonic flaw detector eliminates manual installation and removal of adapters, saving time on auxiliary work. The wheel ultrasonic flaw detector operates continuously and automatically, enabling efficient inspection of an entire train and meeting maintenance cycle requirements. — Technical Section, Shanghai EMU Depot, China Railway Shanghai Group Co., Ltd. 3. Primary thematic focus area: Embodied AI, Industrial Robotics and Smart Manufacturing
Summary: Beijing Sheenline has automated ultrasonic inspection of railway wheelsets and axles with a robot carrying the probe, in service at more than 80 Chinese depots and one Indonesian depot since 2023. The defect record over 36 months is among the hardest evidence in the field; the social and environmental account is thin.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry; Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Embodied AI, Industrial Robotics and Smart Manufacturing

Title: Makanika: Formalising Africa's Vehicle Repair Industry on WhatsApp
Subtitle: A WhatsApp platform that uses AI to verify mechanics and estimate prices, giving informal garages in Uganda customers, payments, skills and a record of work.
Problem Statement: Uganda has more than 2.3 million vehicles on the road, and the fleet is growing at close to 6% a year. The repair and maintenance industry that keeps these vehicles running is worth an estimated US$650 million annually, yet more than 80% of it operates informally. It runs through roadside garages, parts dealers and towing operators that sit outside the formal industrial economy. Most garages are run by young men with no formal training, no digital presence and no way to prove the quality of their work. That keeps them out of the supply contracts, credit and insurance that would let them invest in tools, skills and safe working practices. Manufacturers and distributors of lubricants, batteries and parts cannot see or finance the workshops that decide which products reach the motorist. Dealer credit is therefore costly to extend and difficult to collect, and counterfeit parts circulate freely. Motorists, from boda boda riders to small fleet owners, cannot easily find a mechanic they trust or know what a fair price is. When a repair fails they have no record and no recourse, which means lost income as well as a lost vehicle. Young women make up less than 10% of the trade, and refugees and young people from rural districts have few routes into it. The sector also produces avoidable emissions from poorly maintained vehicles, waste from counterfeit parts and unsafe disposal of used oil and lead-acid batteries, because nothing in the chain is traceable. The same gaps in finance, skills and market access recur across East Africa, where we have mapped 4,859 motor-trade businesses in 8 countries. Most of them operate in markets where connectivity is limited and smartphone apps see little use.
Solution Overview: Makanika Dot Com is a Ugandan automotive services platform, founded in Kampala in 2015, that works to formalise and dignify work in Africa's automotive sector. It connects the four sides of the repair economy, which are motorists, garages, parts suppliers and manufacturers, on one platform. Our WhatsApp platform, launched in 2026, lets a motorist, a mechanic or a parts dealer use the service on any phone, in English or Luganda, without downloading an app. A motorist chooses a service from a simple menu and is matched to the nearest suitable vetted garage. In the same conversation the motorist can request towing, buy parts and insurance and pay by mobile money, and every job produces a quote, an invoice, a receipt and a service record. Garages and mechanics join by WhatsApp and receive a verified profile, a stream of customers, invoicing and payment tools, cashback and access to quality parts. This turns an informal workshop into a business that can be found, paid and trusted. When a provider joins, a Claude vision model compares the photograph on their identity document with a selfie taken at sign-up. Google Cloud Vision reads the business cards and documents they submit, so that a roadside workshop can build a verified profile from the paperwork it already holds. The platform also offers a used-car price estimate generated by Claude, which gives buyers and sellers a reference point in a market with little price transparency. Our team runs the network through a Claude-based operations assistant and an AI content engine. Garage matching, quotes, invoices and the protection of users' contact details run on deterministic rules, which keeps every customer-facing step predictable. Manufacturers and distributors use our portal to run their dealer networks, credit and collections, and to reach the mechanics who decide which products motorists buy. The Makanika Foundation trains young people as mechanics, with deliberate inclusion of young women and refugees. It onboards every graduate onto the platform as a verified provider, so that training leads directly to paid work. Our collaboration model brings multinational fuel retailers, insurers and battery manufacturers together on the supply side. A Dutch vocational-training partner and a Mastercard Foundation–linked youth programme work with us on the skills side, and the platform is the shared channel through which each partner reaches the garages. Revenue comes from commissions on completed jobs and payments, margins on parts and lubricants, partner commissions, and software and data services for manufacturers and insurers. The commercial platform therefore carries the cost of the network that the Foundation's training feeds.
Solution Provider(s): Multinational fuel retailers (lubricant and fuel supply, energy sector), insurers (motor insurance, financial services sector), a Dutch vocational-training organisation (mechanic training, technical and vocational education sector), a Mastercard Foundation–linked youth programme (youth employment and skills, development sector), battery manufacturers (automotive batteries and take-back, manufacturing sector, partnership in development)
Implementation location(s): Uganda: platform live nationally from Kampala, with 600+ connected garages and 3,000+ active users. Mapped and contactable network of 4,859 motor-trade businesses across 87 cities in Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia, DR Congo, Rwanda, South Sudan and Burundi.
Implementation timeline(s): 2015 to present (Makanika platform, Uganda); 2026 to present (WhatsApp platform with AI provider verification and price estimates); ongoing, no end date.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 to 6 months, starting from our existing mapped network in the target country and adding local language menus, mobile-money integration and garage onboarding.
Desired impact: The main objective of Makanika is to bring Africa's informal vehicle repair industry into the formal economy. We do this by giving garages, mechanics and parts dealers the finance, skills and market access that formal businesses take for granted, and by giving motorists a trusted, recorded and fairly priced service. A second objective is to open the trade to young women, refugees and young people from rural districts by connecting every person we train directly to paid work on the platform. A third is to make the automotive supply chain traceable, so that quality parts displace counterfeits and used oil and lead-acid batteries can be taken back and recycled. Our demonstrated impact begins with regional reach. We have mapped 4,859 motor-trade businesses across 8 countries and 87 cities, including 1,344 that trade in spare parts and 445 that specialise in auto-electrical work. We can reach more than 5,900 businesses and motorists directly by WhatsApp and SMS. Within that network, 600+ connected garages and 3,000+ active users already transact on the platform in Uganda. They have processed more than 25,000 service transactions, each with an invoice and a service record. Through a Mastercard Foundation–linked youth programme, the Makanika Foundation is training 1,000 young people across 8 districts, 70% of them women, with a quota for refugees and people with disabilities. Our targets for 2026 to 2028 are to train 10,000+ young people and connect them to employment or enterprise, and to formalise 5,000+ garages across Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda. Through Women In Auto we aim to build 2,500 women-owned or women-inclusive automotive micro-enterprises, 500 of them in refugee settlements. We also aim to reach 50,000+ active platform users and 30,000+ motorists with maintenance and environmental awareness. Our 10+ planned climate initiatives cover electric-vehicle servicing skills, emissions tracking, battery take-back and recycling, and safe used-oil handling. Together with vetted garages and quality parts, they will reduce the excess emissions of poorly maintained vehicles and the waste from counterfeit parts.
Key technologies: The platform runs on WhatsApp, which lets motorists, mechanics and parts dealers use the full service through a channel they already know. It reaches people without data through SMS. Payments run through mobile money, and every job generates a quote, an invoice, a receipt and a service record as structured data on vehicles, faults, parts, prices and providers. Menus and replies are available in English and Luganda, and the platform can send replies as voice through text-to-speech for users who prefer to listen. A manufacturer and distributor portal handles dealer networks, credit and collections. AI is used today at the points where trust is hardest to establish in an informal market, which are the identity of providers and the fairness of prices. A Claude vision model compares the photograph on a new provider's identity document with a selfie taken at sign-up, which lets us verify mechanics and garage owners automatically. Google Cloud Vision reads the business cards and documents that providers submit. A used-car price estimate generated by Claude gives buyers and sellers a reference point. Our team works through a Claude-based assistant that turns plain-English instructions into actions on the platform, and an AI content engine helps produce our published material. Bookings, garage matching, quotes, invoices and the protection of users' contact details run on deterministic rules. This keeps every customer-facing step predictable while we test language models against the risk of incorrect answers. The next stage brings AI into the customer conversation itself. It will add understanding of free-text requests in English and Luganda, intake of voice notes from riders and mechanics who prefer to speak, and triage of faults before a vehicle reaches the garage. It will also match each job to a provider by skill, record and location. The structured data that every job already produces gives these models a local foundation on which to be built and tested.
Unique Characteristics: Makanika's first distinctive feature is its delivery approach, which carries the whole repair economy inside WhatsApp, on any phone, in English or Luganda, with no app to download. A mechanic with a basic phone and limited data can join, receive customers, invoice and be paid in the same conversation that a motorist uses to book. This design suits the low-connectivity settings in which most of East Africa's motor trade operates. It also gives a landlocked least developed country such as Uganda a route into the digital economy that works on the devices people already own. The second is the use of AI to verify providers who hold little formal paperwork. An identity check that compares a document photograph with a selfie, combined with automated reading of business cards and documents, lets a roadside workshop build a verified profile. A corporate client, an insurer or a manufacturer can then rely on that profile. Every completed job adds an invoice and a service record to it, which builds the history of work that informal garages have never been able to show a lender. The third is the hybrid business and partnership model. Makanika Dot Com (U) Limited runs the commercial platform, and the Makanika Foundation trains young people, with deliberate inclusion of young women and refugees, and onboards every graduate as a verified provider from the first week. Commissions on jobs and payments, margins on parts and lubricants, partner commissions and data services for manufacturers and insurers pay for the network. The Foundation's training keeps that network supplied with skilled mechanics. The fourth is the way the platform links the industrial supply chain to the street. Manufacturers and distributors use our portal to run their dealer networks, credit and collections. This gives multinational fuel retailers, insurers and battery manufacturers a traceable channel to the garages that decide which products reach the motorist. The same traceability makes it possible to take back used oil and lead-acid batteries. Our mapping of 4,859 motor-trade businesses across 8 countries gives us a ready base for expansion beyond Uganda.
Sustainable Change: The deepest change Makanika can bring about is a shared and trusted record of work in an industry that has never had one. Every job on the platform produces an invoice, a payment trail and a service record. Together these build a garage's reputation, a young mechanic's career history and a manufacturer's understanding of its market. Once that record exists, garages can show insurers and lenders evidence of steady trading. That opens the way to working-capital credit, insurance and supply contracts that informal workshops cannot obtain today. The finance that follows lets them invest in quality tools, safe waste handling and electric-vehicle servicing. The follow-on effects reach beyond the garage itself. Traceable supply of lubricants, batteries and parts allows manufacturers and distributors to extend dealer credit with more confidence and to displace counterfeit parts. It also allows them to organise the take-back and recycling of used oil and lead-acid batteries. The Foundation's training, connected directly to paid work on the platform, creates a pathway into a skilled trade for young women and refugees who have been almost entirely absent from it. The structured data on vehicles, faults, parts, prices and providers will support baseline studies of the automotive services sector for manufacturers, insurers, policymakers and development agencies. Those studies can inform vocational-training curricula, standards for garages and policy on vehicle emissions and waste. The model is built to be replicated, because it runs on WhatsApp and mobile money, which are already in wide use across the region, and it needs no proprietary hardware. We have mapped 4,859 motor-trade businesses across 8 countries and 87 cities. Our plan for 2026 to 2028 is to formalise 5,000+ garages across Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania and Rwanda and to train 10,000+ young people and connect them to employment or enterprise. We also plan to build 2,500 women-owned or women-inclusive automotive micro-enterprises. The matchmaking that this Call offers with UN programmes on industrial skills, MSME development and the circular economy would help us adapt the model to new countries. It would connect us with partners that already work with governments and training institutions in those countries.
Funding Sources: The commercial platform is funded through its own revenue, which comes from commissions on completed jobs and payments, margins on parts and lubricants, partner commissions, and software and data services for manufacturers and insurers. The Makanika Foundation's training of young mechanics is funded through grant support, currently from a Mastercard Foundation–linked youth programme that targets 1,000 young people across 8 districts, 70% of them women, together with a partnership with a Dutch vocational-training organisation.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access
Summary: Makanika runs the vehicle repair economy on WhatsApp, matching motorists to vetted garages and recording quotes, payments and jobs. Its strength is genuine adoption and a commercial revenue model; its weakness is a thin technical record, with no named model or measurement, which holds technical capability and demonstrability at band 3.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems
