Title: Adaptive Embodied AI for Logistics and Industrial Automation
Subtitle: Powered by X Square Robot’s WALL-series embodied AI models and robotic platforms, the solution enables adaptive 3D goods feeding, dual-arm logistics sorting, and industrial assembly.
Problem Statement: Logistics and manufacturing operations still depend heavily on repetitive manual work or rigid automation designed for predefined objects, fixed positions, and highly controlled workflows. In real-world environments, however, parcels, components, and materials vary in shape, size, orientation, and placement, while workflows and production requirements change over time. In logistics, mixed parcels may arrive in irregular arrangements with labels facing away from scanners, making reliable induction and sorting difficult. In 3D goods feeding, robots must perceive objects at different depths and orientations, select suitable grasping strategies, and place or feed them accurately into downstream equipment. Industrial assembly adds further complexity through precise positioning, coordinated manipulation, multi-step task execution, and adaptation to object or process variation. Conventional automation often requires task-specific fixtures, extensive programming, and repeated engineering whenever products, layouts, or processes change. This limits flexibility, increases deployment and changeover costs, and makes it difficult to automate high-mix or dynamic operations. Industry therefore needs more adaptive robotic systems that can perceive changing environments, understand task objectives, manipulate diverse objects, and transfer the same core intelligence across multiple industrial scenarios.
Solution Overview: How dose the Solution Works X Square Robot provides an embodied AI solution that connects visual perception, task understanding, decision-making, and physical manipulation across multiple robotic platforms and industrial applications. The system uses visual observations and task instructions to identify objects, assess their positions and orientations, determine appropriate manipulation strategies, and execute actions through continuous closed-loop control. Instead of depending exclusively on predefined rules for each object or workflow, the embodied AI model adapts its actions to the current operating conditions. The solution currently supports three representative application areas: - 3D goods feeding: QUANTA X1 Pro perceives goods positioned at different depths and orientations, selects appropriate grasping actions, reorients objects when required, and feeds them into downstream logistics or production processes. - Dual-arm logistics sorting: Coordinated robotic arms identify, grasp, reorient, scan, transfer, and place mixed parcels, supporting continuous parcel induction and sorting under changing object arrangements. - Industrial assembly: The system performs precise, multi-step manipulation and coordinated operations for assembly-related tasks, adapting actions to component position, task sequence, and environmental variation. By applying a shared embodied AI architecture across different robot configurations and workflows, the solution creates a scalable foundation for adaptive automation in logistics and manufacturing. Methodologies and Technologies The solution integrates X Square Robot's proprietary WALL-series embodied AI foundation models, including WALL-B, with visual and spatial perception, multimodal task understanding, model-driven manipulation, motion control, and coordinated dual-arm operation. QUANTA X1 Pro provides a mobile dual-arm robotic platform for flexible goods handling and task execution, while dedicated robotic workcells support higher-throughput logistics and industrial operations. Closed-loop perception and control allow the robots to update their actions as object positions, orientations, and environmental conditions change. The modular architecture is designed to connect with existing conveyors, scanners, production equipment, warehouse systems, and industrial workflows, reducing the need to redesign an entire facility around the robot. Partnership and Collaboration Model X Square Robot works with logistics operators, manufacturers, and system-integration partners to identify suitable workflows, collect operational requirements, validate performance, and progressively deploy embodied AI systems in real operating environments. Collaboration with industry partners, including SF Express, combines X Square Robot's capabilities in foundation models, robotic hardware, and system development with partners' expertise in operational processes, infrastructure, safety requirements, and deployment management. This model supports application-specific testing and optimization while building reusable implementation practices that can be transferred across facilities, industries, and geographic markets.
Solution Provider(s): SF Express (S.F. Holding Co., Ltd.) Sector: Logistics, Express Delivery, and Supply Chain Services SF Express is a leading integrated logistics service provider offering express delivery, freight transportation, and supply chain solutions. Its collaboration with X Square Robot supports the exploration and validation of embodied AI-powered automation for logistics operations.
Implementation location(s): Wuhan China、Shenzhen China
Implementation timeline(s): September – Present
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Not sure for now
Desired impact: Main Objectives The solution aims to: - Extend adaptive automation across 3D goods feeding, logistics sorting, and industrial assembly. - Improve the flexibility, consistency, and continuity of industrial material-handling and manipulation workflows. - Reduce dependence on repetitive, physically demanding, and difficult-to-staff manual tasks. - Reduce the engineering effort required when object types, workflows, or operating conditions change. - Enable more effective use of existing logistics and manufacturing infrastructure through adaptable robotic automation. - Establish a reusable and scalable approach to deploying embodied AI across industrial operations. Demonstrated and Expected Impact The solution has been tested and applied in real-world logistics and industrial scenarios, demonstrating the potential of model-driven robotic systems to operate beyond fixed, single-task automation. Expected operational benefits include more flexible object handling, more consistent goods feeding and parcel induction, reduced manual workload, faster adaptation to workflow changes, and opportunities to improve throughput and operating efficiency. The broader solution may also improve workplace ergonomics by reducing repetitive lifting, sorting, feeding, and assembly activities. However, additional verified operational data is required before claiming quantified improvements in productivity, cost efficiency, energy use, greenhouse-gas emissions, or job creation.
Key technologies: The solution combines X Square Robot's WALL-series embodied AI foundation models with visual and spatial perception, multimodal task understanding, model-driven manipulation, closed-loop motion control, coordinated dual-arm robotics, and the QUANTA X1 Pro platform. This shared technology stack supports adaptive 3D goods feeding, logistics sorting, and industrial assembly while integrating with existing industrial equipment and workflows.
Unique Characteristics: Unlike conventional automation built around fixed rules and task-specific programming, the solution applies a shared embodied AI architecture across multiple robot configurations and industrial tasks. It enables robots to perceive changing environments, reason about task objectives, and adapt manipulation actions in real time-supporting 3D goods feeding, dual-arm logistics sorting, and industrial assembly within one scalable technology framework.
Sustainable Change: The solution demonstrates how general-purpose embodied AI can move industrial automation from isolated, task-specific machines toward adaptable robotic systems that share a common intelligence layer. By reducing dependence on fixed workflows, extensive manual programming, and dedicated automation for every object or process, the approach can make advanced robotics more accessible to operations with high product variation, changing demand, or limited automation engineering resources. X Square Robot aims to scale the solution through collaboration with logistics operators, manufacturers, and system integrators. Reusable deployment methods, accumulated task data, validated integration practices, and technical training can shorten the path from initial site assessment to pilot and broader rollout. As deployments expand across goods feeding, sorting, assembly, and other industrial workflows, experience and data from each application can strengthen the common embodied AI platform. This creates the potential for continuous capability improvement, faster replication across sites, and broader adoption of intelligent automation throughout logistics and manufacturing ecosystems.
Primary thematic focus area: Embodied AI, Industrial Robotics and Smart Manufacturing
Summary: X Square Robot deploys WALL-series embodied models for goods feeding, sorting and assembly, with SF Express as its lead logistics partner in Wuhan and Shenzhen. The architecture is credible; absent measurement, single-country scope and an empty finance field hold it to 55.

Name of your organization: Geo-setting Intelligent Computing Laboratory, East China Normal University; Kairos Meridian Joint Research Working Group
Title: Kairos Meridian: helping small factories act on price, policy and trade shocks
Subtitle: Decision cards from a computable model of industrial chains tell small factories what a price, policy or trade change costs them, what to do and whether it was right. First case: 24 enterprises.
Problem Statement:
Small and medium-sized enterprises are around 90% of all businesses and more than half of global employment (World Bank). In manufacturing they are also the firms least equipped for a world in which costs, orders and compliance duties are set far from the factory gate. Large corporations meet this with intelligence teams, data scientists and trading desks; an SME owner meets it alone.
The gap is widest in inland and resource-based industrial parks, a structure found across developing and middle-income economies: one anchor producer supplies dozens of small downstream processors, and a park authority oversees both. Our first case, an aluminium park in Guizhou, western China, is typical. Five problems recur:
1. Prices move between order and purchase. A processor that quotes 'metal price plus processing fee' can lose a month's margin between taking an order and buying the metal. Between late March and early June 2026 the LME aluminium cash price rose from about USD 3,294 to USD 3,855 per tonne, a four-year high. Most owners price by gut feel and buy on market bets.
2. Rules reach further down the chain. The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism entered its definitive period on 1 January 2026; China's measures on minimum renewable-electricity consumption for key energy-using industries took effect on 1 August 2026 (NDRC Order No. 42). Both change costs for firms that never read the regulation, and support windows close before owners hear of them.
3. Exposure is invisible. Shocks travel through second- and third-tier suppliers and customers the factory cannot see.
4. Existing tools do not fit. ERP systems see only what happens inside the company; generic AI tools assume prior digitalization and an in-house data team; consulting and industry reports are expensive, one-off and not specific to one factory.
5. Nobody checks the advice. The owner rarely learns afterwards whether a decision was right, and park authorities lack firm-level evidence for investment-promotion and early-warning decisions.
This is a structural capability gap, not a lack of diligence. Kairos Meridian is built to close it: read the change, quantify what it means for this factory, recommend an action, and check the result.
Solution Overview:
WHAT IT DOES. When a price, regulation or trade rule changes, Kairos Meridian tells a small factory in three sentences what happened, how much money is at stake and what it can do - and afterwards checks whether the advice was right. STATUS: all steps below run in a demonstration environment (textiles, lithium battery materials; aluminium being completed); the first park-level case used real data from 24 enterprises; no enterprise uses it in live operation yet.
ARCHITECTURE - three layers. (1) Data foundation: an industrial knowledge graph of regions, industry segments, enterprises, products and their supply, trade and ownership links, fed by market prices, policy texts, trade data, news and park registries. (2) Model layer: each external change is described in a common form (Eight-Force Simulation) and routed to an established economic or network model. (3) Decision service: three-sentence cards for enterprises; a chain ledger and risk-exposure map for park authorities; and a decision ledger that checks every forecast against its outcome. We call the whole an economic-industrial world model: a knowledge graph plus a library of economic models that run 'what if' calculations on it - not a learned neural world model.
HOW IT WORKS - six steps. (1) Sense: collects market prices, policy and regulatory texts, trade data and news. (2) Map: matches each change to the regions, segments and enterprises it touches, including second- and third-tier supply-chain exposure. (3) Simulate: sector- and chain-level models give the size and timing of the shock; the factory's own figure comes from applying it to the enterprise's parameters (products, key inputs, pricing mode, export markets). (4) Decide: a three-sentence card with several action paths, each with an estimated result, a confidence level (low, medium or high) and the evidence behind every number. (5) Execute: the owner adopts, postpones or dismisses the card; adopted actions are handed over as an export template or a link opened in the supplier's or customer's system (direct ERP write-back is planned), so no prior digitalization is required. (6) Reconcile: the outcome is compared with the forecast and booked in the decision ledger as verified, projected or pending; deviations recalibrate the next simulation.
ILLUSTRATION (not a measured result). An aluminium processor quotes 'metal price plus processing fee'. Holding 200 tonnes of orders quoted at last week's metal price, it is exposed to RMB 100,000 if the metal rises by RMB 500 per tonne before it buys. The card shows this exposure, compares three paths (lock the price now, lock part of it, wait), and after the purchase records what happened.
METHOD. Eight-Force Simulation codes any external change under eight groups of forces - institutional rules, market demand, industrial supply, trade linkages, capital and cost, technology and data, collaborative governance, and enterprise behaviour - each with a direction, strength and time lag, traced along industrial chains. These descriptions feed models chosen by question type: input-output and network propagation for supply-chain shocks, partial equilibrium for trade policy, system dynamics for inventory and recovery, Monte Carlo and Bayesian updating for uncertainty. Each question is routed to one model; the models are not coupled into a general-equilibrium system, and results are short-run estimates given as ranges. Large language models read and explain (extracting clauses from policy texts, recognising events, wording cards); they do not compute impacts, and extracted rules are shown beside their source clause for checking.
SAFEGUARDS. AI output is always a candidate; a person makes the final call. Every number shows its source, date and confidence, and facts are labelled separately from model inferences. An enterprise starts with public data only and decides step by step what else to share.
Solution Provider(s): The solution is developed jointly by two organizations: the company builds the product and delivers it to enterprises and parks; the laboratory contributes the research capabilities listed below. 1) Kairos Intelligent Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd. - private sector; industrial AI software. A women-led start-up founded by an all-female, interdisciplinary R&D team with backgrounds in industrial analysis, policy research, international industrial chains and intelligent computing. It develops the Kairos Meridian economic-industrial world model and decision service and proposed the Eight-Force Simulation method. 2) Geo-setting Intelligent Computing Laboratory, East China Normal University, Shanghai - academia; research. An interdisciplinary research platform of the University on geo-environmental simulation, monitoring and early warning (cultivated since 2018, formally established as a University platform in 2023). Capabilities it contributes to this solution: acquisition, fusion and processing of multimodal, multi-source data; construction of large-scale corpora and databases; a locally deployed domain large language model and the architecture of an intelligent-system platform; and applied policy research, with more than 100 advisory reports a year. Its wider research collaborators (not partners in this solution) include Shanghai AI Laboratory, the Institute of Geographic Sciences and Natural Resources Research of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, and the Institute of International and Area Studies of Tsinghua University.
Implementation location(s): Shuicheng Economic and Technological Development Zone, Liupanshui, Guizhou Province, China (aluminium and aluminium processing; an inland province of western China): a park dataset built on real park data - 24 enterprises registered, 17 key enterprises examined product by product. Enterprise decision-card pilot in preparation. Industry solution packages have also been developed and demonstrated for Shaoxing, Zhejiang Province (textiles) and Yichun, Jiangxi Province (lithium battery materials); enterprise pilots at these two sites have not yet started. Beyond these sites, the wider multi-country, multi-industry data foundation is partly built and is being extended step by step towards its design scope of 60 countries and 210 industrial chains.
Implementation timeline(s): March 2025 - September 2026: development and demonstration of the first version of the textile (Shaoxing) and lithium battery materials (Yichun) solution packages; a second iteration is under way. 2026: aluminium-industry case in Shuicheng Economic and Technological Development Zone; the park dataset is completed and the case is due for completion in December 2026. Planned next: a decision-card pilot with downstream SMEs in Shuicheng, and a textile pilot with 20-30 enterprises in Shaoxing from February 2027.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: The solution is modular and can be adopted in three levels, so a park with limited funds and little enterprise data can start at Level 1. All durations are design estimates, not yet demonstrated in a second geography. Level 1 - Park view (about 1 month). Public data plus the park's enterprise registry are loaded and the industrial-chain ledger and risk-exposure map are delivered to the park authority. No enterprise data, no hardware, no digitalization on the enterprise side. Level 2 - Enterprise decision cards (about 3 months in total). Each pilot enterprise fills a short parameter sheet (about eight items) during one field visit; the industry package (profile dimensions, scenario list, card templates, regulatory list) is configured and back-tested on historical prices and events; cards are then delivered weekly and the first forecasts are checked against outcomes. After the field visit the pilot runs largely remotely through a local liaison. Level 3 - Closed loop with enterprise systems (6-12 months, on demand). Direct ERP write-back, opt-in sharing of verified records with financial institutions, and on-premises deployment for sites that must keep data local. Each level follows three steps: data ingestion, calibration to the local industry, and pilot operation with KPI verification. Prerequisites: a host park or cluster body that can supply an enterprise list and a local liaison; users need a smartphone and mobile data. Outside China, the interface language, delivery channel, regulatory list and data-protection compliance must be localised with the host partner, which may add time. A new industry in the same geography needs only a new industry package, not engine changes.
Desired impact:
OBJECTIVES
1) Close the decision-capability gap: give SME manufacturers an ability that today sits mostly in large corporations - to see an external change, quantify its effect on their own costs and orders, and act in time - without building a data team.
2) Replace gut feel with checked calculation: every recommendation is computed by an explicit model, shown with its evidence, and its forecast is checked against what actually happened.
3) Connect enterprise and park decisions: park authorities and enterprises work from the same industrial-chain model, so policy making sees firm-level responses and firms see the regional and policy environment.
4) Build a template that industrial parks in developing and middle-income economies can adopt in about three months per park (design target, not yet tested in a second geography).
DEMONSTRATED SO FAR
- A working end-to-end system in a demonstration environment: sensing, mapping, simulation, decision cards, execution hand-off and the decision ledger, for textiles and lithium battery materials, with the aluminium package being completed.
- A real-data case at park level: in Shuicheng Economic and Technological Development Zone, Guizhou, 24 aluminium-chain enterprises were registered and 17 key enterprises examined product by product; together they represent RMB 13.308 billion in related output value (the size of the enterprises covered, not an effect of the product). Working with incomplete data, the case took one external rule, identified which local enterprises it applies to, and listed the data still needed and the actions required of each.
- Not yet demonstrated: no enterprise uses decision cards in live operation, so we report no savings, accuracy figures or user numbers.
EXPECTED IMPACT AND HOW IT WILL BE MEASURED
The planned pilot with downstream SMEs in Shuicheng will be judged against criteria fixed in advance, in four areas: (a) data - how much of the anchor smelter's metal flow the chain ledger covers; (b) accuracy - forecast error against a no-change baseline and an industry-average baseline, and whether stated ranges contain the outcome as often as claimed; (c) use - how many owners open their cards every week and what share of recommendations they adopt; (d) governance - whether the park authority uses the ledger in a real investment-promotion, allocation or reporting decision. Dismissed recommendations and forecasts that missed are recorded as well.
Wider expected effects: fewer margin losses from price and policy surprises; earlier access to policy support that SMEs are entitled to; evidence-based investment promotion and early warning for park authorities; and, as a possible later use, an operating record that an enterprise may choose to share with a bank to support a credit application.
ROLLOUT TARGETS
(1) 2026-2027: complete the Shuicheng aluminium case and run the first enterprise pilot there; start the textile pilot in Shaoxing (20-30 enterprises) from February 2027. (2) 2027: extend the aluminium park template to a second park of the same structure (one anchor producer, many small processors), including a first partner park outside China sought through this Call. (3) From 2028: add industry packages on demand; each new industry needs a package, not engine changes.
ENVIRONMENT. The system does not itself reduce emissions; it shows small processors which carbon and renewable-electricity rules apply to them and what data they must prepare.
GDC OBJECTIVE 2: lets small manufacturers with no ERP and no data staff use AI for pricing, purchasing and compliance decisions. SDG 9.3 (small enterprises in value chains), SDG 8.2 and 8.3 (MSME productivity and growth), SDG 17 (company-university partnership; replication outside China is sought through this Call and has not yet started).
Key technologies: Main technologies: artificial intelligence (knowledge graphs, large language models, machine learning) combined with economic simulation models and data engineering. 1) Industrial knowledge graph - the data layer of the world model: a property graph of enterprises, products, technologies, industry segments and countries/regions with supply, trade, customer and ownership relations; cross-source entity disambiguation through a hybrid of rule constraints and vector similarity; graph path-reachability algorithms that follow trade and customer relationships to compute hidden second- and third-tier supply-chain exposure. 2) Language and machine-learning layer: large language models accessed through a unified gateway with multi-model routing, quota and cost governance; a privately deployed workflow engine for four dedicated tasks - clause-level extraction and applicability determination for policy and regulatory texts, event extraction from news, impact attribution, and decision-card wording; retrieval-augmented generation mixing vector and graph retrieval so that generated text is source-traceable; change-point detection to separate trend from noise; gradient-boosting models for enterprise profiling and counterparty risk scoring. Language models do not compute impacts; extracted rules are shown beside their source clause, and the accuracy of this extraction has not yet been measured. 3) Simulation layer (Eight-Force Simulation): input-output-table-driven propagation models for supply-chain shocks; partial-equilibrium models for trade policy; system dynamics for inventory, orders and recovery; network models for cascading risk; Monte Carlo simulation and Bayesian updating for parameter uncertainty; multi-criteria decision methods for comparing options. The eight forces give a common description - direction, strength, time lag - of how each external change enters these models. Each question is routed to one model; the models are not coupled. 4) Trust and data-governance layer: each number shows its source, date and confidence level and can be traced to the original data; facts and model inferences are labelled separately; a decision ledger checks forecasts against outcomes; a four-tier progressive authorization (public data, park ledgers, targeted entities, quantitative parameters) with row- and column-level access control lets an enterprise decide step by step what to share. Known failure modes - sparse data, wrong entity matching, misread rules - are the reason a person always decides. 5) Delivery: one codebase. The standard cloud service (multi-tenant SaaS) needs no new hardware and no prior digitalization; on-premises and integrated software-hardware edge options exist for sites that must keep data local. Web front end in Chinese and English, plus a mobile mini-program in China; hand-over to existing enterprise systems through export templates and links, with direct ERP write-back planned.
Unique Characteristics:
1) Checked forecasts vs. issued forecasts. Industrial-intelligence tools typically deliver dashboards or forecasts and stop there. Kairos Meridian is built to record every recommendation, what the owner did with it (adopted, postponed or dismissed) and what happened afterwards, in a decision ledger with three categories - verified, projected and pending. Only results confirmed against actual outcomes count as value delivered, and forecast deviations are shown to the user. The gain from an adopted action is an estimate against the modelled alternatives and is labelled as an inference.
2) Explicit mechanisms vs. black-box prediction. The component models are established; what we add is packaging them around one SME's own parameters and checking each forecast against its outcome. External changes are described as forces with direction, strength and time lag and passed to economic and network models selected by question type; language models read and explain but do not compute impacts. Each card shows its evidence chain, alternative action paths and a confidence level, so an owner or a park official can challenge any step.
3) Start with public data vs. digitalize first. An enterprise starts with public data plus a few parameters and decides step by step what else to share. Actions are handed over by export templates and links, so factories without an ERP can still close the loop. In China, cards reach owners through a mobile mini-program; elsewhere through the web front end.
4) One model, two sides vs. separate tools for government and enterprises. Park authorities and enterprises share the same industrial-chain model: the park gets a chain ledger and risk-exposure map for investment promotion and early warning; enterprises get decision cards. Enterprises pay RMB 999 per month (about RMB 12,000 a year); a park authority, cluster body or development partner can pay on their behalf.
5) New success metrics for SME AI tools. Instead of counting dashboards delivered or enterprises connected, the decision ledger measures the share of recommendations adopted, how often stated forecast ranges contain the outcome, and whether the park authority used the ledger in a real decision. These are the pass criteria fixed for the first pilot.
6) Human in command. AI suggestions are always candidates and the business owner makes the final decision; every conclusion carries source, timestamp and confidence and can be traced layer by layer.
7) Partnership and what is hard to copy. A women-led start-up and a university laboratory develop the solution jointly and have built the first park-level case on real data from an industrial park in a less-developed inland region; enterprise pilots are in preparation. What is hard to copy is not the models but the park-level chain ledger built with a park authority and, over time, the record of decisions and their outcomes.
Sustainable Change:
OUR ASK THROUGH THIS CALL: one industrial park or cluster body outside China, with an anchor producer and small downstream processors, that can supply an enterprise list and a local liaison. We supply the software, the industry package and remote support.
(1) A replicable park template. Many industrial parks in developing and middle-income economies share one structure: an anchor producer (a smelter, mill or refinery) supplying dozens of small downstream processors, overseen by a park authority. The Shuicheng aluminium case is being built as a template for this structure: the data checklist, template cooperation memorandum, industry package and pass criteria are being standardised so that the next park can start from them, at Level 1 with public data and a registry alone.
(2) Low-cost extension to new industries. Industry differences are captured in configurable industry packages - profile dimensions, scenario lists, card templates and regulatory lists - so adding an industry needs no engine change. Packages have been developed for textiles and lithium battery materials, and the aluminium package is being completed in Shuicheng.
(3) From decision records to SME finance (a possible later use). If an enterprise chooses, it can share its verified operating record with a financial institution to support a credit application. Sharing is opt-in.
(4) Evidence-based industrial governance. Park authorities see chain-level exposure built from public data and park ledgers; an enterprise's own parameters, cards and decisions reach the park only with its authorization. This moves investment promotion, resource allocation and early warning from experience towards evidence.
(5) Capability transfer. Regular decision cards are intended to build data-driven habits and AI literacy among factory owners themselves - a capability that remains after any project ends.
(6) Designed to improve with use. Every checked forecast adds calibration data for later users.
(7) Global cooperation. If selected, we would offer the solution through the UNIDO Solutions Platform and the AIM Global network, share the park template (data checklist, pass criteria, lessons from the first pilot) in AIM Global knowledge-sharing sessions, and adapt the solution through South-South and triangular cooperation. No deployment outside China has been made yet. On-premises deployment lets enterprise data stay in the host country; host-country data-protection and cross-border transfer rules would be assessed with the host partner before any pilot.
Funding Sources: Development to date has been funded by the operating funds of the Geo-setting Intelligent Computing Laboratory, East China Normal University, and by the own funds of Kairos Intelligent Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: Kairos Meridian models an industrial chain so that a small factory can see what a price, policy or trade change means for its own costs, and records whether its advice proved right. The ledger idea is the strongest in the field; absent accuracy data and a public demonstration, it scores 53.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry;Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems;Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making;

Title: Bwat, a general AI agent for Africa to bring intelligence to all
Subtitle: An AI agent that writes code, does deep research and creates documents autonomously, built in Uganda for Africa and supporting payments by mobile money
Problem Statement: The most capable AI agents are built abroad, priced in dollars and sold to people with international bank cards. Most people and small businesses in Africa cannot pay for them or even access them, so they are shut out of the tools that now speed up coding, research and basically all other knowledge work. A large percentage of Africans still have no internet access. By the time they get connectivity, the productivity gains of AI will have already been largely unfairly distributed, as they already are now. This widens the gap in skills and productivity between African workers, students and enterprises and their counterparts elsewhere. Bwat closes that gap with an AI agent that does actual work for you, is built in Uganda, and accepts mobile money, the way most Africans already pay in addition to being connected to African datasets and lots of other niche capabilities.
Solution Overview: Here's a scenario. A university student wants to solve a problem in their community, say food delivery. They are able to use the Bwat App (Android or IOS) or Desktop app (Windows) or website (And later, a normal phone call to Bwat. No internet needed) to launch a deep research and really immerse themselves into the problem. When the results of this research point toward building a software (Video game, website, etc), they're able to simply install VS code, install the Bwat extension and in natural language, build the software they need to. Bwat breaks a request into steps, uses tools to do each step, checks its own output, and corrects it before reporting back. It's powered by opensource and openweight models and is a highly capable tool in the right hands. We track what every task costs and set prices from those measurements. Mobile money checkout and apps on the platforms people already use. Our planned next step is an Ugandan-owned computing facility at Mbarara University of Science and Technology, so the service can run on local infrastructure with lower and more stable costs. Campus ambassadors: we are building a student ambassador programme. Elton, a student at Mbarara University of Science and Technology and President of its computing students' association, is the first ambassador and our campus lead. Ambassadors introduce Bwat on their campuses, run sessions and send back what works and what fails. On 6 September we ran a hands-on Bwat training with the Mbarara University Computing Students Association (MUCOSA). This was organised entirely by Elton, and we reached more than 120 students in the span of 2 hours. On 8 October we ran a three-hour live training for final-year software development students at Makerere University, at the invitation of a lecturer from the School of Computing and Informatics Technology. More than 80 students joined and about 60 stayed to the end. This shows how much interest and demand there is for the technology, especially among University students, and it shows how effective the campus ambassador program can be, because look how much one did, with zero budget. Now imagine if we had the compute and the budget to pull off a bigger version of that. Implementing partners: Lucky Nation Foundation, a Ugandan youth skills organisation, is set to lead youth training and delivery, while Casa Management Solutions, the company behind Bwat, provides the technology, free Pro accounts and support. Government and development finance: we are seeking partnerships for pilots and for a Ugandan-owned computing facility at a university site and we believe government and financial organizations would be perfect clients for our enterprise offerings.
Solution Provider(s): Casa Management Solutions (Ugandan technology company that owns and operates Bwat; sector: software and AI), Lucky Nation Foundation (Ugandan non-profit that runs youth digital skills and employment programmes, including Digital Horizons with the Mastercard Foundation; sector: education, skills and youth employment), Mbarara University Computing Students Association (student association of computing students at Mbarara University of Science and Technology; sector: higher education and student technology community), Makerere University School of Computing and Informatics Technology (Uganda's largest university computing school; sector: higher education and research)
Implementation location(s): Uganda: Kampala (Makerere University), Mbarara (Mbarara University of Science and Technology). Available online to users anywhere. We have users in Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda and Zimbabwe
Implementation timeline(s): Bwat was launched on 24th May 2026. It's still running to date.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately two weeks.
Desired impact: Our objective is to give every African student, worker and small business access to a highly capable AI agent that does real work, such as writing code, researching a topic and producing finished documents, and answering questions. We want it to be easy to pay for, so Bwat supports payments by mobile money. We also aim to build AI skilling through campus training and a student ambassador programme in which students teach their peers to use Bwat and to understand AI technology in general. We want those students to see that the people who solve African problems with technology can be Africans, and that they can start now with the tools in front of them. Our longer-term objective is to build AI infrastructure in Africa, starting with a computing facility hosted at Mbarara University of Science and Technology. The impact so far is early but real. About 600 people have registered, and about 180 were active in a single month (August 2026). Bwat is live on web, iOS, Android, Windows, npm and VS Code. In the last six weeks we have trained students at two universities: the Mbarara University Computing Students Association on 6 September, and Makerere University on 8 October, where more than 80 final-year software students joined a three-hour session and 60 stayed to the end. New sign-ups followed within the hour. We have also started a student ambassador programme, and our first ambassador is in place. We expect users to finish tasks such as reports, data analysis and small tools in minutes instead of days. Ambassadors will gain skills, work experience and a route into AI work, and they will pass that knowledge on to their classmates. We expect the ambassador programme and campus trainings to produce the next generation of local innovators. Data sovereignty and safety are a core part of the objective. Today, most African users send their documents, code and questions to AI services run in other countries under other countries' rules. We are building Bwat to comply with Uganda's Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019. Our data policy commits to keeping training on user data off by default and requiring explicit opt-in (We're not yet training any models but we will in the future), deleting user data within 30 days of a request, and never training on enterprise customers' data. Our planned Ugandan computing facility would let sensitive work, such as that of government bodies, hospitals and universities, run on infrastructure inside the country. We also want to work with regulators and policy makers early. We plan to share what we learn about how people in Africa actually use AI, where it fails them, and what safeguards they need, so that national and regional AI policy is based on real usage and not on assumptions imported from elsewhere. Research is the other half of this work. Our Bwat for Science effort, led by a machine learning researcher on our team, is building a research workspace for African universities and scientists. It will connect to open datasets and models with respect for their licences, and offer managed computing so that a researcher in Mbarara or Kampala can run serious experiments without needing a foreign cloud account. A Ugandan-owned computing facility would create technical jobs and keep more of the value of AI in the country, so that Africa stops being a mere consumer of AI and starts actively participating in the building of the technology safely.
Key technologies: AI, PostgresSQL, E2B, Inngest, Retrieval Augmented Generation, KV Cache Optimisation, Digital Twins, Flutter, Typescript etc.
Unique Characteristics: The novel thing about Bwat starts with the range of work it covers. It is a general AI agent that writes code, does deep research and creates finished documents, and we also build it on niche datasets that general AI products do not cover well. Bwat for Legal and Bwat for Trade, for example, are grounded in East African law and trade material, so a lawyer, a trader or a small business owner gets answers that fit their own market and not a generic global one. The same approach extends to other sectors where local data is thin, such as health, agriculture and manufacturing. Though, admittedly, these ones are still a work in progress. Not yet as solid as Trade or Legal. Bwat for VS Code puts the agent inside the code editor, which lets anyone build any software. A person with an idea and little programming background can describe the program they want, and Bwat writes it, runs it and fixes it with them. This opens software building to students and small business owners who could never afford a development team. Payment is built for the region. Users pay by mobile money, the way most people in Uganda already pay for everything, so no international bank card is needed. Subscriptions are weekly, which suits users who earn and spend in small amounts and lets a student try a paid plan for a week before deciding whether to continue. Bwat is built on open-source models. This keeps our cost per task low enough to price for African incomes, and it means we can run the models on infrastructure we control. For organisations, we offer enterprise versions of Bwat that analyse company data and automate document and reporting work, with a commitment not to train on enterprise customers' data. Our delivery approach is the campus ambassador programme. Students learn Bwat in live hands-on trainings, such as the three-hour session at Makerere University where 60 final-year software students stayed to the end, and the training with the Mbarara University Computing Students Association. The best of those students become ambassadors who teach their classmates, report back what works and what fails, and gain skills and experience for the job market. This keeps our cost of reaching a new user low and gives us product feedback from the people we most want to serve. Our longer-term plan is a Ugandan-owned computing facility hosted at a university. Because Bwat runs on open-source models, we can host them there and serve sensitive users such as government bodies, hospitals and universities from infrastructure inside the country, under Uganda's own data protection law. Alongside it, Bwat for Science will give African researchers a workspace with open datasets and managed computing for serious experiments. We pursue all of this with local partners. Lucky Nation Foundation brings youth training and delivery experience, universities bring students and research expertise, and Casa Management Solutions provides the technology, free Pro accounts and support. Training programmes funded by partners and donors reach more young people with Bwat, and the subscription and enterprise business grows alongside them.
Sustainable Change: With Bwat, we can show generations to come that advanced technology can be built in Africa to solve African problems. Bwat can also prompt African regulatory institutions to test and put in place rules that support the safe scaling of this transformative technology. The success of a company like ours would add to the economy through jobs, taxes and local spending. Our compute facility would give developers across Africa affordable access to computing and encourage innovation in the field, because we are certainly not the only team facing the compute bottleneck. If we solve it for ourselves, we solve it for everyone. The campus ambassador programme equips the next generation with the knowledge they need to thrive in an AI-driven economy, which is where the world is heading. Without Bwat, Africa risks arriving under-prepared for an increasingly AI-powered future and remaining a market for technology that others build. Bwat for Science can put this power in the hands of our own scientists and researchers, and lead to breakthroughs on problems that have affected Africa for a long time, medical problems among them. Throughout all of this, we will protect data sovereignty, so that the data of African people and institutions stays under African control.
Funding Sources: Entirely bootstrapped. I have used my personal funds plus money from paying Bwat Pro subscribers to pay for everything. We haven't yet gotten funding from VCs or Angel Investors.
Testimonials and Endorsements: Here's a post on LinkedIn from the MUCOSA event: https://lnkd.in/p/eEPjeFPR, Here's another: https://lnkd.in/p/eqikPRa3,
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: Bwat is a general-purpose AI agent for African users, with code, research and document tasks and mobile-money payment. Its reach across four countries on subscriber revenue is notable; unmeasured capability and thin capital keep it in the middle of the field.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems; Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access

Unexpected high demand. We brought It out of maintenance mode later) : https://lnkd.in/p/e_jWvfa7 Here's a post about the training with Year 4 Software engineering students on 8th October: https://lnkd.in/p/eYkgSdBq Here's an article written about us by AfriqIQ, a company that curates startups in Africa: https://blog.afriqiq.com/what-bwat-reveals-about-the-access-problem-nobody-was-solving-in-uganda/.

Title: Groundshift: AI-Powered Industrial Climate Intelligence Infrastructure
Subtitle: Groundshift Technologies provide AI-powered infrastructure connecting industrial operational, energy, and emissions data to actionable intelligence for cost optimization, resource efficiency, and decarbonization.
Problem Statement: Global commitments under the Paris Agreement and the 2030 Agenda have set clear goals for climate action and sustainable development. Yet a major gap remains between these ambitions and real-world implementation, especially in the private sector. Businesses, particularly SMEs and mid-sized manufacturers in emerging markets, often lack the tools, expertise, and reliable data needed to measure their environmental impact and take action. Information is scattered across machinery, utility bills, spreadsheets, and disconnected systems, making it difficult to establish accurate baselines or understand how energy use, emissions, and operating costs are connected. The green transition also comes with financial challenges. Businesses must invest in consultants, audits, software, training, and compliance, often without a clear picture of the potential savings or business opportunities. Many existing solutions focus on reporting emissions rather than helping businesses decide what to do next. Groundshift addresses this gap by bringing fragmented data together and turning it into practical environmental and financial intelligence, helping businesses identify cost-saving opportunities, improve efficiency, and make informed decarbonization decisions.
Solution Overview: Groundshift Technologies develops an AI-powered industrial climate intelligence infrastructure that connects fragmented operational and environmental data and transforms it into actionable business and climate insights. The solution integrates 3 complementary components: 1) Industrial Data Acquisition and Integration Tools Groundshift provides hardware-enabled data collection interface designed to connect with existing industrial equipment. These include manual and structured data imports, API integrations, and hardware-enabled collection systems: Groundshift Edge: An industrial gateway designed to connect with programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and compatible machinery. Sentinel: A sensor-based data acquisition solution for relevant physical and environmental measurements. Planar: A geospatial data solution incorporating satellite and drone-based observations service for applicable environmental use cases. 2) Data Intelligence and Orchestration (Bifröst OS) Bifröst OS serves as the intelligence backbone, integrating data from industrial equipment, enterprise systems, utility records, and other relevant sources through APIs and interoperable data pipelines. Its architecture supports data normalization, emissions calculations, AI-assisted analysis, and the development of operational intelligence capabilities that connect environmental performance with financial and production considerations. 3) User-Facing Intelligence (Groundshift Platform) The Groundshift platform provides interfaces for data input, emissions assessment, operational monitoring, and decision support. It helps organizations understand their climate and operational performance and identify opportunities for efficiency improvements. Title: UseCaseLibrary.AI: An AI Advisor That Finds Where AI Pays Off in Your Factory
Subtitle: Manufacturers describe a production problem in plain language; the AI matches it to verified, sector-specific use cases and helps them decide what to implement first, without hiring a consultant.
Problem Statement: AI is becoming cheaper and easier to use, yet most small and mid-sized manufacturers in developing and middle-income economies have not adopted it. Large firms are pulling ahead, and the benefits of industrial AI are concentrating where expertise and budgets already exist. For a small manufacturer, the first obstacle is usually not the technology but knowing where to start. Owners and plant managers struggle with three questions: which of our problems can AI solve, which solutions have already worked in a business like ours, and what should we do first? The expert advice that answers these questions is priced for large companies and is scarce outside major industrial hubs. Without that guidance, firms either postpone adoption or risk buying tools that do not fit their operations, which deepens scepticism about AI. Public programmes face a related problem: they can fund training and pilots, but they lack a scalable way to help each firm identify the opportunities relevant to it. What is missing is a trusted, affordable and easy first step that turns a factory’s own problems into concrete, proven AI use cases it can act on.
Solution Overview: How the solution works usecaselibrary.ai is a web platform that acts as a first AI advisor for manufacturers. It turns the long, consultant-led path from defining a problem to adopting an AI use case into one guided process. Firms no longer need an intermediary to diagnose their problems and choose solutions, so the platform is accessible to any manufacturer, regardless of size, location or budget. It works in five steps: Describe the problem. A plant manager or owner explains a challenge in their own words, such as high scrap on one line, unplanned downtime or rising energy costs. No technical vocabulary or data upload is needed. Clarify through conversation. The AI asks follow-up questions about the sector, process, scale and available data to understand the real problem behind the description. Match to proven use cases. The platform searches a curated library of [number] industrial AI use cases across [number] sectors. It returns the cases that fit, each with its source, the type of AI involved, the data it needs and the results reported where it was applied. Rank and sequence. A dependency analysis checks what each use case requires, such as data, systems, skills or another use case being in place first. It then ranks the options and arranges them into a logical, step-by-step guide: what to do first, and what each step makes possible next. Receive a detailed report. The user gets a report covering the selected use cases, their prerequisites and the recommended sequence. Organisations use it to build their own AI adoption trajectory and to align their teams around it. The library grows continuously as new cases are verified and added. Methodologies and technologies Source-referenced knowledge base. Every use case comes from open, verifiable sources such as published case studies, research and public programmes, and keeps a link to its source. Recommendations can be checked rather than taken on trust. Consistent case structure. Each case records sector, process, problem addressed, AI technique, data requirements, implementation complexity and reported outcomes, so options can be compared like for like. Dependency analysis and ranking. Use cases are mapped against their prerequisites and against each other. This lets the platform rank options and sequence them into a plan the firm can actually carry out. Conversational AI grounded in the library. A large language model interprets the user’s description and asks clarifying questions. Recommendations come from the curated library rather than being generated freely, which limits invented answers. Problem-first and vendor-neutral. Matching starts from the factory’s problem, not from a product. Technology vendors cannot pay to be recommended. Practitioner-designed question flow. The conversation reflects the team’s experience running Industry 4.0 assessments and industrial training programmes for manufacturers. Partnerships and collaboration models Studio i2x develops and operates the platform and works with partners in five ways: Public programmes. Industrial development agencies, ministries and chambers offer the platform to their manufacturer cohorts at no cost to the firms, as an entry point to national digitization and AI adoption programmes. Training and capability building. The platform is embedded in industrial AI training, so participants apply it to their own factories during and after the course. Knowledge partners. Universities, technology centers and solution providers contribute verified use cases. Every contribution goes through the same source check, and contributors gain no influence over recommendations. Delivery partners. Firms need no intermediary for diagnosis and planning. Partners come in only when a firm decides to implement: local consultancies and technology centers help it move from its plan to a pilot. UN collaboration. Through UNIDO and AIM Global, we aim to localize the platform for new countries and languages, add country-specific cases an
Solution Provider(s): The partners are still under discussion, we are working closely with MEXT Technology Center, Universities, Research Institutions and Public Authorities to finalize the content and scope.
Implementation location(s): United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia (discussions)
Implementation timeline(s): Started implementation by Sept 2026.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 1 second, as the platform is open for everyone, but 1 week as we may need time to onboard region specific challenges and use cases.
Desired impact: 1)Objectives *Give every manufacturer, regardless of size, location or budget, free access to trustworthy guidance on where AI can help them, without needing a consultant. *Turn the path from a production problem to an adoption decision into one guided process that ends in a ranked, step-by-step plan the firm owns. *Raise the success rate of AI adoption in small firms by steering them to use cases they are ready for, in an order that respects dependencies. *Give public programs, training providers and development partners a way to support many manufacturers at once, at almost no extra cost per firm. 2)Demonstrated impact to date 70+ verified industrial AI use cases across 10 sectors, with new cases added continuously. 25+ registered users from 10+ companies in 3 countries. 100+ detailed reports and adoption plans generated. 3)Expected impact by the end of 2027 Reach: 1000 manufacturers in developing and middle-income countries, at least 30% of them small or mid-sized. Adoption: 30% of users start implementing at least one recommended use case within six months. Value of free access: 1.000 users × 250 $annual platform value = 250.000$ of advisory support provided at no cost to firms. In real terms, the value of the advise could sum up to $15MM value of advisory considering the average price of industrial consulting.
Key technologies: The solution is built on five components. It deliberately needs no hardware, sensors or data integration from the user. 1)Generative AI (large language models). Interprets problems described in everyday language, asks clarifying questions and writes the explanations in recommendations and reports. 2)Retrieval over a curated knowledge base. A structured database of verified, source-referenced industrial AI use cases. The AI retrieves and matches cases from this base instead of generating answers freely, which keeps recommendations grounded and checkable. 3)Dependency modelling and ranking. Each use case is linked to its prerequisites: data, systems, skills and other use cases. An analysis engine uses these links to rank the options and sequence them into a feasible step-by-step plan. 4)Automated reporting. Produces a detailed report and adoption plan for each organisation, which it can keep, share and update as it progresses. 5)Cloud-based web platform. Runs in a standard browser with nothing to install, so any firm with an internet connection can use it.
Unique Characteristics: Today a small manufacturer that wants to use AI has three options: hire a consultant, which few can afford; read vendor material, which promotes one product; or ask a general-purpose AI chatbot, which can produce confident but unverified answers. usecaselibrary.ai differs from all three. 1)Problem-first, not technology-first. The starting point is the factory’s own problem, described in everyday language, rather than a technology or product looking for a buyer. 2)Grounded and verifiable. Every recommendation is drawn from a curated library of real, source-referenced use cases, so firms can check the evidence behind it instead of relying on generated text. 3)From options to a plan. Most case collections stop at examples. The platform’s dependency analysis ranks the options and sequences them into a step-by-step adoption plan, with the prerequisites for each step made explicit. 4)Vendor-neutral by design. No technology provider can pay to be recommended. This independence is what makes the guidance trustworthy for firms with no in-house expertise. No intermediary needed for diagnosis. Firms define their problem and build their own plan directly. Consultants, 5)technology centres and solution providers come in only when a firm decides to implement, which puts each partner where it adds the most value. 6)A model that scales without consultants’ hours. Each additional user costs almost nothing to serve. Public programmes, training providers and development partners can offer the platform to whole cohorts of manufacturers at no cost to the firms, reaching numbers that advisory services cannot. Built by practitioners. The question flow and case structure come from a team with long experience running industrial transformation and capability-building programmes for manufacturers.
Sustainable Change: The platform’s immediate effect is one better decision in one factory. Its broader effect comes from how it changes the way AI adoption works in an industrial economy. 1) From vendor push to demand pull. Today small firms mostly meet AI through vendors selling a product. When firms arrive with a clearly defined problem and a sequenced plan, the market reorganises around their needs. Local solution providers can offer what firms actually require, which strengthens the domestic supply side over time. 2)A shared knowledge commons that grows with use. Every verified case added to the library benefits every user in every country. As cases from developing and middle-income economies are documented, firms in similar contexts gain evidence that fits their reality. Much of the published evidence today describes large companies in advanced economies. 3) Evidence for policy and programme design. With user consent and anonymisation, aggregated results can show which problems manufacturers face and which use cases they choose, by sector and country. Governments and development partners could use this to target support programmes, training curricula and financing where demand actually is. 4) A bridge to financing. A structured adoption plan with explicit prerequisites is the kind of document banks, development funds and grant programmes need. It could help small firms present credible investment cases and access finance they currently struggle to reach. 5)Capability that stays in the firm. The firm builds and owns its plan, so the understanding remains inside the organisation after any project ends. Embedding the platform in training programmes extends this to a wider workforce. 6)Replication at almost no extra cost. Because the platform needs no hardware and costs almost nothing per additional user, it can be replicated country by country through local partners: technology centres, industry associations and public programmes. Localisation into new languages and country-specific cases is the main step. The rollout starts in UAE and expands through UNIDO and AIM Global partners.
Funding Sources: To date, usecaselibrary.ai has been funded entirely by Studio i2x as part of its in-house lab programme, with no external investment, grants or public funding. Studio i2x has covered platform development, hosting and the ongoing curation and verification of use cases [optional: total investment to date of approximately 50.000$. Self-funding has also protected the platform’s independence. With no vendor or investor influencing which solutions it recommends, it can stay vendor-neutral. Going forward, the platform will be sustained through a mix of sources that keeps it free for manufacturers: Programme-funded access, in which public programmes, training providers and development partners fund use by their cohorts. Institutional and development partnerships for localisation into new countries and languages. Grants and technical-cooperation funding, including opportunities identified through UN-led initiatives.

Title: PureFlow: AI-Powered Industrial Water Intelligence for Sustainable Industry
Subtitle: An AI powered platform transforming industrial wastewater treatment through real-time monitoring, predictive intelligence and data-driven optimisation for sustainable water management.
Problem Statement: Industries in developing and middle-income economies face growing challenges in wastewater management, water scarcity, rising operational costs and environmental compliance. Many industrial effluent treatment plants (ETPs) rely on manual monitoring, fragmented data and reactive decision-making, resulting in inefficient water, energy and chemical use, delayed detection of treatment failures and inconsistent effluent quality. Limited access to real-time operational intelligence, predictive analytics and affordable digital technologies makes it difficult for industries, particularly SMEs, to optimize treatment processes, maintain regulatory compliance and scale sustainable practices. These challenges contribute to freshwater depletion, industrial water pollution, higher production costs and risks to public health and ecosystems. There is an urgent need for accessible, scalable AI-powered solutions that transform existing wastewater infrastructure into intelligent, efficient and environmentally responsible systems without requiring complete infrastructure replacement.
Solution Overview: PureFlow is an AI-powered industrial water intelligence platform developed by Smart Build, Bangladesh, to modernise wastewater treatment operations, improve resource efficiency and support environmental compliance. It integrates Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) sensing, real-time data acquisition, machine learning, predictive analytics and operational decision support into a unified digital platform. PureFlow is designed to work with existing industrial effluent treatment plants (ETPs), reducing the need for costly infrastructure replacement. How the Solution Works PureFlow connects treatment processes, instrumentation and operational data through IoT gateways and compatible industrial control systems. It monitors key water quality and process parameters, including pH, temperature, dissolved oxygen (DO), total dissolved solids (TDS), total suspended solids (TSS), chemical oxygen demand (COD), biological oxygen demand (BOD), flow rates and tank levels, subject to the instrumentation available at each site. Collected data are structured, validated and analysed to identify abnormal conditions, treatment inefficiencies, emerging compliance risks and opportunities for operational improvement. AI-enabled analytics support trend analysis, early warnings, predictive maintenance and recommendations for improving water, energy and chemical efficiency. Operators and management teams can use dashboards, alerts and analytical reports to make timely, evidence-informed decisions. Deployment can be phased, beginning with monitoring and decision support before progressing towards deeper integration with existing SCADA and automation infrastructure. Methodologies and Technologies PureFlow combines IIoT, industrial data integration, machine learning, time-series analytics, anomaly detection, predictive modelling and data-driven process optimisation. Its architecture is designed to support interoperable industrial systems, scalable data processing and deployment across facilities with differing levels of digital maturity. Its operational methodology follows a continuous improvement cycle: establish a baseline, monitor performance, analyse deviations, recommend corrective actions and measure verified outcomes. Smart Build targets improvements of approximately 30–40% in water consumption and 10–20% each in energy and chemical use, depending on plant conditions and implementation scope. These figures represent optimisation objectives rather than independently verified results across all deployments.
Solution Provider(s): Industrial Partners – Approximately 20 factories across Bangladesh’s RMG, textile, dyeing, washing and wet-processing sectors; Technology Partners – SION Corporation (Japan) and Fraunhofer IVV (Germany); Academic and Research Collaborators – University College London (UK), Arizona State University (USA) and International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI).
Implementation location(s): Bangladesh – Dhaka, Gazipur, Narayanganj and Chattogram; industrial facilities across the Ready-Made Garment (RMG), textile, dyeing, washing and wet-processing sectors.
Implementation timeline(s): February 2026 – Present (Ongoing implementation and industrial pilot activities in Bangladesh).
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 8–12 weeks, including site assessment, sensor and IoT integration, platform configuration, AI model calibration, operator training and initial performance validation, subject to site readiness and infrastructure availability.
Desired impact: PureFlow aims to transform industrial wastewater treatment into an intelligent, resource-efficient and environmentally sustainable process through AI, IoT and predictive analytics. Its primary objectives are to reduce freshwater consumption, optimise energy and chemical use, improve wastewater treatment efficiency, strengthen environmental compliance and enable data-driven industrial operations. Expected Quantifiable Impact: • Water consumption: Target reduction of 30–40% through process optimisation and improved water reuse. • Energy consumption: Target reduction of 10–20% through operational optimisation and improved equipment efficiency. • Chemical consumption: Target reduction of 10–20% through more precise treatment process management. • Environmental protection: Improved effluent quality monitoring, early detection of compliance risks and reduced potential for untreated or inadequately treated wastewater discharge. • GHG emissions: Expected indirect reductions through lower electricity consumption; site-specific CO₂-equivalent savings will be calculated from verified energy data. • Economic and social benefits: Lower operational costs, improved industrial competitiveness, enhanced operator capabilities and opportunities for skilled employment in industrial AI and environmental technology. Implementation activities in Bangladesh began in February 2026 and are ongoing, with engagement across approximately 20 industrial facilities in the RMG, textile, dyeing and wet-processing sectors. The percentage improvements above are performance targets, not independently verified results across these facilities. Site-level baseline measurements and pilot evaluations will be used to establish demonstrated savings and environmental impact. PureFlow supports inclusive industrial transformation by making AI-enabled water management more accessible to industries in developing and middle-income economies, contributing to SDGs 6, 9, 12 and 13.
Key technologies: PureFlow integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), real-time sensor networks, predictive analytics, time-series data processing and industrial automation technologies. Key technologies include: • AI and Machine Learning: Predictive modelling, anomaly detection, operational intelligence and data-driven optimization of industrial wastewater treatment. • Industrial IoT and Smart Sensors: Real-time monitoring of pH, temperature, DO, TDS, TSS, COD, BOD, flow and water levels, depending on available instrumentation. • Predictive Analytics: Early identification of treatment inefficiencies, equipment abnormalities and environmental compliance risks. • SCADA and Industrial Data Integration: Connectivity with existing treatment infrastructure and industrial control systems. • Cloud and Edge Computing: Scalable data collection, processing, monitoring and analytics, with deployment architecture adapted to site requirements. • Digital Dashboards and Decision Support: Real-time visualization, automated alerts, performance reporting and AI-assisted operational recommendations. The platform is designed to support future digital twin capabilities and deeper automation integration as deployment requirements evolve.
Unique Characteristics: PureFlow differentiates itself by transforming conventional industrial wastewater treatment plants into intelligent, data-driven systems through an integrated combination of AI, IoT, predictive analytics and environmental intelligence. 1. AI-Driven Industrial Water Intelligence: Unlike conventional monitoring systems that primarily display sensor readings, PureFlow combines real-time water quality and operational data with AI-powered analysis, anomaly detection, predictive insights and actionable recommendations. 2. Retrofittable and Cost-Effective Architecture: PureFlow is designed to integrate with existing effluent treatment plants (ETPs), sensors and industrial control infrastructure, reducing the need for complete plant replacement and supporting phased digital transformation. 3. Integrated Resource Optimisation: The solution addresses water, energy, chemical consumption and environmental compliance within a unified platform, targeting 30–40% water savings and 10–20% reductions in energy and chemical consumption, subject to site-specific validation. 4. Adaptability for Developing Economies: Its modular implementation approach can accommodate different industrial scales, infrastructure conditions, digital maturity levels and operational budgets, making advanced industrial AI more accessible to resource-constrained facilities. 5. Collaborative Innovation Model: Smart Build combines industrial engagement in Bangladesh's RMG and textile sectors with signed technology cooperation agreements involving SION Corporation (Japan) and Fraunhofer IVV (Germany), alongside exploratory academic and research engagements. 6. Scalable Deployment Model: A phased approach covering site assessment, monitoring integration, AI configuration, operator training and performance validation enables replication across industrial facilities and new geographical markets. PureFlow's distinctive value lies in combining practical industrial AI, resource-efficiency optimisation and international technology cooperation to support affordable, scalable and sustainable industrial transformation.
Sustainable Change: PureFlow has the potential to drive systemic change by transforming industrial wastewater management from reactive, manually operated processes into AI-enabled, data-driven and resource-efficient systems. Its long-term vision extends beyond individual factories to industrial clusters, supply chains, cities and national water management ecosystems. 1. Industry-Wide Replication: PureFlow's modular, retrofittable architecture enables adoption across textile, RMG, dyeing, food processing, chemical and other water-intensive industries without requiring complete infrastructure replacement. Successful pilots can establish replicable deployment models for industrial clusters in Bangladesh and other developing economies. 2. Sustainable Resource Transformation: By targeting 20–30% reductions in water consumption and 10–20% reductions in energy and chemical use, subject to site-specific validation, PureFlow can contribute to freshwater conservation, lower industrial operating costs, reduced environmental pollution and improved resource productivity. 3. Data-Driven Environmental Governance: Standardized monitoring, digital reporting and early-warning capabilities could strengthen industrial environmental accountability, support regulatory oversight and enable more effective sustainability policies through cooperation with government agencies and industrial associations. 4. Inclusive Digital Industrialization: Its phased implementation approach can help small and medium-sized enterprises access industrial AI, while creating opportunities for workforce upskilling, local technology service providers and environmentally focused employment. 5. International Replication and Technology Transfer: Smart Build's cooperation with SION Corporation (Japan), Fraunhofer IVV (Germany) and international research networks provides a foundation for potential joint innovation, knowledge transfer and adaptation across new markets in Asia, the Middle East and other developing regions. 6. Long-Term Ecosystem Impact: Aggregated operational insights could support industrial benchmarking, water reuse strategies, circular-economy initiatives and coordinated water-energy-environment optimization across multiple facilities. By combining scalable technology, industrial collaboration and international knowledge exchange, PureFlow aims to establish a replicable model for sustainable industrial transformation, supporting SDGs 6, 9, 12 and 13 and the Global Digital Compact's objective of expanding the benefits of digital technologies.
Funding Sources: PureFlow has primarily been funded through Smart Build’s internal resources and founder-led investment, supporting research and development, AI platform development, IoT integration and initial industrial pilot activities in Bangladesh.
