Title: Jazarai: an AI chief surveyor for concrete construction sites
Subtitle: An AI agent that reads construction drawings in AutoCAD and prepares every stake-out point and level for site engineers to review. Piloted with Saudi Binladin Group, 20 to 40x faster.
Problem Statement: Before every concrete pour, a surveyor has to mark on site exactly where each column, wall and slab edge goes, and at what level. That work starts at the computer: the surveyor reads the drawings and types out every point and level by hand. It takes 3 to 4 hours for one pour, then the staking on site. A surveyor costs a contractor about SAR 400 ($107) a day in Saudi Arabia, and big sites pour every day. Experienced chief surveyors are few, so their checks don't reach every site, and smaller contractors often have none. The same manual work happens on every concrete site in the world.
Solution Overview: How it works: 1. The site engineer gives Jazarai the pour drawings. 2. Our AI agent opens them in AutoCAD, reads the geometry and levels, and works out every stake-out point using a chief surveyor's rules. 3. It produces a point list and a total-station file, with the points drawn on the plan. 4. The site engineer reviews and approves before anything goes to site. If they reject a stake-out, the contractor doesn't pay. Technology: an AI agent built on large language models that works inside AutoCAD, plus a rule set written by our co-founder Mohamed Fouda from 35 years as a chief surveyor at Saudi Binladin Group (Jeddah airport, Jamarat Bridge). Partnership model: we pilot on a contractor's real pours first, then move to paid work, priced per approved stake-out. Our first pilot was with Saudi Binladin Group in October 2026, under a month after we started. Their site team approved the results and used them on site.
Solution Provider(s): Saudi Binladin Group (SBG), one of Saudi Arabia's largest construction contractors, construction sector, pilot customer
Implementation location(s): Saudi Arabia, on a Saudi Binladin Group construction site
Implementation timeline(s): October 2026: free pilot with Saudi Binladin Group, completed and approved. Paid pilot in talks.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: About 4 weeks. The agent runs in AutoCAD, which contractors already use. A new country needs its local coordinate system and survey rules added and checked on the first jobs.
Desired impact: Objective: give every construction site a chief surveyor's stake-out, prepared in minutes, so building work isn't held up by manual point entry. Demonstrated in our pilot with Saudi Binladin Group: - 20 to 40x faster than by hand, including the engineer's review time. - Results approved by the SBG site team and used on site. Expected impact: - Hours of computer work saved on every pour. At SAR 400 a surveyor-day, that cost repeats on every pour of every project. - Surveyors spend more of their day checking work on site. - Smaller contractors and survey offices get the same chief-surveyor checks as the largest firms.
Key technologies: - AI agent built on large language models that reads construction drawings and works inside AutoCAD. - A rule set from 35 years of chief surveyor practice, applied to every stake-out. - Outputs in the formats site teams already use: point lists and total-station files. - A human review step: the site engineer approves every stake-out before it goes to site. - Every approved job becomes a test case from a real site, used to check the agent before each change.
Unique Characteristics: - It delivers the finished stake-out. Survey tools and layout robots need someone to prepare the point file first; Jazarai prepares it. - Rules from a chief surveyor with 35 years on Saudi megaprojects are built into the agent. - It works inside AutoCAD, where the drawings already are, so there's no new software for the site team to learn. - Business model: contractors pay per approved stake-out, 30 to 40% below the cost of doing it by hand. If the site engineer rejects it, they don't pay.
Sustainable Change: Stake-out is our first step. The same agent can take on the other survey jobs on a site, then more civil engineering work that still runs on manual drawing reading. Replication: every country that pours concrete has this work. Moving to a new country means adding its coordinate system and survey rules, and the agent runs on the AutoCAD setups contractors already have. Scale: survey offices serve many contractors at once, so each office that uses Jazarai brings the checks to many sites. Each approved job adds a real-site test case, so the agent improves as it spreads.
Funding Sources: Founder-funded. No outside funding so far; we're raising a pre-seed round.
Testimonials and Endorsements: "Work that takes days, we finished in 1 day." Mohamed Amin, Construction Manager, Saudi Binladin Group (pilot, October 2026)

Title: AI-Powered Digital Infrastructure for African Innovation Ecosystems
Subtitle: Connecting entrepreneurs, innovation hubs, mentors and investors through AI-powered tools that strengthen business development, programme management and access to opportunities across Africa.
Problem Statement: African entrepreneurs and MSMEs often face fragmented support systems, limited access to mentors, investors, digital tools and markets. Innovation hubs and entrepreneurship programmes frequently lack integrated systems to manage cohorts, track progress, engage alumni and measure impact. This fragmentation limits collaboration, productivity and opportunities for sustainable business growth.
Solution Overview: Wakisha Connect is a Pan-African digital platform connecting entrepreneurs, MSMEs, innovation hubs, incubators, mentors, coaches and investors. It supports entrepreneur onboarding, cohort management, business development, progress tracking, networking and alumni engagement. AI-powered tools help users structure business ideas, analyse information and prepare business documents. The solution combines digital workflows, shared information and ecosystem collaboration. It is designed to support partnerships between hubs, entrepreneurship programmes, institutions and private-sector actors. Deployment can be adapted to local needs through pilot partnerships with selected hubs and support organisations.
Solution Provider(s): Wakisha Holding SAS — technology venture developing and driving Wakisha Connect; Wakisha Hub — entrepreneurship support and innovation hub providing ecosystem experience and a potential environment for solution validation.
Implementation location(s): Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Uganda, République du Congo, Gabon, Tanzanie
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 8–12 weeks, subject to partner onboarding, local adaptation, technical integration requirements and pilot scope.
Desired impact: Wakisha Connect aims to strengthen African entrepreneurship ecosystems by improving access to digital tools, knowledge, mentors, investors and market opportunities. It helps hubs and programmes coordinate entrepreneur support, monitor progress, maintain alumni engagement and improve operational efficiency. Expected impacts include stronger MSME development, improved collaboration across ecosystems, better access to opportunities and more effective programme monitoring. Quantitative impact indicators will include entrepreneurs onboarded, hubs connected, businesses supported, partnerships established and opportunities accessed. Impact figures will be measured through pilot implementations.
Key technologies: Artificial Intelligence (AI), web and mobile technologies, cloud-based digital infrastructure, data management and analytics, digital collaboration tools, workflow automation and dashboards for programme and entrepreneur progress tracking.
Unique Characteristics: Wakisha Connect goes beyond a standalone entrepreneurship platform by providing a digital layer that extends innovation hubs beyond their physical spaces. It combines AI-powered business support, entrepreneur journey tracking, hub programme management, alumni engagement and cross-border networking in one ecosystem. Its collaborative model enables hubs to connect entrepreneurs with mentors, investors and opportunities across markets. The platform is designed to improve productivity, reduce fragmentation and make entrepreneurship support more connected, continuous and measurable.
Sustainable Change: Wakisha Connect can help shift African entrepreneurship support from fragmented, location-based programmes towards connected, data-informed and cross-border ecosystems. Its model can be replicated across countries and adapted to different hubs, incubators and development programmes. As adoption grows, the platform could enable knowledge sharing, collaboration between support organisations, broader access to markets and investment networks, and improved measurement of entrepreneurial outcomes. Strategic partnerships and scalable digital delivery can support expansion while strengthening local innovation ecosystems.
Funding Sources: Wakisha Connect has been developed under Wakisha Holding SAS through entrepreneurial initiative and internal resources. The current funding structure and any external financial contributions can be detailed based on confirmed records. The solution is seeking strategic partnerships and funding opportunities to support further development, pilot implementation and expansion across Africa.

Stakeholder feedback and testimonials will be collected through engagement with innovation hubs, entrepreneurs and ecosystem partners as the solution progresses through validation and pilot implementation.

Title: Maadco TwinAI: Agentic Digital Twins for Industrial Decision-Making
Subtitle: A digital twin platform where AI agents use a knowledge graph and plant documents, predict failures and test what-if cases on a physics-based twin corrected by AI. Built on 15 years of Maadview.com.
Problem Statement: Industrial plants collect large amounts of data, yet most maintenance and operating decisions still rest on fixed alarm limits and calendar schedules. Slow degradation is noticed late, and parts are replaced too early or too late. The information needed to decide is spread across separate systems: sensor data, maintenance records, failure histories, manuals and shift notes. Knowing what an alert means, what caused it and what to do about it depends on a few experienced people. When they are unavailable, that knowledge is lost. Engineering simulations could help test options, but they take hours to run, so they are seldom used for day-to-day decisions. Predictive models face a further limit. Real failures are rare, so plants seldom hold enough fault history to train them, and a model that only flags anomalies leaves the engineer with the investigation still to do. The challenge is to move from detecting that equipment may be failing to supporting an informed decision about its cause, its consequences and the options, while keeping people in control and keeping control systems untouched.
Solution Overview: TwinAI keeps a live digital twin of each asset and process unit. Plant data arrive through standard industrial protocols (OPC UA, MQTT, Modbus) and are stored by type: time series, relations and documents. A knowledge graph links equipment, sensors, operating parameters, past failures, maintenance work and technical documents. When a model reports abnormal behaviour, the platform reads it against this structure. It can see which component feeds or loads the one in question, which failure modes it has had before and which procedures apply. Time-series models learn each device’s normal behaviour, flag deviations and estimate remaining useful life as a distribution of likely failure times, not a single date. A physical simulation of the device is calibrated against measured data and corrected by learned terms. Graph-based surrogate models are trained on it, so what-if cases run during a shift. The same simulation generates fault and degradation scenarios that supply training data for predictive-maintenance models, since real failures are rare. AI agents coordinate these tools. They search the knowledge graph and the plant’s documents together, show the source of each figure and draft a recommendation. A person reviews and approves it. Methodologies and technologies. Forecast-residual anomaly detection and models that capture relationships between signals. Remaining-life estimation with checked interval coverage. Graph-based simulation with MeshGraphNets, graph transformers and physics-informed graph neural networks, with the architecture chosen per device by benchmark. Extended and ensemble Kalman filters for state estimation. A knowledge graph with graph-based retrieval-augmented generation. Language-model agents with defined tool access. Agents are read-only by default and send no commands to control systems. The platform can run on site, in the cloud or air-gapped, and is designed with reference to IEC 62443 zoning. Partnerships and collaboration models. TwinAI is built on Maadview, Maadco’s industrial software platform, which has run for 15 years in oil and gas, petrochemical, steel and power plants, with installations of more than 30,000 signals. Delivery is phased with the client: a 2-month assessment that sets baselines, a 4–6-month pilot on one asset class, then 6–12 months of wider deployment, with a gate review after each phase. In Oman, the product has been supplied to Nafun Electronics under a two-year contract.
Solution Provider(s): Maadview (industrial data logger - industrial monitoring - SCADA)
Implementation location(s): Refinery interactive 3D Virtual Twin using WebGL (integrated with Maadview real-time monitoring system) / Muscat, Oman
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6 to 8 months
Desired impact: Objectives: Reduce unplanned stops by finding developing faults early and estimating remaining useful life. Move from calendar-based to condition-based maintenance, so parts are replaced when needed. Support engineers with evidence-based recommendations; likely cause, likely consequences and options, instead of bare alarms. Lower energy and utility use through earlier detection of efficiency losses and by testing operating options in simulation. Keep plant knowledge in a structured form, the knowledge graph, so it does not depend on a few individuals. Improve safety by anticipating failures and testing changes virtually before making them. Demonstrated base: The platform behind TwinAI, Maadview, has run for 15 years in oil and gas, petrochemical, steel and power plants, in installations of more than 30,000 signals. Maadco’s projects cover more than 50,000 signals. The digital twin product has been supplied to Nafun Electronics in Oman under a two-year contract. Maadco has also delivered a digital twin simulation for Oman Oil Company. Expected impact: Targets are set from each client’s own baselines in the first two months, and progress is reported against them at each gate review. The measures are warning lead time, false-alarm rate, remaining-life error, surrogate error against the reference solver, downtime hours avoided and energy use.
Key technologies: Digital twins: physics-based device and process models, calibrated against measured data and corrected by learned terms. Kalman filters keep them synchronised with the plant. Machine learning for time series: forecasting, anomaly detection and remaining-useful-life estimation, including models that capture relationships between signals. Graph-based simulation: MeshGraphNets, graph transformers and physics-informed graph neural networks that make simulations fast enough for use during a shift. Knowledge graph: assets, sensors, failure modes, work orders and documents, with graph-based retrieval-augmented generation. Agentic AI: language-model agents that use defined tools, with read-only access by default and human approval. Industrial IoT and edge computing: OPC UA, MQTT and Modbus; on-site, cloud, hybrid or air-gapped deployment. Security: design with reference to IEC 62443 zoning, an audit log, and no commands to control systems.
Unique Characteristics: A standard physical model rarely matches the real machine, so TwinAI calibrates it and trains learned corrections on the remaining difference. Live data then keep it current. Real failures are rare. The validated twin generates fault and degradation scenarios, which become training and test data for predictive-maintenance models. Simulated data supplement recorded data, and every model is tested on real events. The knowledge graph reads each alert against the asset’s structure, history and procedures. Agents that search the graph and documents together; They show the source of each figure and draft a recommendation for a person to approve. Several graph-based simulation architectures are benchmarked on the client’s own device, and the best is used, with fallback to the full solver. Delivery approach. A phased pilot with gate reviews and baselines agreed before any commitment
Sustainable Change: Replication: The structure is the same across sectors. What changes from site to site is the asset library, the equipment-specific models and the operating constraints, so each new site is an extension, not a new system. A pilot in a new geography takes about 6 to 8 months. Scale-up path. One asset class, then a whole site, then several sites. Models trained on one plant can be transferred to similar assets elsewhere, which helps where failure records are few. Open standards and on-site deployment: OPC UA, MQTT, ISA-95 and FMI, with an on-premises or air-gapped option, let local engineers and integrators run and extend the system and keep control of their data. Capacity that stays: Client engineers are trained during the pilot and at handover. The knowledge graph keeps plant knowledge in a form that outlasts staff changes. Follow-on effects: Longer equipment life, less waste of spares, lower energy use and safer operation, extended from one plant to a fleet
Funding Sources: Previous implementations were funded commercially through client contracts, for example the Virtual Twin Project, Maadview projects or smart factory/Industrial AI solutions delivered to industrial clients.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: Maadco TwinAI keeps a live digital twin of each asset, reads anomalies against a knowledge graph of equipment, sensors, failures and documents, and tests options on the twin before they are applied. The Muscat refinery twin ran through 2024 and 2025 on the Maadview platform.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making

Title: RIFFAI: Satellite AI for Sustainable Agriculture and Industry
Subtitle: Transforming satellite imagery into actionable AI intelligence for crop health, water and nutrient monitoring, environmental assessment, and more efficient field operations.
Problem Statement: Agricultural producers and resource-intensive industries face increasing challenges in monitoring land conditions, managing resources efficiently, and responding to environmental changes. Conventional field inspections can be time-consuming, costly, and difficult to scale across large or geographically dispersed areas. Meanwhile, satellite imagery and other Earth-observation data can be difficult for end users to interpret and translate into practical operational decisions. These challenges can limit the ability of farmers and agricultural businesses to identify variations in crop health, soil moisture, vegetation conditions, and field performance. Without timely, location-specific information, users may struggle to prioritize field inspections, optimize agricultural operations, and allocate resources efficiently. RIFFAI addresses these challenges through AI-powered Earth-observation intelligence that transforms satellite imagery and geospatial data into field-level information. By making environmental and agricultural conditions easier to monitor and interpret, the solution helps users make more informed decisions, prioritize interventions, and integrate digital intelligence into everyday operations.
Solution Overview: RIFFAI is a satellite and artificial intelligence company specializing in Earth-observation intelligence for monitoring environmental changes and critical infrastructure. Its RIFFAI Intelligence platform processes satellite imagery and complementary data sources to generate actionable geospatial information for agriculture, forestry, energy, environmental monitoring, and other operational applications. How the solution works 1. Data acquisition: The platform uses satellite imagery, including multispectral imagery and synthetic aperture radar (SAR), together with relevant weather information and other geospatial data. Drone imagery and field observations can complement satellite-derived information where required. 2. AI-powered processing: RIFFAI processes Earth-observation data using AI-based image analysis, geospatial modelling, and spatial data processing to extract information about land conditions, vegetation, and field characteristics. 3. Field-level intelligence: The platform generates spatially organized outputs that can include plant-health indicators, vegetation indices, moisture-related indicators, nutrient-related assessments, growth monitoring, field segmentation, overall field-health assessments, and crop or tree counting. These outputs help users identify spatial variation and areas requiring further investigation. 4. Operational integration: The resulting intelligence can support field operations, farm management, and targeted drone activities. The platform also supports deployment through data, platform, and model delivery, including cloud or on-premises configurations and end-to-end mission workflows, according to project requirements. Methodologies and technologies The solution combines satellite remote sensing, multispectral image analysis, SAR data processing, artificial intelligence, geospatial analytics, field-level modelling, spatial segmentation, and the integration of Earth-observation information into operational workflows. The specific analytical methods depend on the application, available imagery, crop or land characteristics, and validation data. Existing applications and case studies In Thailand, RIFFAI works with Chadhai Leasing, an agricultural leasing company supporting farmers' access to agricultural technology. RIFFAI provides multispectral satellite analysis and field-level modelling to help farmers monitor crop health, assess environmental conditions, and make more informed resource-use decisions. In Hokkaido, Japan, RIFFAI's farmland-monitoring case study with AGRIER demonstrates applications for open-field agriculture, including soil-moisture assessment, harvest-readiness monitoring, ground-operation planning, and farm-record integration. Partnerships and collaboration model RIFFAI's approach connects Earth-observation technology with agricultural businesses, drone-related operations, and local implementation partners. For new deployments, RIFFAI can collaborate with industrial users, agricultural enterprises, research institutions, data providers, and local organizations to identify operational needs, configure the analytical workflow, validate results against local conditions, and evaluate the solution through agreed performance indicators.
Solution Provider(s): Chadhai Leasing (Thailand) — agricultural leasing and agricultural-technology access; AGRIER (Japan) — agricultural production and technology-enabled farmland monitoring; drone-sector partners involved in agricultural field operations, as applicable to the specific deployment.
Implementation location(s): Hokkaido, Japan. Saraburi and Chanthaburi, Thailand.
Implementation timeline(s): Hokkaido: since 22 April 2026 and still on going. Chanthaburi and Saraburi: since 25 September 2026 and still on going.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 2-4 weeks, subject to data availability, geographic coverage, local validation requirements, and partner readiness. The proposed deployment process includes defining the use case, acquiring and processing relevant satellite imagery, configuring the analytical workflow, validating outputs against local conditions, and conducting a controlled pilot using agreed technical and operational indicators. More complex applications may require additional time.
Desired impact: Main objectives 1. Transform satellite imagery and geospatial data into actionable intelligence for agricultural and industrial decision-making. 2. Improve the accessibility and usability of Earth-observation information for agricultural producers, businesses, and other operational users. 3. Support the monitoring of crop health, vegetation, moisture-related conditions, field characteristics, and changes in land conditions. 4. Help users prioritize field inspections and interventions through spatially detailed monitoring and analytical outputs. 5. Enable the adaptation of AI-powered Earth-observation workflows across different locations and resource-intensive sectors. Existing applications and reach RIFFAI's company presentation describes agricultural monitoring applications in Thailand and Japan. Its reported agricultural-impact figures include 1,011 farms, 2,500 farmers, three countries, 160 million hectares, and more than 18 specimens. These figures are company-reported indicators; their measurement periods, definitions, and attribution to specific deployments should be confirmed before they are used as formal impact metrics. Expected impact The solution aims to improve monitoring efficiency, provide more timely information about field conditions, and support better-informed resource-management decisions. In agricultural applications, it can help identify areas requiring attention, guide targeted field operations, and support the more efficient allocation of water, agricultural inputs, and inspection resources. For industrial and environmental applications, the technology can support land monitoring, environmental assessment, and location-specific operational planning. The proposed pilot will evaluate performance through indicators such as the number of hectares monitored, time required to generate actionable information, cost per monitored area, accuracy against field-verified observations, frequency of field inspections, and user adoption. Where suitable baseline data are available, the pilot will also assess changes in water use, agricultural input consumption, operational costs, and greenhouse-gas emissions. Quantified reductions in resource use or emissions are not claimed without supporting baseline measurements and post-implementation evidence.
Key technologies: 1. Artificial intelligence and machine learning: AI-based processing and analysis of Earth-observation data to generate task-specific intelligence. 2. Satellite remote sensing: Satellite imagery for monitoring agricultural fields, vegetation, land conditions, and environmental changes. 3. Multispectral image analysis: Analysis of spectral information to generate vegetation and plant-health indicators and support field-level assessments. 4. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR): Radar imagery as an additional Earth-observation data source, where appropriate for the application. 5. Geospatial analytics and geographic information systems (GIS): Spatial analysis, field segmentation, mapping, and the integration of location-based information. 6. Field-level modelling: Spatially detailed analysis of agricultural conditions to support operational monitoring and decision-making. 7. Drone and field-data integration: Complementary observations to support targeted field operations and verification of satellite-derived results. 8. Digital platforms and deployment infrastructure: Delivery of analytical outputs through data, platform, and model workflows, with cloud or on-premises deployment options according to project requirements.
Unique Characteristics: 1. Converting satellite imagery into actionable intelligence RIFFAI focuses on transforming complex Earth-observation data into practical information that users can apply to field monitoring and operational decisions, rather than relying solely on conventional satellite-image visualization. 2. Field-level spatial analysis The platform provides spatially detailed outputs, including plant-health indicators, moisture-related assessments, field segmentation, growth monitoring, and overall field-health visualization. This allows users to examine variation within monitored areas and prioritize locations for further investigation. 3. Integration of complementary Earth-observation sources RIFFAI's technology approach incorporates satellite imagery, multispectral data, SAR, weather information, and, where relevant, drone observations. Combining suitable data sources can provide complementary information for monitoring and assessment. 4. Linking digital intelligence with field operations The platform's field-level outputs can inform operational workflows, including the planning of targeted drone activities and field inspections. This creates a practical connection between remote observation, analytical outputs, and on-the-ground decision-making. 5. Adaptability across sectors and geographies RIFFAI's Earth-observation capabilities can be configured for different agricultural and environmental contexts and have broader potential applications in energy and infrastructure monitoring. New deployments require appropriate data selection, local validation, and adaptation to the needs of each user. 6. Collaboration-based deployment RIFFAI's agricultural case studies demonstrate collaboration with organizations operating directly in agricultural production and technology access. Such partnerships can connect AI-powered monitoring with existing field operations and provide a foundation for further adoption. The distinguishing feature of the solution is its combination of satellite-based observation, AI-powered geospatial analysis, field-level outputs, and operational integration within a deployable digital platform.
Sustainable Change: RIFFAI has the potential to support a wider transition toward data-driven, geographically detailed, and more efficient monitoring across agriculture and resource-intensive industries. Replication across geographic contexts: The underlying Earth-observation workflow can be adapted to different locations and agricultural systems. RIFFAI's agricultural case studies in Thailand and Japan provide examples of applications in different operating environments. Further replication would involve local data validation, adaptation to regional conditions, and collaboration with implementation partners. Improved access to digital intelligence: By converting satellite imagery into more accessible operational information, RIFFAI can help agricultural enterprises and other users benefit from Earth-observation technology without independently building all the required data-processing and geospatial-analysis capabilities. More targeted resource management: Field-level monitoring can help users identify areas requiring further inspection or intervention. If validated through implementation, these insights could support more targeted agricultural inputs, water management, field operations, and maintenance planning. Digital transformation of operational workflows: Integrating geospatial intelligence into existing agricultural and industrial processes can encourage organizations to incorporate data-driven monitoring into routine planning, resource allocation, and performance assessment. Knowledge transfer and local collaboration: Partnerships with agricultural businesses, drone-sector organizations, research institutions, and local technology providers can facilitate the adaptation of analytical workflows and the development of local expertise in Earth observation and AI. Potential for broader sustainability benefits: At scale, more accessible and consistent environmental monitoring could strengthen the evidence available for resource-management and sustainability decisions. The extent of these benefits will depend on user adoption, analytical reliability, and demonstrated improvements in operational and environmental performance. RIFFAI's proposed pathway to systemic change is to establish validated use cases, document operational outcomes, develop repeatable deployment processes, and expand through partnerships into additional regions and sectors. This approach can help move AI-powered Earth observation from specialized analysis toward broader practical use in sustainable agriculture and industry.
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: RIFFAI converts satellite imagery into crop, water and infrastructure intelligence, with sites in Thailand and Japan. The sensing approach is sound and partners are in place; unvalidated models, no public product and an empty finance field keep the score at 55.

Title: PhaseSense: AI-Powered Grid Intelligence for Monitoring Secondary Electric Distribution Networks
Subtitle: Energy-efficient edge AI that detects and corrects phase imbalance in low-voltage networks, cutting energy losses, transformer failures and machine downtime for small manufacturers in Tanzania
Problem Statement: In Tanzania and across much of Africa, small manufacturers such as grain mills, welding workshops and food processors share the same low-voltage power lines as homes and shops. Customers are connected unevenly across the three phases, so the load on each phase is uneven too. This is called phase imbalance. It overheats motors, stops machines and disrupts production. For utilities, it wastes energy and causes transformers to fail early, which leads to long outages for whole industrial areas. The problem is that power utilities can’t see what is happening on these networks. Monitoring them is costly: meters are expensive to install and power, they produce large amounts of unneeded data, and many sites have unreliable electricity and poor communications. As a result, imbalance is only fixed after damage has happened. Small industries lose money, energy is wasted, and productivity suffers just when growing economies need reliable power most.
Solution Overview: PhaseSense is an end-to-end, AI-driven monitoring and decision system for low-voltage distribution networks that serve small industries. It has three layers: 1. Energy-efficient edge sensing. Low-cost sensor nodes are installed at distribution transformers and key feeder points. They measure phase currents, voltages, and power-quality indicators. Each node runs a lightweight machine learning model that adapts its sampling and transmission rate to network conditions. When the network is stable, the node samples sparsely and stays in low-power mode. When the model detects rising imbalance, an anomaly or a fault signature, it switches to high-resolution acquisition and reports immediately. This adaptive approach greatly reduces energy use, data volume and communication cost compared with fixed-rate monitoring, so the nodes can run on small solar or battery supplies and be deployed widely. 2. AI analytics and decision layer. A central platform combines data from the nodes and uses machine learning to: (a) forecast phase loading and imbalance from daily, weekly and seasonal patterns (b) detect abnormal conditions that put transformers and motors at risk (c) recommend the best reassignment of customer connections across phases to restore balance with the fewest field interventions A future version will send control signals to automatic phase-switching devices for real-time balancing. 3. Actionable outputs for utilities and industry. Utility engineers get a dashboard showing transformer health, imbalance levels, estimated losses and prioritized corrective actions. Connected small manufacturers receive simple SMS or app alerts about power quality conditions that could damage their equipment, so they can protect machines and plan production. Methodologies and technologies used >Edge machine learning (TinyML) for event-driven, adaptive data acquisition on low-power microcontrollers >Time-series forecasting and anomaly detection models for load behavior and imbalance prediction >Optimization algorithms for phase load reassignment that minimize imbalance and losses >Low-cost IoT hardware with current and voltage sensing, plus low-power communications (LoRaWAN) >A cloud or utility-hosted data platform with open, interoperable data formats so it can integrate with existing utility systems The team develops and validates the ML models on measured and simulated LV network data. Next comes a field pilot on [one or more transformer zones serving small industries in Dar es Salaam]. Then the system is refined and prepared for utility-scale rollout. Partnerships and collaboration models >Academic lead: College of Information and Communication Technologies, University of Dar es Salaam. The college leads R&D, model development and system integration. >Utility partner: [TANESCO, proposed/confirmed]. Provides network access, pilot sites, operational data and a pathway to adoption. >Industry partners: [SIDO and small-industry associations, proposed/confirmed]. Engage manufacturers as pilot beneficiaries and validate impact on productivity. >Scaling partners: regional utilities, development partners and UN agencies, who would support replication across East Africa and other developing regions. >Collaboration model: co-development with the utility, open methods and capacity building for engineers and technicians, and a low-cost hardware model suitable for local manufacturing and maintenance.
Solution Provider(s): University of Dar es Salaam, College of Information and Communication Technologies (CoICT) – public university leading research, AI model development and system integration – Academia, Tanzania Electric Supply Company Limited (TANESCO) – National electricity utility responsible for distribution networks; pilot sites and operational data – Public sector (Energy), Small Industries Development Organization (SIDO) – Government agency supporting small and medium industries; links to pilot manufacturers – Public sector (Industry/SME development)
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6–9 months, covering site assessment and utility partnership (1–2 months), hardware deployment and data collection (2–3 months), local retraining of the AI models (1–2 months), and pilot operation and evaluation (2 months).
Desired impact: Main objectives: >Give utilities low-cost, real-time visibility of low-voltage networks that serve the distribution networks. >Detect and predict phase imbalance early, and recommend the best way to rebalance loads before damage happens. >Cut the energy and data costs of grid monitoring through AI-driven adaptive data collection. >Protect small manufacturers from power problems that damage machines and stop production. Expected impact (pilot targets): >50–70% less energy use and data transmission by monitoring nodes, compared with fixed-rate monitoring >Phase imbalance at monitored transformers brought within recommended limits (below about 10%) >10–20% fewer technical losses on monitored feeders, giving direct energy savings and lower CO₂ emissions >Fewer transformer failures and outages, so less costly replacement and less production downtime >Fewer motor burnouts and machine stoppages for small manufacturers connected to monitored transformers >Local jobs and skills in installing, maintaining and running the system, and training for utility technicians and engineering students
Key technologies: Key technologies used: >Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: forecasting of load and imbalance, anomaly and fault detection, and optimization models that recommend how to reassign loads across phases. >Edge AI (TinyML): lightweight models running on low-power sensor devices decide when to collect and send data, which saves energy and bandwidth. >Internet of Things (IoT): low-cost sensor nodes measure current, voltage and power quality at transformers and feeders, and connect through GSM or LoRaWAN. >Renewable-powered hardware: nodes can run on small solar panels or batteries, so they work at sites with unreliable power. >Cloud data platform and dashboards: data is stored and analysed centrally, with a dashboard for utilities and SMS or app alerts for small manufacturers.
Unique Characteristics: >Smart, energy-saving data collection: Most grid monitoring collects data constantly, which wastes energy and bandwidth. PhaseSense uses AI at the device to collect detailed data only when it matters, so monitoring becomes cheap enough to deploy widely in low-resource settings. >Built for weak grids: It is designed for African low-voltage networks with low-cost hardware, unreliable power, limited communications and little existing digital infrastructure. >Serves both utility and industry: Utilities get network intelligence, and small manufacturers get direct alerts that protect their equipment. This creates shared value and a reason for both sides to adopt it. >Prediction and action, not just monitoring: It forecasts problems and recommends specific corrective actions, rather than only showing data. >Locally developed and maintained: It is developed by a Tanzanian university with local partners, so skills, hardware assembly and maintenance can stay in the country, and costs and dependence on imported systems stay low. >Open and adaptable: Its open data formats and transferable models let other utilities and countries retrain and adopt it.
Sustainable Change: PhaseSense can change how utilities in developing countries manage low-voltage networks, from reacting after failures to acting early based on data. Once utilities see the savings from fewer transformer failures and lower losses, the system can be built into their normal operations and expanded from pilot sites to whole cities and regions. The problem is common across Africa and other developing regions, so the solution can be replicated widely. Models can be retrained on local data, and the low-cost hardware can be assembled and maintained locally, which creates jobs and builds technical skills. Beyond the pilot, the data it produces can help utilities and governments plan network upgrades, connect new industries more reliably, and integrate solar and other distributed energy. Over time, a more reliable grid helps small industries grow, saves energy and reduces emissions, which supports sustainable industrialization. Training utility engineers and students through the project builds a lasting local capacity for AI in the energy sector.
Funding Sources: The solution has not yet been deployed. Research and development so far has been supported through the “Smart Grid Capacity Development and Enhancement in Tanzania” programme at the University of Dar es Salaam supported by SIDA, with in-kind support from the University of Dar es Salaam, College of Information and communications Technologies
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: PhaseSense proposes edge sensors and TinyML models to detect and correct phase imbalance on the low-voltage lines that supply small Tanzanian manufacturers. The problem and the design are convincing; with no deployment and no measurement it remains a concept.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems; Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making

Title: DataPlus: AI-Powered Data Intelligence Built in Africa for Africa’s Industries
Subtitle: An Ethiopian-built AI platform that collects verified, geo-targeted data from a paid respondent panel via SMS, QR and web, turning it into real-time insights for businesses, NGOs and banks
Problem Statement: Industrial AI and data-driven decision-making depend on reliable, representative local data, yet in Ethiopia and many emerging economies that data barely exists. Manufacturers, SMEs, startups, banks and NGOs make investment, product and policy decisions with little current market intelligence on who their customers are and what they need. Traditional field surveys are slow and expensive, putting them out of reach for most small businesses. Online alternatives suffer from fake, duplicate and out-of-area respondents, and without fair incentives, participation and response quality stay low. Many tools also assume high-speed internet, missing communities that rely on SMS, mobile money and basic smartphones, and most platforms are foreign-owned and not built for local demographics or conditions, leaving local data and insights controlled elsewhere. Without a trusted local data layer, AI models cannot be trained, validated or adapted to local realities, and the benefits of industrial AI stay out of reach for the businesses that need them most.
Solution Overview: DataPlus is an Ethiopian-built, AI-powered data collection and intelligence platform that connects organizations that need reliable data with a paid, demographically profiled panel of survey takers. Corporates, NGOs, banks, universities, startups and researchers create a survey in minutes, either by typing a prompt that the AI turns into a questionnaire or by building it manually. They set a budget and target respondents by location and demographics. The survey is distributed by bulk SMS, link or printable QR code, so it reaches people with and without strong internet access. Respondents complete it on their phones and are paid for every completed response, withdrawing earnings through Telebirr. Title: Stamped: Always-On Process Control for Manufacturing Plants
Subtitle: Stamped reads the data a plant already logs (ERP, SCADA, CNC, quality) and tells the shift lead, while the batch is still running, what is causing rejects, idle time and wasted energy.
Problem Statement: India's manufacturing, forging and auto-component plants are mostly MSMEs running on thin margins. They lose money in four places every shift: machines sitting idle, lines running below rated throughput, parts rejected at inspection, and energy burnt on bad or idle cycles. The data to catch these losses already exists, split across the ERP, SCADA, machine controllers and quality sheets. Nobody joins it in time. Plants find out a batch was bad at end-of-shift inspection, after the material, machine hours and energy are already spent. Fixes today are one-time audits. They go stale within months, because lines change, new parts and recipes come in, and process parameters drift. Large OEMs can afford in-house digital teams to keep up. MSME suppliers can't. This translates to global manufacturing as well.
Solution Overview: Stamped sits on top of the systems a plant already has. There's no new hardware and no rip-and-replace. How it works: Stamped connects to the ERP, SCADA, CNC and VMC machine logs, and the quality records, and lines them up on one timeline per machine, part and batch. It learns which combinations of settings, materials and machine states led to past rejects, slowdowns and energy spikes. It runs all the time, not as a one-off audit. When a live batch starts to look like a past failure, it sends the shift lead one specific action: which machine, which parameter, what to change. The plant's own team sets the limits first, and people make the final call. Methods and technology: data connectors for common industrial systems; time-series alignment across machine, quality and energy data; machine learning models that learn from each plant's own reject and downtime history; and an agent layer that turns findings into plain-language actions for the floor. Partnership model: we work directly with plant owners and their production and quality heads. We start on one line, prove the loss reduction there, then expand line by line. Stamped is part of the NVIDIA Inception programme for startups.
Solution Provider(s): We are currently or starting to work with, Bhatia Alloy, JBM Group, Ashok Leyland, Remsons and others in our sales cycle. We are also in NVIDIA Inception (NVIDIA's startup programme, technology sector: Stamped is a member) and Aws for Startups.
Implementation location(s): India, Faridabad, Bhatia Alloy, and others coming up.
Implementation timeline(s): Analysis and initial procurement is over 1 month, initial deployment is starting
Duration to pilot in a new geography: About 1 week per plant(2 days of survey and scoping, 3 days of deployment and 2 days of verification). Stamped connects to the systems a plant already runs, so most of that time goes on data access and mapping one line.
Desired impact: Objective: cut the four daily losses in MSME forging and auto-component plants (idle machines, lost throughput, quality rejects and wasted energy) using data those plants already collect. Expected impact: our target for first deployments is about 10% lower energy cost per plant. It comes from fewer rejected parts, fewer idle and bad cycles, and better machine utilisation. Every rejected forging wastes the steel, the furnace heat and the machine hours that went into it. So each reject caught early saves material, energy and CO2 together. We'll measure results per plant against that plant's own baseline: rejection rate, machine utilisation, and kWh per good part.
Key technologies: Industrial data integration (ERP, SCADA, CNC/VMC controllers, quality systems); time-series analytics; machine learning trained on each plant's own reject and downtime history; an agent layer that delivers actions to shift teams; and cloud and edge deployment depending on the plant's connectivity.
Unique Characteristics: It runs continuously. Process audits go stale the moment a line changes. Stamped re-learns as new parts, recipes and settings come in, so the guidance stays current. It needs no new hardware. Stamped uses the data plants already log, which keeps the cost within reach of an MSME instead of only large OEMs. It ends in an action, not a dashboard. Each alert names the machine, the parameter and the change, and it goes to the person who can act during the shift. It treats quality, throughput and energy as one problem. A reject is also wasted energy and material, so Stamped optimises all three together instead of selling three separate tools.
Sustainable Change: MSMEs make up most of the supplier base in auto components and forging, in India and across the Global South. Most of them can't afford industrial digital teams. Stamped turns data these plants already have into continuous process control, with no capital spend on new equipment. The same data pattern (ERP, SCADA, machine controllers, quality records) shows up in casting, machining and metal fabrication. So the approach carries across sectors and countries with little rework. Every plant that cuts rejects and energy per good part also gets more competitive in global supply chains that increasingly demand lower-carbon parts. Over time, the shared process knowledge Stamped builds across plants could give MSME clusters the kind of process know-how only large manufacturers have today.
Funding Sources: Bootstrapped by the founders so far. We haven't raised outside investment yet, and Stamped is a member of the NVIDIA Inception startup programme as well as AWS for startups.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: Stamped reads ERP, SCADA, CNC and quality records and tells the shift lead, while a batch is still running, which settings are producing rejects, idle time and wasted energy. The first deployment is at Bhatia Alloy in Faridabad, with several larger groups in the pipeline.

Title: TerraScan: AI Soil Intelligence and Irrigation for Drought Resilient Farms
Subtitle: A low cost hardware system with a phone app, designed and built in Zimbabwe, that uses AI on soil data to guide fertilizer and watering through El Niño droughts.
Problem Statement: Southern Africa is facing more frequent and severe droughts, and the 2023 to 2024 El Niño drought left many Zimbabwean smallholder farmers with failed harvests. Most of these farmers decide how much fertilizer to apply and when to water by guesswork, because laboratory soil tests are slow, costly and far from the farm. In a dry season every wrong decision is expensive. Fertilizer put on dry soil is wasted, water is used too early or too late, and yields fall. Farmers need affordable and timely information about their own soil to make the best use of scarce rain and water.
Solution Overview: As the founder of Grumium Engineering Pvt Ltd, I designed TerraScan to give smallholder farmers the kind of soil advice a large commercial farm gets from an agronomist, at a price they can afford. TerraScan is a hardware system with a software interface. We designed and built both here in Zimbabwe. Sensors placed in the soil measure nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, electrical conductivity and moisture. The hardware collects these readings and sends them to the farmer's phone. The app uses artificial intelligence to process the data. It compares the readings with what the crop needs and turns them into plain advice on which fertilizer to apply, how much and when. The app works offline, so farmers with no internet still get results. The same data switches on automatic irrigation, so water reaches the crop only when the soil needs it. In drought and El Niño years this matters most. The system helps farmers save water and avoid wasting fertilizer on dry ground. We built TerraScan from low cost soil sensors, our own hardware unit and a mobile app with AI models that turn the soil data into recommendations. Grumium Engineering Pvt Ltd earns revenue from selling the kit and from soil testing with recommendations. A subscription for the app's agronomist advice is planned. We want to work with agricultural extension services, input suppliers and farmer cooperatives to reach more farmers.
Solution Provider(s): EU Youth Empowerment Fund (European Union funding programme for youth led projects in the development sector), beVisioneers (fellowship and project scholarship programme for young innovators in the social entrepreneurship sector)
Implementation location(s): Zimbabwe
Implementation timeline(s): 2025 to present
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 to 4 months
Desired impact: The main objective is to help smallholder farmers in Zimbabwe get the most from scarce rain, water and fertilizer, so that dry seasons and El Niño droughts hurt their harvests less. TerraScan is a hardware system with a software interface that we designed and built in Zimbabwe. It gives each farmer a soil test, a clear recommendation and automatic irrigation in one low cost kit. So far it has reached about 300 farmers, and more than 100 of them have used it to increase their yields. Farmers we have spoken with report gains of about 40%. These are their own reports and not a measured trial. Better targeted fertilizer and watering also means less fertilizer lost to the environment.
Key technologies: Artificial intelligence that turns soil data into fertilizer and irrigation advice. Internet of Things soil sensors that measure nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, electrical conductivity and moisture. Embedded hardware that controls automatic irrigation. A mobile app that processes the readings offline on the farmer's phone.
Unique Characteristics: TerraScan joins soil sensing, AI advice and irrigation control in one low cost kit, so a farmer gets a test, a recommendation and an action without a laboratory visit or an agronomist. It works offline, which suits rural areas with weak internet. We designed and built the whole system in Zimbabwe for local soils, crops and prices. The business model pairs a kit purchase with paid soil testing and a planned subscription for ongoing advice, so farmers can start small and grow their use over time.
Sustainable Change: Every farm that adopts TerraScan adds soil data from an area where few farms have been tested. As the founder of Grumium Engineering Pvt Ltd, I expect this data to help extension services, input suppliers and planners understand soil health and water stress. They can then prepare earlier for El Niño years. The kit can be repeated in other southern African countries with similar smallholder farming and drought risk. Local partners would handle sales and training. Farmers who waste less fertilizer and water spend less on inputs and are better placed to protect their harvest in dry seasons.

Title: From Pilot to Scale: Governed Enterprise AI Agents for Manufacturing
Subtitle: A staged, low-risk-to-scale approach to deploying enterprise AI agents in manufacturing, with built-in guardrails that keep company, sensitive and personal data protected.
Problem Statement: Enterprises in developing and middle-income economies want to adopt AI but face three barriers. They fear exposing company, sensitive and personal data. They lack the governance and skills to keep AI agents under control. And their pilots often stall before reaching scale. Without a safe, proven path, the benefits of enterprise AI stay with a few large players, while employees and the public carry the data and security risks.
Solution Overview: The solution is a staged, governed approach to deploying AI agents across a manufacturing enterprise. It moves from low risk to wide scale while the organization stays in control, in three stages: 1. Embedded AI, no customization: AI assistance built into existing enterprise systems for a low-risk function such as HR. Data stays inside existing security and access controls. 2. External-facing AI agent: a public-facing agent that gives real-world feedback. Guardrails are added in response to actual use. For example, when the public began asking it to verify suspicious job offers, the team built protections for that use. 3. Internal AI assistant with guardrails: a workforce-wide assistant with access rules and data-protection controls that keep company, sensitive and personal data from being exposed. The same approach is now being extended to AI agents for logistics and for data-intensive technical work. Methodologies and technologies • Staged adoption: each stage is piloted and governed before access widens. • Responsible AI governance: risk assessment, guardrails, data-protection controls, human oversight, and alignment with AI ethics, regulation and compliance practice. • Technologies: enterprise-embedded AI, web-based conversational agents, internal AI assistants and custom AI agents.
Solution Provider(s): Contributed to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance (Geneva), sharing practical lessons from governed enterprise AI deployment. • Engaged with ITU-T work on trust and identity for humans and agentic AI. • Aligned with international AI governance and standards frameworks. • Cross-functional collaboration among AI strategy, IT, HR, legal, security and business teams.
Implementation location(s): United Arab Emirates (Dubai)
Implementation timeline(s): 2025 to present
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 to 6 months
Desired impact: Main objective 1. Provide manufacturing enterprises with a safe, repeatable pathway to adopt AI agents, progressing deliberately from low-risk use cases to enterprise-wide scale. 2. Protect company, sensitive and personal data at every stage through guardrails, access controls and human oversight. 3. Build trust and accountability in enterprise AI through responsible governance aligned with international standards. 4. Offer a practical playbook that other enterprises, including those with fewer resources, can adapt to their own context. Demonstrated impact • A governed, three-stage deployment is live, spanning embedded AI for HR, an external-facing agent and an internal assistant with guardrails. • The deployment has delivered measurable efficiency gains and freed capacity for higher-value work. • Governance proved responsive to real-world use. When the public began relying on the external agent to verify suspicious job offers, protections were built in response, helping safeguard job seekers from fraud. • The approach is now being extended to AI agents for logistics and for data-intensive technical work. • Lessons from the deployment have been shared through contributions to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and engagement with ITU-T work on trust and identity. Expected impact Faster, lower-risk AI adoption, with reduced exposure of sensitive data. • Stronger employee and public trust in enterprise AI. • A replicable, governance-first model that organizations and regions can adapt, supporting more inclusive access to the benefits of AI.
Key technologies: • Artificial intelligence: generative AI and large language models, deployed as conversational AI agents. These include enterprise-embedded AI assistants, a public-facing web agent and an internal AI assistant. Custom AI agents are being developed for logistics and data-intensive technical work. • Agentic AI: task-oriented agents that act within defined permissions and workflows, with human oversight. • Data protection and security controls: guardrails, role-based access controls and data-boundary enforcement that keep company, sensitive and personal data from being exposed to AI systems. • Responsible AI governance tooling: risk assessment, monitoring and policy controls aligned with international AI governance and standards frameworks. • Enterprise systems integration: connections to existing enterprise platforms, so AI works inside trusted environments rather than outside them.
Unique Characteristics: 1. A staged, risk-graduated delivery approach Most AI initiatives either stall at the pilot stage or scale without sufficient controls. This solution takes a deliberate path: embedded AI with no customization, then an external-facing agent, then a guardrailed internal assistant. Each stage is governed before the next widens access, which builds capability and trust while keeping the organization in control. 2. Data protection by design Company, sensitive and personal data are protected from the first deployment through guardrails, access controls and human oversight, rather than added later. This addresses the main barrier that keeps many enterprises from adopting AI. 3. Governance that learns from real use Governance is treated as a continuous feedback loop. When the public began using the external agent to verify suspicious job offers, protections were built in response. Real-world use directly shapes safeguards, so the solution is practical, not theoretical. 4. Technology-agnostic and replicable The approach is a delivery model, not a single product. It can be adapted to different enterprise systems, sectors and country contexts, including organizations with limited resources, because it starts with low-risk, no-customization AI. 5. Connected to international governance practice The solution is informed by contributions to the UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance and engagement with ITU-T work on trust and identity, aligning enterprise practice with emerging global norms
Sustainable Change: From one enterprise to a replicable model The solution is a delivery model, not a single product. Its staged, governance-first path (low-risk embedded AI, then external-facing agents, then a guardrailed internal assistant) can be adopted by other manufacturers in different sectors and countries.
