Title: AYIVI AI-Native Enterprise Intelligence System
Subtitle: A deployable AI-native architecture that embeds governed intelligence, human oversight and auditable decision support into enterprise and institutional digital systems.
Problem Statement: Organizations across developing and middle-income economies increasingly want to use artificial intelligence, but many operate with fragmented data, legacy workflows, limited technical capacity, unreliable connectivity and systems that were not designed for safe AI integration. The result is often a choice between conventional software with limited intelligence and externally hosted AI tools that operate outside core institutional workflows, governance controls and accountability structures. This creates risks around data sovereignty, hallucination, opaque decision-making, uncontrolled automation, vendor dependence and weak auditability. The challenge is therefore not simply access to AI models. It is the absence of a practical enterprise architecture for integrating AI safely into real operational systems while preserving human authority, institutional controls, traceability and adaptability to local infrastructure constraints. AYIVI AI-Native addresses this implementation gap by providing a governed intelligence architecture through which AI can assist institutional operations, analyse data, support decisions and automate bounded tasks without becoming an uncontrolled decision-maker.
Solution Overview: AYIVI AI-Native is an enterprise intelligence architecture developed by AYIVI Systems Limited in Ghana for embedding governed artificial intelligence directly into operational digital systems. Rather than treating AI as a standalone chatbot or external add-on, the solution integrates intelligence into the application's data, workflow, authorization, audit and decision-support layers. The architecture combines structured institutional and operational data; role-based access control and policy enforcement; AI-assisted analysis and decision support; bounded agentic workflows; human-in-the-loop approval for consequential actions; decision and trajectory logging; verification and confidence controls; model/provider identification and traceability; audit trails and incident handling; API-based interoperability; and reusable intelligence services that can be adapted across institutional domains. The governing principle is that AI may assist, analyse, recommend and execute explicitly bounded operations, but institutional authority remains with authorized human users for consequential decisions. The solution is designed as a reusable architecture rather than a single-purpose application. It can therefore support enterprise and institutional systems across education, health, energy, commerce, agriculture and public-service environments. The technology approach combines modern web and cloud architecture, relational data systems, API-based services and large language models integrated through controlled application layers. AI interactions are governed through explicit permissions, verification mechanisms, audit logging and human escalation pathways. AYIVI develops the core architecture internally and applies it progressively across its digital product ecosystem. The model also supports collaboration with institutional clients, technology providers, implementation partners and domain specialists where deployments require sector-specific expertise or integration with existing infrastructure.
Solution Provider(s): None. The solution is developed and implemented by AYIVI Systems Limited.
Implementation location(s): Ghana. The architecture is being progressively implemented and validated through AYIVI Systems Limited's enterprise and institutional digital products, including operational and pilot systems serving education, health, financial/operational management and institutional intelligence use cases.
Implementation timeline(s): 2026 – ongoing. Progressive implementation and validation across AYIVI Systems Limited's AI-enabled enterprise and institutional systems.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 4–8 weeks for an initial pilot, depending on the target institution, data availability, required integrations, regulatory requirements, localization and deployment environment.
Desired impact: The principal objective of AYIVI AI-Native is to make governed, auditable and context-appropriate artificial intelligence practically deployable within enterprises and institutions in developing and middle-income economies. The solution aims to: • enable organizations to integrate AI directly into operational systems rather than rely on disconnected AI tools; • improve the speed and quality of data analysis and institutional decision support; • reduce repetitive administrative and analytical workloads; • preserve human accountability for consequential decisions; • create auditable records of AI-assisted actions and recommendations; • enable organizations to adopt different AI models and providers without rebuilding their core applications; • support AI deployment in environments with infrastructure, connectivity and technical-capacity constraints; and • create reusable AI capabilities that can be adapted across sectors and geographies. The architecture is currently being validated progressively across AYIVI's enterprise and institutional technology portfolio in Ghana. Its present impact is therefore best measured through deployment capability, reusable architecture, operational integration and reduction of the engineering effort required to introduce governed AI into multiple systems, rather than through unsupported large-scale beneficiary claims. As deployments mature, the architecture is designed to support measurable indicators including processing-time reductions, administrative workload reduction, decision-response times, AI recommendation acceptance/correction rates, system availability, user adoption and operational cost efficiency.
Key technologies: The solution combines: • Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative AI; • AI-assisted natural-language interaction and analysis; • controlled agentic workflows; • retrieval and context-aware AI integration; • structured relational databases; • API-first application architecture; • cloud and edge-compatible web technologies; • role-based access control (RBAC); • human-in-the-loop decision controls; • automated verification and validation mechanisms; • decision, trajectory and audit logging; • provider/model identification and observability; • secure API integrations; and • modular enterprise application architecture. The architecture is model-agnostic by design, allowing appropriate AI providers and models to be selected according to task, cost, performance, governance and deployment requirements.
Unique Characteristics: AYIVI AI-Native differs from conventional enterprise AI implementations by treating intelligence as a governed architectural layer of the operational system rather than as an external chatbot or isolated AI feature. Its distinguishing features include: 1. Governed AI by design: AI permissions, human authority, verification, escalation and audit requirements are built into the system architecture. 2. Human authority over consequential decisions: AI can analyse, recommend and perform bounded actions, while consequential institutional decisions remain subject to authorized human control. 3. Auditable intelligence: AI-assisted decisions and operational trajectories can be logged and traced, enabling organizations to understand what the system recommended, what action followed and where human correction occurred. 4. Model-agnostic architecture: Organizations are not structurally locked into one AI provider. Models can be selected or changed according to capability, economics, availability and governance requirements. 5. African operating context: The architecture is designed from a developing-economy implementation perspective, including constrained connectivity, affordability, institutional capacity and the need to integrate AI progressively rather than replace entire technology estates. 6. Reusability across sectors: The same governed intelligence architecture can be adapted to education, health, energy, agriculture, commerce and institutional administration, reducing the cost and time required to introduce safe AI capabilities into new systems.
Sustainable Change: AYIVI AI-Native has the potential to shift AI adoption in developing economies from isolated experimentation toward governed institutional deployment. Because the solution is an adaptable architecture rather than a single-sector application, successful implementation in one organization can generate reusable components, governance patterns, intelligence services and implementation knowledge for deployment in other institutions and sectors. This creates three pathways for systemic change. First, organizations that cannot economically develop proprietary AI infrastructure can adopt governed AI capabilities through existing enterprise systems. Second, the architecture can enable local software companies and institutional technology providers to build AI-enabled solutions while maintaining human oversight, auditability and compatibility with local regulatory requirements. Third, its model-agnostic and API-based approach can support technology cooperation across countries without requiring every market to reproduce the same underlying infrastructure. At scale, this approach could help create an ecosystem in which African enterprises and institutions become active implementers and adapters of AI rather than merely consumers of generic AI services developed for other operating environments. Replication can occur through direct deployments, institutional partnerships, technology-transfer arrangements and integration into sector-specific platforms. The architecture is designed so that lessons and reusable components from each deployment strengthen subsequent implementations, reducing deployment time and cost as the ecosystem expands.
Funding Sources: AYIVI AI-Native has been funded internally by AYIVI Systems Limited through founder investment, company resources and the reinvestment of resources from AYIVI's software development and technology activities. The research, architecture design, engineering, testing and progressive integration of the solution into AYIVI's enterprise technology ecosystem have therefore been undertaken without external grant funding or institutional investment to date. This internally funded development model has enabled AYIVI to retain ownership of the core intellectual property and to develop the architecture around practical operational requirements encountered while building digital systems in an African operating environment.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems
Summary: AYIVI embeds governed AI, with access control and audit, directly into enterprise systems for Ghanaian institutions. The architectural thinking is sound; with no external deployment and no media, it cannot be verified.

Title: PROACT :Predict. Alert. Act Before the Crisis.
Subtitle: An AI platform that predicts climate shocks and their impact on food security and humanitarian supply chains enabling earlier, lower-cost response before crises escalate.
Problem Statement: Food insecurity emergencies are increasingly driven by climate related shocks including droughts, floods, and extreme heat that simultaneously affect agricultural production, household livelihoods, and humanitarian supply chains. While early warning information exists, it is often fragmented across climate, market, and logistics systems, limiting its operational usefulness for timely humanitarian action. As a result, humanitarian responses are frequently reactive, leading to higher delivery costs, disrupted supply chains, delayed assistance, and, in some cases, ration cuts. There is a critical need for integrated, anticipatory decision-support tools that enable early action before shocks escalate into food insecurity crises
Solution Overview: PROACT is an AI-driven anticipatory action platform that predicts climate shocks — floods, droughts, and heatwaves and translates them into food security and supply chain risk alerts before a crisis occurs. The system monitors climate and environmental data continuously, assigns district-level risk levels (Low / Medium / High) with time windows of days to weeks, and links each alert to specific recommended actions such as pre-positioning food stocks, rerouting transport, or triggering cash assistance. Outputs are delivered through a real-time risk dashboard, automated alerts, and weekly partner briefing reports. Methodologies and Technologies The platform ingests weather forecasts, satellite-derived hazard layers, market price signals, and historical incident data through automated pipelines. It computes district-level risk features — including rolling rainfall anomalies, floodplain exposure, slope-risk indices, and food price volatility and scores each district using an explainable hybrid rules-and-statistics model (Phase 1), with an upgrade path to machine learning models (XGBoost/LightGBM with SHAP explainability) in Phase 2. The backend uses PostgreSQL/PostGIS for spatial data, object storage for raw and curated datasets, and a Next.js dashboard with SMS/WhatsApp alerting. The system is designed for low-connectivity environments and built to scale across regions and hazard types. Partnerships and Collaboration PROACT works through partner organizations rather than around them. Two NGO partners have been onboarded in the first three months, using platform outputs to inform storage management and community response. Alert thresholds are co-designed with partners and humanitarian actors including alignment with WFP’s anticipatory action framework to reflect real operational contexts. Partners also feed back on alert accuracy, driving a continuous model improvement cycle.
Solution Provider(s): UNDP-timbuktoo,WFP
Implementation location(s): Uganda
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 8 months
Desired impact: PROACT’s core objective is to shift humanitarian and agricultural response from reactive to anticipatory enabling organizations to act on climate risk before it becomes a food security crisis. Specifically, the platform aims to: Provide district-level early warning for climate shocks (floods, droughts, heatwaves) with enough lead time for meaningful preventive action Reduce post-harvest food losses by giving farming communities and food security organizations advance visibility into storage and supply chain risks Lower the cost and improve the efficiency of humanitarian response by enabling pre-planned, upstream interventions rather than emergency reactions Expected and Demonstrated Impact Demonstrated (first 3 months): 5 NGO partner organizations onboarded and actively using the platform 100% platform availability throughout the reporting period Partner organizations report improved visibility into storage risks and a shift toward proactive operational planning Expected (next 12 months): Expansion from 5 to 20 organizational partner organizations Reduced post-harvest food losses across monitored storage facilities, with loss-reduction metrics to be formally tracked and reported Measurable lead time gained ahead of climate shocks enabling earlier, lower-cost interventions compared to reactive emergency response Cost savings on humanitarian logistics through pre-positioned supplies and proactive route adjustments Strengthened food security and climate resilience for smallholder farming communities reached through partner networks
Key technologies: Ai
Unique Characteristics: Innovative and Differentiating Features PROACT’s core innovation is integration most existing early warning tools operate in silos, covering either climate forecasting, food security monitoring, or supply chain risk separately. PROACT is distinctive in combining all three into a single operational platform that goes from climate signal to recommended action in one workflow, making it immediately usable by field teams rather than requiring analysts to manually connect data across systems. Key differentiators: From warning to action. Unlike traditional early warning systems that stop at issuing alerts, PROACT links every risk trigger to specific recommended actions pre-positioning food stocks, rerouting transport, initiating cash readiness co-designed with partners to reflect real operational contexts. The platform supports decisions; it does not just report risk. Anticipatory rather than reactive. By acting upstream of a crisis when lead times are still available PROACT enables interventions that are faster, cheaper, and more dignified than emergency responses. This shifts the cost curve of humanitarian action significantly. Explainability built in. Risk scores come with plain-language driver explanations (e.g., “exceptional rainfall + saturated ground + high floodplain exposure”), making outputs trustworthy and actionable for non-technical users in the field. Phase 2 adds SHAP-based ML explainability for deeper accountability. Designed for real-world constraints. The platform is built for low connectivity environments, uses low cost monitoring infrastructure, and delivers alerts via SMS and WhatsApp not just web dashboards making it viable in the contexts where food insecurity risk is actually highest. Co-designed thresholds. Alert trigger levels are not set algorithmically and imposed they are co-designed with partner organizations and humanitarian actors on the ground, ensuring the system reflects operational reality rather than technical defaults. This drives trust and adoption. Scalable by design. The architecture supports incremental expansion across districts, countries, and hazard types without rebuilding core infrastructure, making it cost effective to grow.
Sustainable Change: PROACT’s systemic impact lies in changing how climate risk is acted on across humanitarian and agricultural systems not just in individual districts. By demonstrating that early, data driven intervention is feasible and cost-effective in low-resource settings, the platform builds a documented evidence base that can reform standard response protocols at institutional level shifting the default from reactive emergency response to anticipatory action. The architecture is replicable by design, built on open climate data and configurable thresholds that can be adapted to any country facing similar climate food security dynamics. The Uganda pilot is explicitly scoped as a proof-of-concept for national and regional scale up across East and West Africa. Over time, the district level risk data PROACT generates can be integrated into national meteorological and disaster management systems, creating a pathway from a private platform to a public good. This also supports the broader adoption of forecast-based financing where donor funds are released automatically when risk thresholds are crossed by providing the measurable evidence that development banks and humanitarian funders require. At the partnership level, every organization onboarded builds internal capacity in anticipatory, data-driven decision making, creating sustained demand for evidence based early action across the sector. The underlying model is also transferable beyond food security to health, water, and infrastructure risk multiplying the long-term value of the initial investment.
Funding Sources: Grants from UNDP
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: PROACT aims to turn climate forecasts into district-level food security and supply chain alerts with recommended actions. The problem and the partnerships are real; the technical case is essentially undocumented.

Title: IDWorthy: Trusted Identity and Evidence for Robots and Drones
Subtitle: Neutral digital infrastructure linking robots and drones to permanent identities, responsible organizations and lifecycle evidence, supporting accountable and inclusive industrial AI adoption.
Problem Statement: Industrial robots and professional drones are increasingly software-defined, AI-enabled systems. However, information about their identity, configuration, responsible organizations, maintenance and supporting evidence remains fragmented across manufacturer portals, spreadsheets, documents and specialist operational platforms. A serial number alone cannot establish which software or AI configuration applied during an operation, who was responsible, or which evidence supports a capability claim. Changes in ownership, components, software and service providers can further disrupt continuity. For micro, small and medium-sized enterprises in developing and middle-income economies, this fragmentation can create additional administrative costs and technical barriers to adopting advanced industrial technologies. It also makes maintenance, equipment transfers, supplier evaluation and evidence sharing more difficult. IDWorthy addresses the need for a continuous, attributable record that follows each physical machine across organizations, systems and lifecycle changes.
Solution Overview: IDWorthy is a digital identity and operational-record platform developed by AT Worthy Technology, Inc. It connects each physical machine to a permanent identity and an evolving, permission-controlled record. Professional drones are the initial commercial focus, with a broader architecture for robots and other Intelligent Physical Agents. The platform works through four connected functions: - Identify and reconcile. Organizations submit equipment information through structured onboarding and import workflows. Records are reviewed and reconciled before registration, reducing duplicate or conflicting identities. Each registered unit receives a permanent identifier and web address. - Connect responsibility and configuration. The record distinguishes manufacturers, owners, operators, maintainers and other participating organizations. It links the machine to product information, components, batteries, software and AI references, maintenance and lifecycle changes. - Preserve evidence and history. Documents and assertions retain their source, contributor, applicable time and review status. Corrections preserve earlier history. The platform distinguishes a submitted claim from reviewed evidence or an external regulatory decision. - Share information under controlled access. Authorized users access relevant information through organizational workspaces and structured interfaces. Public identity information is separated from confidential operational and commercial evidence. The methodology combines persistent identification, provenance, structured evidence, temporal records and explicit human responsibility. The technical foundation includes a web application, relational database, APIs, private document storage, cryptographic integrity checks and organizational access controls. The proposed collaboration model brings together equipment manufacturers, operators, integrators and maintenance providers. Local industry associations, research institutions and development partners could support onboarding, contextual adaptation and pilot evaluation. Participation can begin with assisted onboarding and structured files, with deeper integrations introduced where justified. IDWorthy complements specialist flight, fleet and industrial systems by preserving identity and evidence across them. Mission and flight workflows are part of the drone roadmap and would be included only as they become validated.
Solution Provider(s): AT Worthy Technology, Inc. — United States-based private technology company and lead developer/operator of IDWorthy, specializing in physical AI identity, evidence infrastructure, technology research and governance, Enova Robotics — Tunisia-based robotics manufacturer and signed strategic design partner, RobotLAB Fairfax — independently operated robotics solutions provider in Fairfax, Virginia, United States, and signed partnership collaborator.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 8–12 weeks
Desired impact: IDWorthy’s main objective is to make industrial physical AI easier to identify, document and govern across its operational life. Its specific objectives are to: - Establish continuous identity across ownership, configuration and service-provider changes. - Reduce repeated data entry, fragmented documentation and time spent retrieving equipment information. - Improve visibility into organizational responsibility, maintenance and supporting evidence. - Support repair, reuse and equipment transfers through preserved component and lifecycle records. - Help smaller organizations participate in industrial AI ecosystems through accessible onboarding and shared record conventions. Expected benefits include lower administrative effort, better-informed maintenance and deployment decisions, improved evidence availability and stronger continuity when machines change hands or systems. These are expected benefits rather than demonstrated field outcomes. Pilot evaluation would measure onboarding time per machine, record completeness, unresolved identity discrepancies, evidence retrieval time, maintenance-history availability and administrative effort compared with existing practices. Where participating operators provide suitable data, evaluation could also examine equipment utilization, repair and reuse outcomes. No quantified emissions reductions, energy savings or job-creation results are claimed at this stage.
Key technologies: IDWorthy combines: - Persistent digital identity: Permanent UUID-based identifiers, canonical web addresses and QR-accessible identity references. - Structured operational data: PostgreSQL records connecting machines, organizations, configurations, components, batteries, maintenance and evidence. - Temporal history and provenance: Records distinguish when information applied from when it was recorded, preserving corrections and attribution. - Secure evidence management: Private object storage, document access controls, malware-scanning gates and cryptographic integrity checks. - Web applications and APIs: TypeScript-based services and organizational workspaces supporting structured onboarding and information exchange. - Identity and access management: Authentication, organizational membership, scoped permissions and audit records. Robotics and embodied AI are the application domain. The platform records software, AI-model and learned-behavior references where relevant; its documented foundation does not depend on training or operating an AI model.
Unique Characteristics: IDWorthy’s distinctive approach combines permanent machine identity with attributable operational evidence across manufacturers and organizations. Its principal differentiators are: - Identity continuity: Ownership transfers, software updates, battery replacement and maintenance do not automatically create a new machine identity. - Cross-manufacturer records: Operators can organize information around their equipment rather than relying exclusively on separate manufacturer portals. - Responsibility distinctions: Manufacturer, owner, operator, maintainer and software provider remain separate relationships. - Configuration-specific evidence: Claims and supporting records can be associated with the relevant machine, configuration and time. - Preserved corrections: Historical assertions remain attributable when information is corrected or superseded. - Controlled disclosure: Different participants can access appropriate information without exposing the full operational record. - Flexible delivery: Self-service software, assisted administrative services and API integration are intended to use the same underlying records. The platform organizes evidence for evaluation and decision-making. Registration or document submission does not itself establish safety, legal compliance or certification.
Sustainable Change: IDWorthy could help establish a common information foundation for industrial ecosystems in which machines, software and responsibility move between multiple organizations. For individual enterprises, continuous records could reduce repeated onboarding and improve access to maintenance and operational evidence. Across supply chains, the same approach could help manufacturers, integrators, operators and service providers exchange information using consistent identities and attributable records. For developing and middle-income economies, replication through local partners could help smaller enterprises adopt advanced equipment without having to build equivalent record infrastructure themselves. Assisted onboarding provides an entry point for organizations with limited technical capacity, while structured interfaces create a path toward deeper integration. Over time, preserved maintenance, component and transfer histories could support repair, refurbishment and secondary equipment markets. Authorized access to reliable machine records could also support future research and AI-assisted workflows. The proposed expansion path begins with focused professional-drone use cases, validates operational value, and then adapts the shared identity and evidence foundation to additional industrial robots and physical AI systems. Sustained impact would depend on partner participation, data quality, affordable delivery and demonstrated benefits in field pilots.

Historical financing raised by AT Worthy supported its broader business activities and is not presented as funding awarded specifically to IDWorthy. No externally funded field implementation is claimed in this submission.

Title: ATAWI-3A3 – AI-Enabled Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV)
Subtitle: An African-developed intelligent marine robotic platform for environmental monitoring, port operations and aquatic infrastructure inspection.
Problem Statement: Ports, coastal industries and environmental authorities in Africa face growing challenges in monitoring aquatic ecosystems, detecting pollution, inspecting submerged infrastructure and ensuring compliance with environmental protection requirements. Traditional water quality monitoring and maritime inspection operations often depend on crewed vessels, manual sampling, specialized equipment and costly field operations. These approaches can expose personnel to hazardous environments, limit monitoring frequency and make continuous or geographically extensive data collection difficult. In Cameroon, port operators face specific challenges related to ballast water management, unauthorized discharges, water pollution, sedimentation and the monitoring of sensitive aquatic environments. Access to locally developed marine robotic systems remains limited, while imported solutions can be expensive, difficult to adapt to local operating conditions and dependent on external technical support. There is therefore a need for affordable, modular and locally maintainable robotic platforms capable of collecting reliable environmental data, supporting maritime inspections and improving operational decision-making. ATAWI-3A3 addresses these challenges through an African-developed Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) integrating robotic navigation, environmental sensors, sonar, embedded software and AI-enabled data analysis. The solution aims to strengthen local technological capabilities while supporting smarter, safer and more sustainable management of ports, coastal waters and aquatic ecosystems.
Solution Overview: ATAWI-3A3 is an African-developed Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV) designed and developed by SPARTE ROBOTICS CLUSTER SARL in Cameroon. It is a modular marine robotic platform intended for environmental monitoring, port surveillance, aquatic inspection and data acquisition in coastal, inland water and industrial maritime environments. The solution combines a remotely operated and autonomous-capable surface vehicle, environmental sensing instruments, acoustic measurement systems, embedded electronics and dedicated software for mission management and data processing. 1. How the solution works ATAWI-3A3 operates as an unmanned surface platform that navigates across selected aquatic areas to collect environmental and operational data. Depending on mission requirements, the platform can carry different sensors and scientific instruments, enabling users to perform water quality measurements, bathymetric surveys and maritime infrastructure inspections. The collected data are acquired through onboard electronic systems and processed through ATAWI eSoft, Sparte Robotics' dedicated software environment for mission management and environmental data handling. The modular architecture allows the platform to be configured for different missions without redesigning the entire vehicle. 2. Main technical configuration The current ATAWI-3A3 prototype has the following characteristics: Platform type: Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV). Dimensions: Approximately 92 × 31 × 16.5 cm, excluding protective structures. Weight: Approximately 12 kg. Power system: 24 V lithium battery system, rated at 25 Ah. Operational endurance: Approximately 1–2 hours, depending on operating conditions and mission configuration. Navigation: Remote operation with autonomous navigation capabilities under development and integration. Communication and mission supervision: Remote control and onboard electronic systems. Software: ATAWI eSoft.
Solution Provider(s): SPARTE ROBOTICS CLUSTER SARL , Solution developer and lead technology provider; Cameroon-based robotics and applied AI company specializing in the design, development, integration and deployment of aerial, terrestrial and aquatic robotic systems, embedded electronics, intelligent sensing and robotics software. Sector: Robotics, Artificial Intelligence, Marine Technology and Industrial Automation. PORT AUTONOME DE KRIBI (PAK) – Technical and financial partner; Cameroon's deep-water port authority, providing operational insights and support for the development of solutions addressing port environmental monitoring, ballast water management, unauthorized discharges and smart port applications. Sector: Maritime Transport, Port Infrastructure, Logistics and Industrial Development. PAKAZUR / PAK AZURE – Port data and smart-port cooperation framework associated with the Port Autonome de Kribi, providing a context for exploring the integration of ATAWI environmental data into broader port digitalization and data valorization initiatives.
Implementation location(s): This is the most defensible classification because ATAWI-3A3 is no longer just a concept or laboratory prototype. It has: - Been developed as a functional marine robotic platform. - Been publicly presented on 27 February 2026 in Douala. - Undergone field tests in several aquatic environments along the Cameroonian coast. - Demonstrated environmental data collection and monitoring capabilities. The next stage is to consolidate operational performance and conduct structured deployments with port and environmental stakeholders.
Implementation timeline(s): Cameroon – Douala, Littoral Region. ATAWI-3A3 was developed by SPARTE ROBOTICS CLUSTER SARL in Cameroon and publicly presented in Douala on 27 February 2026 during the COCKTECH technology event. Field tests have been conducted in several aquatic environments along the Cameroonian coastline. The project is also connected to port environmental monitoring requirements identified through collaboration with the Port Autonome de Kribi (Kribi, Southern Region, Cameroon).
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3–6 months. ATAWI-3A3 has a modular architecture that allows adaptation to different aquatic environments and operational requirements. The deployment process includes: Initial assessment of local environmental and operational requirements. Identification of a port authority, research institution or environmental monitoring partner. Adaptation of sensor configurations and mission parameters. Integration of local positioning, communication and data-processing requirements. Operational testing and validation in representative aquatic environments. Training of local technical personnel and establishment of maintenance procedures. The estimated timeframe may vary depending on regulatory requirements, environmental conditions, communication infrastructure and the complexity of the required sensor configuration.
Desired impact: The primary objective of ATAWI-3A3 is to provide an accessible, locally developed and intelligent marine robotic platform that improves environmental monitoring, maritime inspection and operational decision-making in African aquatic and industrial environments. Specific objectives include: Improve the frequency, accessibility and efficiency of water quality monitoring through unmanned robotic platforms. Support port authorities in identifying potential pollution events, unauthorized discharges and environmental anomalies. Reduce the need to expose personnel to potentially hazardous or difficult-to-access aquatic environments. Facilitate bathymetric data collection and inspection of submerged or partially submerged infrastructure. Strengthen African capabilities in marine robotics, sensor integration, embedded software and AI. Develop locally adaptable technologies for sustainable port operations and aquatic ecosystem management.
Key technologies: ATAWI-3A3 integrates several complementary technologies: Marine Robotics and Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USV): An unmanned floating robotic platform for remote operation and autonomous-capable navigation. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: AI components for environmental data interpretation, anomaly detection, predictive analysis and mission optimization, with further development planned using field-collected datasets. Internet of Things (IoT): Connected environmental sensors and onboard electronics for data acquisition and transmission. Environmental Sensing Technologies: Multiparameter instruments measuring turbidity, pH, temperature, dissolved oxygen and electrical conductivity. Acoustic Sensing and Sonar: Mini Ping echosounder for depth measurements and bathymetric data acquisition. Embedded Systems and Electronics: Onboard processing units, electronic controllers, power management systems and sensor interfaces. Robotics Software and Data Processing: ATAWI eSoft, Sparte Robotics' software environment for mission management, sensor integration and environmental data handling. Navigation and Positioning Systems: Marine navigation, remote supervision and optional high-precision positioning equipment depending on mission requirements. Modular Engineering: A configurable architecture allowing different payloads, sensors and instruments to be integrated according to operational needs.
Unique Characteristics: ATAWI-3A3 introduces a locally developed approach to marine robotics and intelligent environmental monitoring, combining physical robotic systems, modular instrumentation and AI-enabled data processing. 1. African-developed Marine Robotics ATAWI-3A3 is engineered and integrated by a Cameroonian technology company. It demonstrates the ability of African engineering teams to develop specialized marine robotic systems rather than relying exclusively on imported turnkey equipment. 2. Modular and Mission-Adaptive Architecture The platform can accommodate different environmental sensors, acoustic instruments and mission-specific payloads. This enables a single robotic platform to support multiple applications, including water quality monitoring, bathymetry, port surveillance and aquatic infrastructure inspection. 3. Integration of Robotics, IoT and AI The solution combines an unmanned surface vehicle with multiparameter sensors, embedded electronics, dedicated software and AI components. This creates a pathway from physical environmental data collection towards intelligent data interpretation and operational decision support. 4. Contextualized Technology for African Environments ATAWI is designed around operational challenges identified in African maritime and port environments, particularly ballast water management, unauthorized discharges, water quality monitoring and the inspection of aquatic infrastructure. Its development approach prioritizes local technical support, adaptability, maintainability and progressive technology improvement. 5. Multi-Application Industrial Platform Rather than addressing a single monitoring task, ATAWI provides a configurable marine robotics architecture with applications across port logistics, environmental management, maritime infrastructure, research and industrial inspection. 6. Local Data and AI Development The solution creates opportunities to generate environmental datasets from African aquatic environments. These locally collected datasets can support the development and validation of AI models better adapted to regional environmental conditions. 7. Technology Transfer and Local Value Creation ATAWI creates opportunities for collaboration with international robotics manufacturers, sensor providers, research institutions and industrial stakeholders while strengthening local capabilities in integration, software, maintenance and future manufacturing. Its long-term differentiation lies in combining locally engineered marine robotics with contextualized environmental intelligence and an adaptable industrial deployment model.
Sustainable Change: ATAWI-3A3 has the potential to contribute to the transformation of environmental monitoring and marine industrial operations in Africa by introducing locally developed robotic technologies into sectors traditionally dependent on conventional inspection and data collection methods. 1. Building African Marine Robotics Capabilities The project demonstrates that African technology companies can develop, integrate and maintain advanced marine robotic systems. Its continued development will contribute to local engineering expertise, technical employment and the emergence of a regional marine robotics industry. 2. Improving Environmental Governance and Monitoring By facilitating more accessible and repeatable water monitoring operations, ATAWI can help port authorities, environmental agencies and research institutions obtain additional information about aquatic ecosystems and potential pollution events. The availability of more frequent and geographically distributed measurements can support more informed environmental management and monitoring decisions. 3. Strengthening Smart Port Development ATAWI can become part of broader smart port ecosystems through the integration of environmental measurements, bathymetric data and inspection information into digital port management and monitoring systems. Its potential integration with port data platforms can support the transition towards more intelligent and environmentally responsible maritime infrastructure. 4. Developing Locally Relevant Environmental AI One of the major long-term opportunities is the creation of localized environmental datasets from African coastal and inland water environments. These datasets can support the development of AI models capable of identifying abnormal environmental patterns, improving monitoring operations and assisting decision-making under different regional conditions. 5. Reducing Dependence on Imported Turnkey Solutions Through local engineering, modular design, maintenance and software development, ATAWI can strengthen technological sovereignty and reduce dependence on external service providers for selected marine monitoring applications. 6. Enabling Regional Replication The solution's modular architecture and adaptable deployment methodology make it suitable for replication in other African coastal and inland water environments, subject to local operational and regulatory requirements. Potential applications extend to port authorities, maritime operators, environmental agencies, hydrographic institutions, industrial facilities and research organizations. 7. Supporting Sustainable Blue Economy Development By connecting marine robotics, environmental intelligence and industrial applications, ATAWI can contribute to responsible management of aquatic resources, improved environmental oversight and more sustainable development of Africa's maritime economy. Ultimately, ATAWI seeks to establish a replicable African marine robotics model that combines local engineering, environmental intelligence, international technology cooperation and industrial deployment. Its ambition is not only to introduce a new robotic product, but also to strengthen Africa's capacity to design, develop, operate and maintain intelligent technologies for its own industrial and environmental priorities.
Funding Sources: ATAWI-3A3 has been developed through a combination of internal company resources, engineering contributions and strategic institutional support. 1. SPARTE ROBOTICS – Internal Development Resources SPARTE ROBOTICS CLUSTER SARL has contributed its own technical and organizational resources to the development of ATAWI-3A3, including engineering expertise, software development, mechanical and electronic integration, prototyping, testing and project coordination. 2. This collaboration emerged from discussions regarding operational challenges in port environmental management, particularly ballast water monitoring, unauthorized discharges and the need for more accessible environmental inspection technologies. Title: Melorin: AI-Powered Flight Digital Twin for Sustainable Aviation
Subtitle: AI-driven flight simulation and operational decision support to identify fuel-efficiency opportunities, improve airline operations, and support aviation emissions management.
Problem Statement: Airlines face increasing pressure to reduce fuel consumption, operating costs, and greenhouse gas emissions while maintaining safety, reliability, and operational efficiency. However, relevant information is often fragmented across flight operations, weather, route and airspace data, aircraft performance, and environmental reporting systems. Limited integration of these data sources makes it difficult to compare operational alternatives, anticipate their consequences, and consistently identify actionable fuel-efficiency opportunities. These challenges can be particularly significant for airlines in developing and middle-income economies, where access to advanced analytics and decision-support capabilities may be constrained by cost, technical capacity, and fragmented digital infrastructure. Melorin addresses this gap by translating aviation and environmental data into explainable, scenario-based operational insights and recommendations.
Solution Overview: Airlines face increasing pressure to reduce fuel consumption, operating costs, and greenhouse gas emissions while maintaining safety, reliability, and operational efficiency. However, relevant information is often fragmented across flight operations, weather, route and airspace data, aircraft performance, and environmental reporting systems. Limited integration of these data sources makes it difficult to compare operational alternatives, anticipate their consequences, and consistently identify actionable fuel-efficiency opportunities. These challenges can be particularly significant for airlines in developing and middle-income economies, where access to advanced analytics and decision-support capabilities may be constrained by cost, technical capacity, and fragmented digital infrastructure. Melorin addresses this gap by translating aviation and environmental data into explainable, scenario-based operational insights and recommendations.
Solution Provider(s): No formal implementation partners have been confirmed to date. Melorin is seeking airline pilot partners and potential collaborators in aviation operations, environmental data, AI, and sustainability. Potential data sources and technology platforms are not presented as formal partners.
Implementation timeline(s): N/A — No completed external implementation period to report.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 3–6 months from pilot agreement and access to the required data, depending on data quality and availability, integration requirements, validation needs, and the airline partner's operational and compliance processes.
Desired impact: Melorin's primary objective is to help airlines make more informed operational decisions by combining aviation data, AI-assisted analysis, and digital-twin-based scenario evaluation. The solution aims to: • Identify potential opportunities to reduce fuel consumption and associated greenhouse gas emissions. • Improve the consistency and explainability of operational decision-making by comparing alternative scenarios. • Help airlines evaluate the operational, environmental, and economic trade-offs of potential actions. • Support more efficient organization of aviation emissions data and CORSIA-related reporting workflows. • Make advanced operational analytics more accessible to airlines in developing and middle-income economies. Expected impact will be evaluated through a pilot using an agreed baseline and representative flight or operational data. Proposed key performance indicators include fuel consumption per flight or distance-adjusted unit, estimated CO₂ emissions, potential fuel and operating-cost savings, quality of scenario predictions, recommendation acceptance, and time required to prepare relevant emissions data. Where sufficient data are available, the pilot will compare modeled opportunities with observed or independently validated outcomes, accounting for weather, route, aircraft, payload, and other relevant operating conditions. No independently validated fuel savings, greenhouse-gas reductions, cost savings, or job-creation figures are claimed at this stage. Quantified impact will be reported only when supported by pilot evidence and a documented measurement methodology.
Key technologies: • Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning: data analysis, predictive modeling, and decision-support capabilities. • Digital Twins: a developing Flight Digital Twin concept for representing flight and operational conditions and comparing scenarios. • Aviation and Environmental Data Integration: pipelines for processing relevant flight, weather, route, airspace, and environmental data. • Weather and Geospatial Intelligence: use of suitable weather and environmental datasets, including potential integration with Copernicus and ERA5. • Explainable, Rule-Based Decision Support: configurable operational rules, constraints, and recommendation checks to support interpretable outputs. • Environmental and Carbon Data Management: data organization and workflow support for aviation emissions monitoring and CORSIA-related reporting. • Software Engineering and APIs: Python-based services, FastAPI, React, and database technologies to support application development and integration. The technology stack and data integrations are being developed and refined as the solution progresses toward airline pilot validation. The solution is designed to support human decision-making rather than autonomous flight control.
Unique Characteristics: Melorin's main differentiator is its focus on operational decisions rather than simply displaying aviation data or reporting historical emissions. First, its Flight Digital Twin approach is designed to combine flight operations, weather, route and airspace conditions, and environmental information within a common decision-support workflow. This enables users to explore alternative scenarios and assess their potential consequences before acting. Second, the solution connects sustainability objectives with operational and economic considerations. Fuel-efficiency analysis and emissions-related data workflows are intended to complement each other, helping airlines consider environmental performance alongside operational feasibility and cost. Third, Melorin emphasizes explainable, human-reviewed recommendations. Its intended workflow allows airline personnel to examine the assumptions, constraints, and potential trade-offs behind a recommendation rather than relying solely on an opaque AI output. Fourth, the proposed deployment model is modular and non-invasive. Initial use cases can be scoped around available data and a specific operational question, without requiring immediate replacement of existing airline systems. Finally, the solution is being designed with the needs of airlines in developing and middle-income economies in mind. A focused pilot can establish the evidence needed to assess technical feasibility, practical value, and the requirements for wider adoption. These features describe Melorin's design direction and intended differentiation. Their performance and comparative advantages remain subject to pilot validation.
Sustainable Change: Melorin could contribute to broader industrial transformation by making data-driven operational decision support more accessible within the aviation sector, including in developing and middle-income economies. At the airline level, the solution could help move operational analysis from fragmented, retrospective reporting toward repeatable scenario evaluation and evidence-based decision-making. If validated, this approach could help organizations identify and prioritize fuel-efficiency opportunities while maintaining human oversight and operational constraints. At the ecosystem level, a modular approach to aviation data integration could encourage more effective use of existing digital infrastructure and environmental data resources. Documented pilot methodologies, measurable performance indicators, and reusable integration patterns could help other airlines assess whether similar approaches are suitable for their operating environments. At the sustainability level, integrating operational analysis with emissions data workflows could improve the connection between day-to-day operational decisions and longer-term climate objectives. Potential benefits include more consistent measurement, better identification of improvement opportunities, and stronger evidence for sustainability initiatives. Melorin's approach could also support digital capability development by giving smaller airlines and aviation organizations a practical pathway to evaluate AI-enabled decision support without immediately undertaking a large-scale systems transformation. The intended pathway to systemic change is staged: validate a focused use case with an airline partner, document results and limitations, refine the solution based on evidence, and then explore replication across aircraft types, operational contexts, and geographic markets. These are potential follow-on effects, not yet demonstrated sector-wide outcomes. Replication and scale-up would depend on pilot results, data access, regulatory requirements, commercial viability, and the willingness of aviation stakeholders to adopt the approach.
Funding Sources: Melorin has been developed through founder-led efforts and in-kind contributions, including time invested in product development, aviation-domain research, software engineering, and the development of AI-enabled operational decision-support capabilities. No external institutional funding or investment is being claimed for the solution at this stage.
Testimonials and Endorsements: No formal customer testimonials or independent endorsements are available at this stage. Melorin is preparing for initial airline pilot engagement and is seeking aviation-sector partners to validate the solution's technical feasibility and operational value.

Title: DiagNXT: AI-Powered Workforce Intelligence for Resilient Industry
Subtitle: Transforms fragmented occupational health data into actionable workforce intelligence, enabling preventive risk management, healthier workplaces, and more resilient industrial operations.
Problem Statement: Industrial employers often rely on periodic medical examinations, fragmented health records, disconnected occupational health systems, and manual reporting. These limitations make it difficult to identify emerging workforce health patterns, detect preventable risks early, evaluate interventions, and make evidence-based decisions. Data fragmentation, inconsistent terminology, limited interoperability, and concerns about sensitive employee health information further restrict the use of AI. DiagNXT addresses these gaps by transforming routine occupational health data into structured, contextual intelligence while supporting privacy, human oversight, and data-sovereign deployment.
Solution Overview: DiagNXT is an AI-native healthcare intelligence platform developed by VectoRise Global Private Limited. Its Occupational Health Intelligence application transforms fragmented occupational health records and routine workforce health data into structured, longitudinal intelligence for industrial employers and occupational health teams. How it works 1. Data integration: Ingests available structured and semi-structured health records from occupational health systems, medical examinations, and compatible enterprise data sources. 2. Standardisation and contextualisation: Applies healthcare terminology processing, medical coding, data normalisation, and contextual mapping to improve consistency across heterogeneous records. 3. Longitudinal intelligence: Links relevant records over time, where permitted, to build a more coherent view of workforce health patterns rather than treating each examination as an isolated event. 4. AI-powered analysis: Analyses available data to identify relevant trends, potential health risks, missing information, and patterns requiring review by authorised occupational health professionals. 5. Decision support: Presents structured insights and relevant indicators to support preventive workplace health programmes, occupational health planning, and evidence-informed resource allocation. Medical and employment-related decisions remain with authorised human decision-makers. 6. Title: ByLoop: AI Discovery and Matching of Industrial By-Products
Subtitle: AI turns plant process descriptions into structured by-product profiles and connects them with nearby buyers, reducing waste and raw material use.
Problem Statement: Manufacturing plants generate large volumes of secondary outputs, such as scrap, residues, excess heat, liquids, and gases, many of which have real economic value for other businesses. Most of this value is lost because plants don’t know which by-products their processes generate, have no simple way to present and exchange them, and rely on consultants, brokers, or rigid public programs. The bottleneck is not demand but knowledge, coordination, and simplicity. As a result, reusable materials are discarded as waste.
Solution Overview: ByLoop is a B2B software-as-a-service platform. Users describe their production process in plain language, and ByLoop’s AI extracts potential by-products and structures them into standardized material profiles. Each profile is enriched with material properties, common reuse cases, and quality considerations, building a shared industrial knowledge base. By-products are then matched with interested buyers: locally for low-value, high-volume flows, and regionally or internationally for high-value materials. A lightweight interface lets companies list materials, initiate contact, and coordinate exchanges at a high level. Logistics and contracts remain flexible and are handled company-to-company. Methodologies: AI-assisted extraction of by-products from process descriptions, structured material profiling, and matching based on material type, location, and industry compatibility. Technologies: AI-based extraction, a structured materials database, and a web application. Partnerships and collaboration models: The business model is a subscription per plant or site, with pricing based on the number of processes and by-products managed, access to the intelligence database, and matching reach.
Solution Provider(s): Currently in customer discovery: EcoTashira, Boratas Machinery, Naftal, Intern2Founder Venture Studio.
Implementation location(s): Algeria
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 4 weeks
Desired impact: Objectives: Help manufacturers discover by-products their processes generate, connect them with reuse buyers, and make industrial by-product exchange simpler than existing consultant- or broker-led approaches. Expected impact: reduced raw material extraction, lower waste treatment and disposal costs, increased reuse across industries, and measurable reductions in industrial emissions.
Key technologies: AI-based extraction of by-products from plain-language process descriptions, a structured industrial materials database with reuse applications, a matching engine (material type, distance, industry compatibility), and a responsive web application with map-based search.
Unique Characteristics: ByLoop starts from the production process rather than from a list of known waste. This surfaces by-products plants don’t know they have. It builds a shared knowledge base with each new plant, offers a simple interface for engineers, uses a transparent match confidence score, and combines local matching for high-volume flows with broader reach for high-value materials.
Sustainable Change: Each plant onboarded adds to a shared by-product intelligence base, so matching improves as the network grows. The approach applies across sectors, including metal and machining, plastics, food processing, chemicals, and construction materials, and can be deployed at industrial parks. Over time, it could reduce dependence on consultants and public programs for industrial symbiosis, making reuse a routine part of plant operations.
Funding Sources: ByLoop is currently self-funded at the MVP stage. The first iteration of the MVP has been built to validate the core user flow and UX.
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: ByLoop reads a plant's process description and turns it into structured by-product profiles matched to nearby buyers. The discovery approach is the best idea in the submission; with no onboarded plant, the network effect it depends on is absent.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry; Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems

Title: L5: Industrial Process Monitoring and Fault Investigation
Subtitle: An open-source workspace combining industrial time-series analysis, nine anomaly detectors, process simulation, fault investigation, and evidence-based reporting.
Problem Statement: Industrial facilities generate large volumes of time-series data from sensors, controllers, and process equipment. However, turning these measurements into actionable fault investigations remains challenging. Operational data often come from multiple sources with different sampling intervals, engineering units, and data quality. Anomaly detection results may be disconnected from the original measurements, making it difficult to investigate potential causes or compare alternative methods. Industrial fault detection also faces challenges involving false alarms, detection delays, and sensitivity to training data. These issues can complicate operational decisions, particularly for smaller organizations with limited analytical resources. L5 addresses these challenges by connecting data preparation, statistical monitoring, comparative experiments, process simulation, and documented fault investigation within a unified, accessible environment.
Solution Overview: **L5 is an open-source industrial process monitoring and investigation platform designed to transform raw operational data into structured, evidence-based analysis.** The solution provides an integrated workflow: **Data Ingestion → Signal Processing → Anomaly Detection → Experimental Comparison → Incident Investigation → Reporting** **1. Industrial Data Integration** L5 imports industrial time-series data from CSV/TSV files and organizes them into persistent workspaces. Users can inspect multiple data sources, synchronize timestamps, identify missing observations, convert engineering units, resample measurements, and construct derived process variables. **2. Statistical and Machine-Learning-Based Monitoring** The platform implements nine anomaly detection methods, including PCA-Q, PCA-T², Dynamic PCA, EWMA, CUSUM, Robust Max-Z, and an experimental adaptive detector. Each method produces numerical monitoring scores, thresholds, abnormal intervals, and supporting diagnostic information. Different algorithms can be compared under consistent experimental settings. **3. Experimental Evaluation and Benchmarking** L5 supports reproducible comparisons across training configurations, algorithms, and test datasets. Its Tennessee Eastman Process benchmark covers 52 process variables, 20 industrial fault types, and nine detection methods. The expanded evaluation and normal-training stability study completed 2,340 successful experimental executions across 1,755 distinct configurations of training source, detector, and test run. The evaluation measures early detection, eventual alarm coverage, detection delay, and false-alarm burden. **4. Incident Investigation** Detected anomalies can be converted into persistent investigation records. Users can compare synchronized timelines, inspect original measurements, evaluate candidate explanations, organize supporting or contradictory evidence, and generate structured reports. **5. Process Simulation** Integrated TripLens and coupled-tank models allow users to simulate process faults, examine signal responses, and compare interventions. Simulation results can enter the same analysis workflow as imported datasets. **6. Technical Architecture** The frontend is implemented with React, TypeScript, and Vite. The computational backend uses Python, NumPy, and pandas, with SQLite providing persistent local data management. L5 operates locally and supports offline investigation and reporting. Its open-source MIT license enables inspection, adaptation, and reuse. **Partnership and Collaboration Model** L5 is currently an independently developed open-source project, with no formal organizational implementation partners. Its public repository, documented experiments, and reproducible research protocols provide a foundation for future collaboration with universities, industrial operators, research laboratories, and technology providers. Future pilots could integrate site-specific historical process data and adapt the existing monitoring and investigation workflow to local operational requirements. Project repository: https://github.com/dongxuelian2/L5
Solution Provider(s): None at present. L5 is independently developed and maintained as an open-source research project. Its developer is an undergraduate student at Hebei University of Technology, China. The university is an academic affiliation, not a formal implementation partner.
Implementation location(s): N/A — The solution has been developed and evaluated using simulation models and publicly available industrial benchmark datasets. No industrial-site deployment has been completed.
Implementation timeline(s): N/A — The software prototype was developed in 2026. Industrial deployment has not yet commenced.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 8–12 weeks for an initial pilot using historical industrial process data, including data integration, signal mapping, detector configuration, validation, and reporting. A pilot involving live operational integration may require approximately 3–6 months, depending on data access, existing industrial systems, cybersecurity requirements, and local implementation partners.
Desired impact: **Main Objectives** L5 aims to make industrial process monitoring and fault investigation more accessible, systematic, and reproducible. Its primary objectives are to: 1. Integrate industrial time-series data from multiple sources into a unified analytical environment. 2. Support early anomaly detection and transparent comparison of monitoring algorithms. 3. Connect detected anomalies with original measurements, investigation records, and evidence-based reports. 4. Reduce the technical barriers to industrial data analysis through an open-source, locally deployable platform. 5. Support reproducible research and practical experimentation in process monitoring. **Demonstrated Technical Results** L5 has been evaluated using the Tennessee Eastman Process benchmark, covering 52 process variables, 20 simulated industrial fault types, and nine anomaly detection methods. The expanded study and normal-training stability evaluation completed **2,340 successful experimental executions**, representing 1,755 distinct training-configuration, algorithm, and test-run combinations. Under fixed configuration A: - PCA-Q produced 51 eventual nominal detections across 60 fault events, including 19 within 30 minutes. - DPCA-Q produced 54 eventual nominal detections, including 20 within 30 minutes. - Both methods produced two alarm samples across 4,800 normal testing samples. The study also quantified substantial changes in false-alarm behavior across different normal-training configurations, demonstrating the importance of evaluating monitoring reliability under varying data conditions. **Expected Industrial Impact** Future applications could help industrial operators identify process abnormalities, investigate their causes, compare monitoring strategies, and improve the documentation of operational incidents. Potential longer-term benefits include reduced investigation effort, improved process reliability, and more efficient resource utilization. These operational and environmental benefits remain targets for future industrial pilots. Quantified energy savings, emissions reductions, and operational cost reductions have not yet been established through real-world deployment.
Key technologies: L5 combines statistical machine learning, industrial process monitoring, time-series data engineering, simulation, and interactive data visualization. **Statistical and Machine-Learning-Based Monitoring** - Principal Component Analysis (PCA), including Q-statistic and Hotelling's T² monitoring. - Dynamic PCA for temporal process monitoring. - Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA). - Page CUSUM and finite-window CUSUM. - Robust Max-Z and experimental adaptive monitoring. **Industrial Data Engineering** - Multisource time-series integration and synchronization. - Resampling, engineering-unit conversion, missing-data processing, and derived signal generation. - Persistent experiment records and reproducible analysis configurations. **Process Simulation** - TripLens process simulation with multiple fault scenarios. - Coupled-tank dynamic process modeling and intervention experiments. **Software Technologies** - Python, NumPy, and pandas for numerical computation. - React, TypeScript, and Vite for the interactive interface. - SQLite for persistent workspace and investigation data. - HTML, JSON, CSV, and browser-based PDF export for reporting and data exchange. The platform uses locally executable analytical methods and an open-source architecture designed for adaptation to different industrial datasets.
Unique Characteristics: **L5's central innovation is the integration of industrial anomaly detection, comparative experimentation, process simulation, and evidence-based investigation within a single persistent workspace.** Its distinguishing features include: **1. Complete Investigation Workflow** L5 connects raw sensor measurements, transformed datasets, anomaly detection results, investigation hypotheses, supporting evidence, and final reports. Users can move between analytical results and their underlying data without losing the investigative context. **2. Multi-Algorithm Evaluation** Nine monitoring methods are available within a shared experimental environment. Users can compare detection behavior, alarm timing, thresholds, and false-alarm burden across the same datasets. **3. Research-Backed Evaluation** The platform includes an extensive Tennessee Eastman Process evaluation covering 20 industrial faults and 2,340 successful experimental executions. The experiments investigate not only nominal detection rates but also detection delays, training-data sensitivity, and normal-background alarm behavior. **4. Integration of Simulation and Investigation** Process simulation models allow users to generate faults, study dynamic responses, compare interventions, and subsequently investigate the resulting data using the same analytical tools. **5. Persistent, Evidence-Based Analysis** Analysis configurations, results, incident timelines, hypotheses, and supporting observations can be saved and revisited. Standalone reports preserve the evidence and parameters associated with an investigation. **6. Accessible Open-Source Delivery** The MIT-licensed software runs locally using widely available technologies. Its modular components can be adapted to different industrial datasets and research environments. Together, these capabilities provide a reusable industrial analysis environment connecting algorithmic research with practical fault investigation.
Sustainable Change: L5 has the potential to support broader adoption of industrial data analytics by providing an accessible, extensible, and reproducible foundation for process monitoring and fault investigation. **1. Expanding Access to Industrial Analytics** As an open-source platform built on widely available software technologies, L5 can be adopted and adapted by research institutions, educational organizations, and industrial enterprises without requiring proprietary analytical licenses. This approach may be particularly relevant to smaller manufacturers and organizations with limited resources for specialized industrial analytics. **2. Supporting Replication Across Industries** L5 separates its general data-processing, monitoring, and investigation capabilities from specific process models and datasets. This architecture creates opportunities to adapt the platform to manufacturing, chemical processing, utilities, and other industries that generate multivariate operational data. **3. Enabling Research and Knowledge Transfer** Public source code, documented experimental protocols, and benchmark results can support collaboration between academic researchers, industrial engineers, and software developers. Additional datasets, monitoring algorithms, and process models could be incorporated through future contributions. **4. Strengthening Evidence-Based Operational Decisions** Combining anomaly detection with traceable investigation records can help organizations move toward more systematic evaluation of process abnormalities. The ability to compare multiple monitoring strategies and examine false-alarm behavior may improve how industrial monitoring systems are selected, validated, and maintained. **5. Building a Path Toward Sustainable Industrial Operations** Future industrial pilots could evaluate whether earlier fault detection and improved investigation workflows reduce unnecessary process interruptions, material losses, energy waste, or equipment-related inefficiencies. The next development stage will focus on expanding process coverage, integrating industrial datasets, and establishing collaborations for pilot evaluation. Through open-source distribution, reproducible research, and adaptable software components, L5 could contribute to a broader ecosystem of accessible industrial intelligence technologies.
Funding Sources: L5 has been independently developed and self-funded by its creator, an undergraduate student at Hebei University of Technology, China. Development has relied on personal computing resources, open-source software, and publicly available industrial research datasets. The project has not received external grants, venture capital investment, corporate sponsorship, or institutional funding. Development and research activities have been carried out independently.
Testimonials and Endorsements: N/A — No formal third-party testimonials or institutional endorsements have been obtained at this stage. The project's source code, technical documentation, and experimental findings are publicly accessible for independent evaluation: https://github.com/dongxuelian2/L5
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: L5 is an open-source workspace that takes industrial time series through anomaly detection, simulation and structured fault investigation. The engineering is solid and inspectable; with benchmark-only validation and no site, it scores on tooling.
