Title: EcoSan AI: Waste, Sanitation & Pollution Intelligence for Green, Resilient Industry
Subtitle: Satellite, climate and citizen data fused to detect, predict and prioritise waste, sanitation and industrial effluent hotspots for operators, utilities and regulators in Nairobi.
Problem Statement: Nairobi’s waste, sanitation and pollution-control industry works largely blind. Waste operators, sewerage utilities, recyclers and regulators learn about illegal dumping, blocked drains, sewer overflows and industrial effluent discharges only after residents complain or damage is done. The pressure is sharpest along the Nairobi River and the Industrial Area corridor, where manufacturing, informal settlements and stormwater drains meet. Untreated effluent and dumped waste degrade the river, block drainage and raise flood and disease risk downstream. Heavier rainfall linked to climate change turns these problems into floods within days. Monitoring today relies on periodic site inspections, manual sampling and complaints. Operators cannot see where risk is building, regulators cannot target inspections, and limited trucks, crews and enforcement budgets are spent reactively. Many operators are MSMEs that cannot afford the monitoring systems larger utilities elsewhere take for granted.
Solution Overview: EcoSan AI is a decision-intelligence platform for the waste, sanitation and pollution-control industry. It turns open Earth-observation data, climate records and citizen reports into a ranked, map-based action list for operators, utilities, recyclers and regulators. It runs a four-stage loop: 1. Detect: computer-vision models analyse Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery with geotagged citizen photos and reports to flag dumping, drainage and sanitation hotspots. An industrial effluent module, now in development, will flag suspected discharge points and pollution plumes along the Nairobi River and Industrial Area corridor using water-colour and turbidity indices from Sentinel-2, thermal anomalies from Landsat 8/9, and citizen reports. 2. Predict: forecasting models combine rainfall, flood history, elevation, drainage networks and land use to estimate where hotspots will emerge or worsen in the coming days and weeks. 3. Prioritise: a transparent risk index scores each grid cell by severity, exposure and urgency, giving each user a short ranked list instead of a whole city to triage. A gradient-boosted model with explainability (SHAP) is being developed against this baseline. 4. Direct intervention: the platform generates work orders for operators, inspection lists for regulators and map layers (GeoJSON), with a human sign-off before any action. Satellite and AI outputs flag suspected sites; field inspection and sampling confirm them. Methodologies and technologies: open satellite data (Copernicus Sentinel, Landsat), open rainfall data (CHIRPS and GPM), geospatial AI, time-series forecasting, a generative-AI layer (Google Gemini) for plain-language briefs and reports, and a cloud backend with a spatial database (PostGIS). Heavy processing runs in the cloud; field teams report and receive priorities on a phone, which suits low-connectivity settings. Partnership and collaboration model: IwazoLab builds and operates the platform and is developing it within the Kenya AI Accelerator Programme (Konza Technopolis Development Authority, the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy, and UNDP Kenya). Pilots will be co-designed with industry users and regulators, who provide ground truth and act on the outputs. Community-based organisations will collect verified field reports. Revenue comes from subscriptions/custom built installations for operators, utilities and regulators, with a free community-reporting tier.
Solution Provider(s): Kenya AI Accelerator Programme — Kenya’s national AI startup accelerator, delivered by Konza Technopolis Development Authority (KoTDA), the Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy (MICDE) and UNDP Kenya; public sector and international development; IwazoLab is a 2026 cohort startup in the Circular Economy & Environment track, receiving technical residencies, mentorship and access to government stakeholders
Duration to pilot in a new geography: About 4–5 months. Month 1: data-sharing agreements with the local authority or regulator, satellite and rainfall ingestion for the new area, and recruitment of a community field partner. Months 2–3: local calibration against field inspections and, for effluent, water-quality sampling. Months 4–5: live pilot with operators and regulators. Because the core inputs are open satellite and climate data, most of the system transfers without new infrastructure; local ground truth is the main lead-time item.
Desired impact: • Give waste operators, utilities and recyclers, many of them MSMEs, an affordable tool to put crews, trucks and maintenance where risk is highest. • Help regulators target inspections of suspected effluent discharge and illegal dumping along the Nairobi River and Industrial Area corridor. • Shift the sector from complaint-driven clean-up to predictive, evidence-based management that cuts pollution and builds flood and climate resilience. Current status: EcoSan AI is a working prototype covering the full detect, predict, prioritise and direct loop on demonstration data. It has not yet been deployed, so no impact has been demonstrated. IwazoLab was selected for the 2026 Kenya AI Accelerator Programme cohort. Pilot targets (first Nairobi pilot, to be measured against field observations): • At least 85% accuracy in detecting and prioritising waste and sanitation hotspots. • At least 30% reduction in response time from hotspot identification to intervention. • At least 20% reduction in unmanaged waste and sanitation hotspots in the pilot area. • For the effluent module, a baseline and target for confirmed effluent hotspots will be set with regulators in Month 1. Wider benefits we will track: less untreated effluent and dumped waste reaching the Nairobi River; fewer drainage-related floods (climate adaptation, SDG 13); less open burning of waste, cutting air pollution and greenhouse-gas emissions; better use of collection fleets; and paid field-reporting roles for community members.
Key technologies: • AI and machine learning: computer vision on satellite and citizen imagery; time-series forecasting; gradient-boosted risk scoring with SHAP explainability. • Earth observation: Copernicus Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery for land and water; Landsat 8/9 thermal imagery for effluent plumes; elevation and land-cover data. • Geospatial data: PostGIS spatial database, grid-based risk mapping and GeoJSON outputs for GIS tools. • Climate data: CHIRPS and GPM rainfall, flood history and drainage networks. • Generative AI: Google Gemini for plain-language briefs, inspection lists and work orders. • Cloud and mobile: cloud-hosted backend and API (Google Cloud) with a lightweight web and mobile interface for field teams.
Unique Characteristics: • Predictive, not just reporting: most tools record dumping after it is reported; EcoSan AI forecasts where risk will build, using rainfall and terrain, before it becomes a flood, outbreak or pollution event. • One platform for the whole value chain: operators, utilities, recyclers and regulators work from the same risk picture, each with outputs suited to their role. • Space plus street: free satellite data combined with verified citizen reports works where official monitoring is thin, as in informal settlements and along the river corridor. • Low-cost by design: open data and cloud processing make it affordable for MSME operators and county departments. • Responsible by design: a transparent baseline index, human sign-off before action, AI that flags suspected sites rather than issuing findings, privacy protection under Kenya’s Data Protection Act, and fairness checks so poorer areas are not over- or under-flagged. • Built in Africa, for Africa: designed for Kenyan institutions and data, within a national AI accelerator.
Sustainable Change: EcoSan AI can move Kenya’s waste, sanitation and pollution-control sector from complaint-driven response to data-driven planning and enforcement. Each pilot builds a reusable data pipeline and ground-truth dataset that lowers the cost of the next. Because the core inputs are open satellite and climate data, the method can be replicated across Kenya’s 47 counties and in other African river basins and industrial zones with modest local calibration. Shared risk maps give operators and regulators a common evidence base, which can inform drainage and treatment investment, waste-collection contracts, effluent-licence compliance and climate-adaptation plans. The same evidence can help operators and counties show measurable risk reduction to climate funds and development partners. Training county staff, operators and community reporters builds lasting local AI and data skills.
Funding Sources: EcoSan AI has been self-funded by IwazoLab Solutions Limited, through founder time and company resources. The Kenya AI Accelerator Programme provides in-kind support through technical residencies, compute credits and mentorship. A five-month single-settlement pilot budget is yet to be decided for which IwazoLab is seeking funding.
Testimonials and Endorsements: Selected as a 2026 cohort startup of the Kenya AI Accelerator Programme (Konza Technopolis Development Authority, MICDE and UNDP Kenya), Circular Economy & Environment track.
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: EcoSan AI ranks waste, sanitation and effluent hotspots in Nairobi from satellite, climate and citizen data to direct crews and inspections. The data design is strong; with no validation and no user, it remains a well-argued prototype.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry

Title: SkillPedigree: origin and licence evidence for AI-agent components
Subtitle: An offline tool that shows where a copied AI-agent component came from, whether it was changed, and what licence it declares. Where the proof is missing, it says so.
Problem Statement: Small firms now build AI agents from free parts. A "skill" or plugin is copied from a public registry, changed a little, and shipped inside a product or a client job. Most firms cannot say where that part came from, who changed it, or what licence it carries. This is a supply-chain gap, and it is growing. AI makes these parts cheap to copy. It does not make them cheaper to check. The gap hurts small manufacturers and software suppliers most. They have no legal or compliance staff. Many work with weak or costly internet. Yet their buyers, and rules such as the EU AI Act and Cyber Resilience Act, increasingly expect them to know what is inside their digital products. The records that exist are not enough on their own. In a public set of 19 agent skills, 17 put a pointer such as "see LICENSE.txt" in the licence field instead of a licence name. Two had no licence field at all. A firm that trusts that field alone can ship a part it has no right to ship.
Solution Overview: SkillPedigree checks one AI-agent component and answers three questions. 1. What does the record claim? Install tools write the source, version and a content fingerprint into the component. We read these as claims, not facts. 2. What does the content actually match? We fingerprint the folder the same way Git does. Then we compare it with each known source. 3. Is the origin really known? Only when the evidence proves it. If it does not, the answer is "not determined", with the reason. It reports the declared licence, the licence file and the source licence side by side. It never guesses a licence from similarity. A person makes that decision. How it works. It is a small Python tool with no outside libraries. It needs no network and no cloud account. It runs on an ordinary laptop. That matters where connectivity is limited or data must stay on site. Methods. Content fingerprints, comparison against pinned sources, and fixed decision rules. We wrote the rules before scoring any case, so results cannot shape the method. The tool was built and tested on our own governed multi-agent engineering platform. Stage. It is a tested prototype. It is not yet a product and has no users. We are honest about its limits: the similarity check is basic, and it knows only four licence types so far. Partnerships. We have no partners yet. We are looking for one pilot partner: an industry association, a quality-infrastructure or standards body, a technology centre, or a UN Centre of Excellence that supports small firms. Together we would run a small pilot on real components that their member firms use.
Solution Provider(s): None yet. SkillPedigree is a founder-led prototype from Hernani Holding B.V. (the Netherlands). We are seeking a first pilot partner, such as an industry association, standards or quality-infrastructure body, or technology centre that supports MSMEs.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: About 6 to 8 weeks after a pilot partner agrees. The tool runs offline on a laptop, so no cloud set-up is needed. Most of the time goes into choosing real components and agreeing the test cases.
Desired impact: Objective. Give a small firm a fast, cheap answer to one question: which of the AI components we ship can we prove the origin and licence of? What is measured so far (prototype, 26 October 2026, our own tests, not externally validated): - The folder fingerprint matched Git exactly for 19 of 19 public agent skills. - A real installed skill was confirmed against its source. An edited copy was flagged as modified. A false claim naming another source was flagged as contradicted. With no source available, the claim was reported as unverifiable, not as false. - 16 written test cases and 34 automated tests pass. Expected impact (planned, not yet shown). In a pilot, we will measure two things: how many components a firm can clear in an hour, and how many unclear licences the check finds that the firm did not know about. We do not yet claim energy, emissions or job figures. We will report the pilot results, including where the method is wrong.
Key technologies: - Content fingerprinting compatible with Git, so any public repository can be checked against. - Reading of the source records that AI-agent install tools already write. - Fixed, written decision rules with a "not determined" outcome. - Licence detection from declared fields, licence files and SPDX identifiers. - Plain Python, offline, with no outside libraries. The tool governs AI components. It does not use a machine-learning model to make its decision today. That is on purpose: a provenance decision must be repeatable and explainable. A learned similarity check is a possible later step, kept separate from the decision rules.
Unique Characteristics: It separates three things that are usually mixed up. A recorded claim is what a file says about its source. Observed identity is what a direct comparison shows. Established origin is only what both support together. It says "not determined" instead of guessing. Most tools give an answer every time. Ours reports what it can prove and what it cannot. A missing proof is a result. It never turns similarity into a licence duty. A content match is not a licence. A person decides that. It works offline and costs almost nothing to run. No account, no cloud and no network. That suits small firms with weak connectivity or strict data rules. It is built for AI-agent components. Software bill-of-materials tools track libraries. Agent skills and plugins are copied as loose folders and slip past them.
Sustainable Change: AI agents are spreading into small firms through free, copied components. If nobody can check those parts, trust in AI supply chains will rest on claims alone. SkillPedigree could help in three ways: 1. A shared evidence format. Its outputs could become a simple, open record that a supplier hands to a buyer, much like a test certificate. 2. Use by intermediaries. Industry associations, technology centres and quality-infrastructure bodies could run it for many member firms at once. One pilot partner can reach many MSMEs. 3. Readiness for rules. Firms that export digital products will meet more questions about what is inside them. A cheap check now lowers the cost of answering later. The first step is small: one pilot with one partner, on real components, with results published.
Funding Sources: Self-funded by Hernani Holding B.V. No grant has funded SkillPedigree to date.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems
Summary: SkillPedigree checks where an AI agent component came from, whether it was altered and what licence it carries, and says so when the evidence is insufficient. The design is rigorous; with no demonstration and no user, it scores 38.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems

Title: Accordock – AI-Powered Freight Invoice Verification and Trade Intelligence
Subtitle: An AI-powered platform helping importers identify freight quotation and invoice discrepancies, improve financial control, and strengthen transparency across international supply chains.
Problem Statement: International freight transactions involve multiple quotations, amendments, emails, supporting documents, currencies, units, and final invoices. Importers frequently struggle to reconcile these documents accurately before approving payments. Discrepancies such as unexpected charges, inconsistent rates, currency differences, unit mismatches, and outdated quotation versions can go undetected because verification is fragmented across PDFs, spreadsheets, emails, and manual workflows. This creates operational inefficiencies, financial exposure, limited auditability, and information asymmetry between importers and logistics service providers. These challenges are particularly significant for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which often lack dedicated freight audit teams or sophisticated financial control systems.
Solution Overview: Accordock is an AI-powered freight invoice verification platform designed to help importers identify and resolve discrepancies between freight quotations, contractual amendments, supporting documents, and final freight invoices before approving payment. The platform processes freight-related documents, extracts relevant commercial information, and compares invoice line items against the applicable quotation terms and subsequent amendments. It identifies potential discrepancies involving charges, amounts, currencies, units, and inconsistencies between document versions. Rather than simply extracting information, Accordock aims to establish traceability between identified discrepancies and their original supporting documents. This enables finance and operations teams to understand why a particular charge has been flagged and review the relevant evidence before making payment decisions. **Methodologies and technologies** - AI-assisted document processing and information extraction. - Structured comparison of freight quotations, amendments, and invoices. - Rule-based and contextual discrepancy identification. - Document version and evidence tracking. - Human-in-the-loop review, with payment approval remaining under the customer's control. The platform is being developed as a digital SaaS solution, with an emphasis on practical integration into existing importer workflows. **Partnerships and collaboration models** Accordock's intended collaboration model includes importers, exporters, freight forwarders, logistics providers, trade associations, and technology ecosystem partners. These collaborations can support access to real-world document workflows, pilot deployments, product validation, and eventual integration with existing logistics and financial systems. The solution is currently undergoing early pilot activity in Dubai and Ethiopia, with the ambition to support international trade workflows across multiple markets.
Solution Provider(s): No formal institutional or commercial technology partnerships are currently being declared. Accordock is pursuing collaboration opportunities with importers, exporters, freight forwarders, logistics providers, and trade ecosystem organizations to support pilot validation and market development.
Implementation location(s): Dubai, United Arab Emirates, and Ethiopia (early pilot activity).
Implementation timeline(s): 2026 – Early pilot and product validation activities.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 8–12 weeks, depending on access to representative freight documentation, local workflow requirements, customer onboarding, and the availability of pilot partners. Initial deployment would involve workflow assessment, document and process configuration, testing against representative shipment records, and validation with participating businesses.
Desired impact: The primary objective of Accordock is to improve financial transparency, operational efficiency, and accountability in international freight transactions through AI-assisted document verification. Its main objectives are: 1. Reduce the manual effort required to reconcile freight quotations, amendments, and final invoices. 2. Help businesses identify unexpected charges, inconsistent commercial terms, and document discrepancies before payment approval. 3. Improve the traceability and auditability of freight-related financial decisions. 4. Give SMEs access to more structured freight verification capabilities without requiring large internal audit teams. 5. Support more transparent and resilient international trade relationships. **Expected impact** Accordock aims to reduce time spent on manual document reconciliation, improve the identification of potential billing discrepancies, and strengthen financial controls across freight transactions. Its expected impact includes fewer overlooked discrepancies, better-informed payment decisions, improved operational productivity, and greater transparency between importers and logistics providers. The solution is still at an early implementation stage. Quantified improvements in financial savings, discrepancy detection accuracy, emissions reduction, and customer productivity have not yet been independently established. These indicators will be measured through pilot deployments.
Key technologies: - Artificial Intelligence (AI) - Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) - Machine Learning-assisted document understanding - Natural Language Processing (NLP) - Optical Character Recognition (OCR) - Structured data extraction and normalization - Rule-based discrepancy detection - Document comparison and version tracking - Cloud-based SaaS architecture - Human-in-the-loop verification and review workflows
Unique Characteristics: Accordock's key differentiation is its focus on verifying the commercial consistency of freight transactions rather than simply digitizing invoices or extracting information from documents. The platform is designed to connect multiple documents belonging to the same shipment, including original quotations, subsequent amendments, and final invoices, to establish which commercial terms should be used during verification. Its distinguishing features include: **1. Cross-document verification:** Compares freight invoices against quotations and amendments instead of treating each invoice as an isolated document. **2. Context-aware discrepancy identification:** Identifies potential inconsistencies involving charges, currencies, units, amounts, and document versions. **3. Evidence-linked findings:** Connects flagged discrepancies to the relevant source documentation, allowing users to investigate and understand the basis of each finding. **4. Human-controlled financial decisions:** Supports finance and operations teams without removing human oversight or transferring payment approval authority to automated systems. **5. SME-oriented accessibility:** Provides a focused verification workflow through a SaaS model, potentially making more sophisticated freight financial controls accessible to businesses that cannot maintain dedicated audit departments. The innovation lies in combining document intelligence, commercial-term comparison, and evidence-based verification within a workflow specifically designed for international freight transactions.
Sustainable Change: Accordock has the potential to contribute to broader digital transformation in international trade by addressing an important but often overlooked part of the supply chain: the verification of freight charges and commercial documentation. Today, many businesses still depend on fragmented communication channels and manual document reconciliation to verify freight invoices. Accordock aims to introduce a more structured, traceable, and scalable approach. **Potential systemic contributions include:** 1. **Greater financial transparency:** Encouraging more consistent verification of freight charges and commercial terms, helping reduce information asymmetry between importers and logistics providers. 2. **SME digital inclusion:** Making AI-assisted financial verification more accessible to smaller businesses, particularly in emerging markets where advanced logistics technology adoption remains uneven. 3. **Stronger international trade infrastructure:** Establishing more standardized digital workflows for comparing freight quotations, amendments, and invoices across different countries, currencies, and logistics providers. 4. **Cross-border scalability:** Developing a platform that can be adapted to different trade corridors, regulatory environments, document formats, and commercial practices. 5. **Improved industry accountability:** Creating more traceable documentation and evidence-based review processes that can support stronger financial governance throughout freight transactions. As adoption expands, Accordock could evolve from an individual business verification tool into an enabling layer within the wider digital trade ecosystem, supporting more transparent, efficient, and resilient international supply chains.
Funding Sources: Accordock has been developed through founder-led, bootstrapped efforts, with no institutional investment or external grant funding currently declared. Product development and early validation activities have been supported through founder contributions and independent execution.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access
Summary: Accordock checks freight invoices against quotations, amendments and supporting documents to surface discrepancies before payment. The use case is financially compelling; with no demonstration and no named user, it scores 41.

Title: Sabixa: AI Proof-of-Skill Passport for Africa’s Entry-Level Hiring
Subtitle: Candidates complete real customer-support tasks, AI scores the work against employer rubrics, and SMEs get ranked evidence instead of CVs. Low scorers get a path to improve.
Problem Statement: Young Africans are not short of certificates. They are short of trusted proof. ILO data shows 20.4% of young people globally were NEET in 2023, and a 10-country African study found 56.9% of employed youth undereducated and 28.9% underskilled. More than 70% of jobs in emerging economies are informal, so hiring runs on referrals and trust rather than paper credentials. CVs show wording and past titles, not tone, judgement or ownership. SMEs and startups cannot afford weeks of screening, and a bad customer-support hire shows up fast as refunds, churn and angry customers. Candidates who are rejected usually hear nothing and have no idea what to fix.
Solution Overview: Sabixa starts with one wedge: entry-level customer support hiring for African SMEs and startups. How it works: 1. The employer describes the hiring need, either by pasting a rough job description or answering short intake questions. 2. AI turns that need into a skill map and a three-task assessment pack (delayed delivery complaint, refund escalation, support ticket summary). The employer can edit the tasks and weights. 3. Candidates complete the tasks on their phones in 10 to 15 minutes each, in a WhatsApp-style format. 4. AI scores each response against a visible rubric. Every score comes with a reason, quoted evidence from the candidate’s own words, and a confidence band. 5. Each candidate gets a skill passport showing strengths, gaps and a work-sample preview. 6. The employer sees a ranked shortlist with evidence detail and a recommended action: interview, trial task, talent pool, or improve first. 7. Candidates below the benchmark get a specific improvement route and a retry task. Methodology: Candidates need 70 or above overall with no critical competency below 60. Low-confidence scores and scores within 5 points of the threshold go to human review. The employer always makes the final hiring decision. Scoring ignores name, school, gender, age, tribe, religion, location and disability, and raw AI outputs are logged for audit. Technology: Open-source models (Qwen3 8B and DeepSeek-R1 8B) run through Ollama, with Nomic Embed for matching. A deterministic fallback evaluator keeps the demo stable, and all outputs are validated as structured JSON. Collaboration model: Employers co-design the rubrics. Training providers and community programme leads sponsor cohort assessments and use the passports to show job readiness.
Solution Provider(s): None for now
Duration to pilot in a new geography: About 6 to 8 weeks. This covers adapting the task scenarios and language to the local market, calibrating the rubrics with local employers, and running a first pilot with around 15 candidates and 10 employers. This figure is my estimate, so change it if your team has a different number.
Desired impact: Objectives: Replace CV guesswork with task evidence in entry-level hiring. Cut screening time and cost for SMEs. Give every candidate a fair, explained score and a route to improve. Pilot targets (Lagos and Abuja). These are targets, not results yet: 70% task completion 60% of employers saying the passport is more useful than a CV alone 30% faster screening At least 10 candidates receiving an interview, trial task or talent-pool invite Disputes below 15% of evaluations 40% of candidates retrying after receiving feedback, with an 8-point average improvement Early prototype feedback from candidates, employers and trainers supported the concept: real tasks were trusted more than CV claims.
Key technologies: AI for competency mapping, task generation, rubric-based scoring, ranking and improvement planning Open-source language models (Qwen3 8B, DeepSeek-R1 8B) running locally through Ollama Embedding models (Nomic Embed Text) to match hiring needs, tasks and improvement routes Structured JSON validation and audit logging A mobile-first web interface built for WhatsApp-style work
Unique Characteristics: It is built for low-trust, high-informality labour markets, not copied from a Western job board. Candidates do real work samples, and employers see the evidence behind every score. Scoring is transparent: visible rubrics, quoted evidence, confidence bands and a human decision point. It scores the work, not the person, with a published list of factors the AI must ignore. Candidates who miss the benchmark get a repair path instead of silence. Open-source models running locally keep costs low and make deployment realistic for African SMEs. Employers start from a hiring need, not a job title.
Sustainable Change: Customer support is the first step because it is common across ecommerce, logistics, fintech, health services and NGOs. The same model extends to sales support, admin, programme support and field operations. As more employers use the passports, a shared and portable proof layer builds up that does not depend on referrals or elite schools, so candidates outside informal networks get a fairer way in. Training providers can use the same assessments to close the loop with employer demand and adjust their curricula. The tasks and rubrics can be localised for other African labour markets, and the open-source stack keeps replication cheap. One honest note on fit: the call is industrial, and Sabixa is a skills and hiring tool. The answers above frame it as a skills and MSME enabler for the industrial ecosystem, which is the strongest honest angle. I’d keep it that way rather than stretch it.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access
Summary: Sabixa scores real customer-support tasks against employer rubrics and returns ranked evidence instead of CVs. The hiring wedge is well chosen and the scoring is transparent; with no pilot and no media, it remains a design.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access; Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems

Name of your organization: Life Analytics株式会社 (LifeAnalytics Co., Ltd.)
Title: IAS: Connecting Food R&D Data for AI-Assisted Decisions
Subtitle: A research workspace connecting laboratory images, omics and analysis records to help food-sector R&D teams turn existing data into traceable, researcher-reviewed decisions.
Problem Statement: Food-sector research and development generates images, molecular measurements and experimental records that often need to be interpreted together. When these data remain in separate tools, teams must spend time reconciling sample identities, checking quality and reconstructing how a result was obtained. Smaller businesses may have access to testing facilities but limited specialist capacity to integrate the results. IAS addresses this data-to-decision gap. Our proposed use case is to support food SMEs and their research partners in developing and middle-income economies through remote analysis of existing, lawfully accessible data. The initial focus would be a bounded ingredient or process-development question, selected with a local partner, rather than a new measurement infrastructure project.
Solution Overview: IAS is a cloud-based research workspace developed and commercialized by Life Analytics in Yokohama, Japan. It connects imaging, genomics, flow cytometry, mass spectrometry and molecular-structure analysis with integrated analysis, electronic laboratory notes, databases and analysis histories. AI-assisted interpretation and report drafting support scientific review. For the proposed food-sector pilot, a participating business or research organization would provide an agreed set of existing images and laboratory results. We would first map samples, experimental conditions and data provenance, then assess missing values, measurement quality and batch effects. Methods appropriate to the available data would be used to extract image features, analyze molecular measurements and examine relationships across data types. Results would be returned with their supporting evidence, analysis conditions and limitations so that the research team can prioritize the next test or development decision. The collaboration model combines Life Analytics' software and analysis support with the partner's domain knowledge and existing laboratory or testing relationships. The pilot would establish an agreed baseline, reusable workflow and researcher-reviewed report. New experimental measurements, if needed, would be separately scoped with a qualified partner. IAS is for research use; scientific conclusions require researcher review.
Solution Provider(s): No external partner is committed to this proposed deployment. Life Analytics株式会社 (LifeAnalytics Co., Ltd.), Japan, is the solution developer and research-analysis provider. We are seeking a food-sector SME or industry research organization in a developing or middle-income economy, with access to suitable existing data and a scientific lead, as an initial pilot partner.
Implementation location(s): N/A for the proposed food-sector deployment in developing and middle-income economies. The existing IAS platform is developed and commercialized from Yokohama, Japan; the new deployment would be scoped with a local pilot partner.
Implementation timeline(s): N/A for the proposed deployment.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: To be agreed after review of the pilot scope, data readiness, data-use permissions and local requirements with a suitable partner. The proposed initial pilot is a narrowly scoped, remote analysis of existing data. New data collection or laboratory work would require separate planning.
Desired impact: Our objective is to help smaller research and industrial teams make better use of data they already generate. The proposed pilot would connect relevant measurements, make quality issues visible and provide a traceable basis for deciding which hypotheses or process conditions to investigate next. Three outcomes would be evaluated against the partner's existing workflow: time required to assemble and review a cross-data analysis; completeness of data provenance and analysis records; and reproducibility of results when the agreed workflow is repeated. A scientific review would also assess whether the output helps prioritize the next experiment or development decision. The expected benefits are more reusable research data, easier collaboration between businesses and scientific partners, and fewer avoidable repetitions caused by fragmented records or analysis errors. Resource-efficiency benefits would be measured where the pilot permits. These are proposed evaluation objectives; quantified industrial, environmental and economic effects have not yet been established for this deployment.
Key technologies: AI-assisted research interpretation and report drafting; scientific image analysis; genomic and multiomics analysis; analysis of mass-spectrometry-derived protein and metabolite data; statistical quality control, normalization and batch-effect assessment; data integration; electronic laboratory notebooks, databases and analysis-history management. The methods selected for each pilot would depend on the research question and available data. Scientific review remains part of the workflow.
Unique Characteristics: IAS brings multiple research-data modalities and their interpretation into a shared workspace. Its value is the connection between an image or molecular result, the relevant sample and experiment, the analysis history and the research team's decision. Teams can choose the analysis functions required by a particular question while retaining a common record of how the evidence was produced. The proposed delivery model builds on existing measurement resources. A food SME can collaborate with its usual laboratory or research partner while Life Analytics supports data organization, analysis and review remotely. This allows a pilot to focus on one practical decision and reuse the resulting workflow for subsequent datasets.
Sustainable Change: A successful pilot could provide a reusable workflow for cooperation among food SMEs, laboratories and research organizations. Shared data dictionaries, explicit quality criteria and documented analysis steps could make future studies easier to repeat and compare, even when different organizations generate the measurements. Replication would start with similar research questions and expand only after checking local data formats, connectivity, language, scientific capacity and data-governance requirements. Partner-led review and practical training could help teams retain the knowledge needed to interpret results and commission better-targeted follow-up work. The longer-term opportunity is wider access to research-analysis capability without requiring every SME to build a full specialist team internally.

Title: Revlog: a safe, traceable first mile for used lithium-ion batteries in Africa
Subtitle: Monitored, fire-resistant units and drop-off points, built in local workshops, with a chain-of-custody record for every battery from collection to recycling or reuse.
Problem Statement: Lithium-ion batteries are spreading across Africa through solar home systems, mini-grids, electric motorbikes, buses and battery swapping networks, and every one will reach end of life. There is no safe first step for them. In Kenya, where we start, standard practice is a steel drum filled with vermiculite: no gas or heat sensing, no alarm, no record of what is inside or who handled it, and a loaded weight of 74 to 160 kg that needs a forklift. Damaged packs can go into thermal runaway while stored or moved, and the risk falls on informal collectors. Because collection is unsafe and unrecorded, used batteries are dumped or burned, recyclers cannot plan on feedstock they cannot see, second-life users cannot trust packs with no history, and regulators cannot enforce extended producer responsibility without records. The lithium, cobalt and nickel inside are lost.
Solution Overview: Revlog combines monitored containment with a custody record. How it works: the RV-K1 is a fire-resistant unit for storing and moving used lithium-ion batteries. It is designed to detect early thermal runaway through gas and heat sensing, send SMS alarms over the cellular network (no smartphone or Wi-Fi needed), contain a failing battery, be cooled in place without being opened, and vent hot gas away from the people carrying it, while staying under 30 kg loaded. The Battery Point is a public drop-off cabinet built around a swappable drum, which battery companies can place at shops and service centres. CycleTrack, our software, gives every unit and battery a chain of custody: location, contents, condition and handler, from producer to recycler. Methodology: we analysed 138 use scenarios, built a risk register and a failure mode and effects analysis, benchmarked 29 existing designs, and used a Monte Carlo simulation of venting to redesign the unit (vents reaching carriers fell from 95 to 98% of runs to 0% in 11 of 13 scenarios). Alarm thresholds will be set from tests on cells driven into failure. Today the system uses sensing and set thresholds, not AI. The sensor and custody data from our pilots is the base we plan to use for AI models that grade returned packs and predict faults earlier. Partnership model: battery producers, solar and e-mobility companies host units at their collection points and lease them with monitoring included; licensed recyclers receive recorded, graded batteries; local workshops build the units from our design pack.
Solution Provider(s): Lab of Tomorrow (cohort 29), an innovation programme with GIZ (German development cooperation agency), Siemens Stiftung (foundation) and Seedstars (emerging-market startup investor), which supports Revlog's market and partner development, NVIDIA Inception (startup programme for AI and accelerated computing companies), of which Revlog is a member
Duration to pilot in a new geography: About 6 to 9 months once the design is fire tested: local workshop build from our design pack, partner and site onboarding, agent training and CycleTrack setup (estimate).
Desired impact: Objectives: make the first mile of used lithium-ion batteries safe and recorded; give producers the evidence they need under Extended Producer Responsibility rules; and send more batteries to licensed recycling and second-life use instead of dumps. Expected impact (targets for our first 20-unit, 3-month pilot in Nairobi; not yet demonstrated): no injuries, with an alarm raised before the first cell vents in every test; 100% of batteries recorded with a full chain of custody; at least half of the trained collection agents women. Wider impact: fewer battery fires, critical materials (lithium, cobalt, nickel) recovered, and safer collection jobs. Battery reuse also cuts emissions: one study found that a second life for LFP batteries cuts about 50 kg CO2e per kWh. We will report results under low, base and high adoption scenarios.
Key technologies: IoT: a sensing pod with gas and heat sensors and a local alarm. Cellular connectivity: SMS alarms that reach any basic phone, for sites with weak internet. Software: CycleTrack, a web platform that records the chain of custody of every unit and battery; our public collection portal is live at portal.revlog.africa. Simulation: Monte Carlo modelling of venting, used to engineer safety before building. Digital design: full CAD model and verification scripts, and a design pack so local workshops can build the units. AI (planned): models trained on sensor and custody data to grade returned packs and predict faults earlier.
Unique Characteristics: Revlog moves the first mile from passive to active, from a container to a record, and from imported to locally built. Unlike a vermiculite drum, the RV-K1 is designed to warn before a fire spreads, cool in place and vent away from people, at under 30 kg loaded instead of 74 to 160 kg. Unlike certified transport containers from high-income markets, it is designed for African cost and heat and to be built in local workshops. Unlike battery tracking software, CycleTrack is tied to physical containment at the point of collection, where most batteries are lost today. Business model: units are leased with monitoring included, so small collectors pay for a service instead of buying equipment, and producers pay for the custody records they need as compliance evidence.
Sustainable Change: Because the units are designed to be built in local workshops from available materials, production can grow wherever batteries are, without importing finished units; a design pack, jigs and an inspection checklist let new workshops build to the same standard. CycleTrack is software, so new sites, partners and countries can be added without new infrastructure. Every recorded battery strengthens Extended Producer Responsibility enforcement and creates a reliable, graded feedstock that recyclers and second-life companies can plan around. The custody data is designed to meet battery passport requirements, so batteries from African markets can enter global recycling and second-life supply chains. We start in Kenya, then East Africa and the wider continent, following the solar and e-mobility companies that collect batteries from their customers.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access
Summary: Revlog proposes a monitored, locally built container and a custody record for the first mile of used lithium batteries in Kenya, with AI planned once sensor data accumulates. The design work is specific and honest; the operation, the test evidence and the money to run it are not yet in place.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems; Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access

Title: AgriFood SystemsCold AI: Intelligent Solar Cold Chains for Sustainable
Subtitle: An AI-powered, solar-enabled cold-chain platform using predictive analytics, IoT monitoring and digital traceability to reduce food loss, improve supply-chain efficiency and expand market access for smallholder farmers.
Problem Statement: Smallholder farmers and agricultural supply-chain businesses face post-harvest losses, fragmented collection systems, inadequate cold storage, unpredictable demand and inefficient distribution. Limited access to reliable temperature monitoring and actionable data makes it difficult to manage perishable produce, coordinate supply with buyers and optimize energy and transport use. These challenges reduce farmer incomes, increase food waste and constrain the growth of sustainable agro-industrial enterprises, particularly in underserved African communities.
Solution Overview: AgriCold AI is a proposed AI-enabled platform designed to improve the collection, preservation, aggregation and distribution of fresh agricultural produce. Led by Reality Escape Ltd in Rwanda, it builds on existing produce aggregation and market-linkage activities while introducing intelligent tools for managing perishable-food supply chains. How it works: Digital produce collection: Farmers and community-based youth agents submit information about available crops, quantities, quality, expected harvest dates and collection locations through mobile forms or a digital platform. AI-powered demand forecasting: Machine-learning models analyze historical sales, buyer orders, seasonal patterns, crop availability and market demand to forecast requirements and support better purchasing and inventory decisions. Inventory and spoilage prediction: Predictive analytics identify produce at risk of deterioration and recommend stock rotation, prioritization, suitable storage duration and faster market allocation. Smart cold-chain monitoring: IoT sensors installed in participating cold-storage facilities monitor temperature and, where appropriate, humidity. Alerts notify operators when readings exceed defined thresholds. Distribution optimization: Data-driven recommendations help coordinate collection schedules, transport routes, storage allocation and deliveries to hotels, supermarkets, wholesalers, processors and other institutional buyers. Traceability and performance reporting: Digital records track produce movements, quantities, storage conditions and transactions, supporting quality assurance, accountability and future impact measurement. Solar-powered preservation: The platform is designed to support solar-powered refrigeration and energy monitoring, reducing dependence on unreliable electricity supplies and supporting lower-carbon food distribution. Methodologies and technologies: The proposed approach combines machine learning, demand forecasting, inventory analytics, IoT sensing, digital data collection, dashboard reporting and route optimization. The initial implementation would use existing spreadsheets and digital records, progressively moving toward integrated data systems as sufficient reliable data becomes available. Partnership and collaboration model: Reality Escape Ltd would coordinate implementation with farmer cooperatives, youth and women-led agent networks, cold-storage and solar-technology providers, logistics operators, agricultural researchers, technology developers and produce buyers. Partnerships would be established according to implementation needs. The first phase would validate data availability, forecast accuracy, monitoring reliability and operational value through a small-scale pilot in Rwanda before replication in other African markets.
Solution Provider(s): Reality Escape Ltd — Rwandan agribusiness and social enterprise leading produce aggregation, market linkage, youth agripreneurship and development of the proposed intelligent cold-chain solution. No formal implementation partners for the AI solution are confirmed at this stage. Prospective partners include farmer cooperatives and associations (agricultural production and aggregation), solar refrigeration and IoT technology providers (renewable energy and cold-chain infrastructure), logistics operators (transport and distribution), research institutions (agricultural data and model validation), and hotels, supermarkets, wholesalers and food processors (commercial demand and market access).
Implementation location(s): N/A — the integrated AI-powered solution has not yet been implemented. Reality Escape Ltd's existing aggregation and market-linkage activities are based in Rwanda, which is the proposed initial implementation country.
Implementation timeline(s): N/A — implementation of the integrated AI solution has not yet commenced.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 3–6 months, subject to funding, partner availability, access to reliable operational data, installation of required monitoring equipment and validation of the initial deployment. The first pilot would be conducted in Rwanda, followed by adaptation to another geography based on local crop patterns, infrastructure, regulations and buyer requirements.
Desired impact: The primary objective of AgriCold AI is to reduce avoidable post-harvest losses and improve the reliability, efficiency and sustainability of agricultural supply chains by combining predictive analytics, digital traceability, smart monitoring and renewable-energy-enabled cold storage. Expected impact and pilot targets: Reduce post-harvest losses among participating supply-chain partners by a target of 20–30% relative to a measured baseline. Improve demand forecasting, inventory turnover and the matching of available produce with buyer requirements. Reduce avoidable collection trips, unnecessary storage and inefficient deliveries through improved scheduling and route planning. Improve visibility of temperature excursions and enable faster corrective action for temperature-sensitive produce. Expand market access and earning opportunities for smallholder farmers, youth and women participating in collection, aggregation, distribution and digital operations. Establish measurable data on produce loss, delivery performance, energy use per unit of produce, farmer income and employment created. Reality Escape Ltd has previously reported RWF 4.8 million in revenue and RWF 720,000 in net profit from produce-market activities, as well as supporting more than 100 young people. These are existing business results, not demonstrated impacts of the proposed AI system. The initial pilot would establish verified baselines and measure changes against them. The 20–30% loss-reduction figure is a proposed target, not a result already achieved. Emissions reductions and energy savings would be quantified after collecting baseline energy, transport and operational data.
Key technologies: The proposed solution will use: Artificial intelligence and machine learning: Demand forecasting, supply-demand matching, inventory recommendations and spoilage-risk prediction. Internet of Things (IoT): Temperature and optional humidity sensors for monitoring storage conditions and generating alerts. Data analytics and business intelligence: Dashboards for produce volumes, inventory, buyer demand, stock turnover, quality and operational performance. Digital data collection: Mobile forms and web-based tools for farmer registration, harvest estimates, collection records and transactions. Optimization algorithms: Collection scheduling, delivery planning, route optimization and storage allocation. Digital traceability: Structured records of produce origin, collection, storage, movement and delivery. Solar-energy monitoring: Where solar-powered refrigeration is deployed, monitoring of energy generation and consumption to assess operational efficiency. The technologies would be introduced incrementally, with appropriate data protection, access controls, data-quality checks and human oversight of operational decisions.
Unique Characteristics: AgriCold AI integrates agricultural aggregation, market access, predictive intelligence and sustainable cold-chain operations into a model designed for resource-constrained African markets. Its distinctive features include: Demand-led preservation: Using buyer demand and crop availability to guide collection and storage decisions, rather than relying solely on reactive purchasing. Affordable, incremental digitalization: Building on existing spreadsheets and mobile data collection before investing in more complex systems, lowering barriers for small enterprises. AI linked to physical operations: Connecting predictive recommendations with collection schedules, storage monitoring, inventory management and delivery decisions. Climate-conscious infrastructure: Integrating the digital platform with solar-powered cold storage where feasible, with the aim of reducing food loss and improving energy resilience. Youth-inclusive delivery: Creating opportunities for young people and women to participate as digital data agents, produce aggregators, cold-chain operators and distribution entrepreneurs. Replicable business model: Combining service fees, aggregation margins, market-linkage services and potential cold-storage services to support commercial sustainability. Rather than treating AI as a standalone software product, the solution applies it to measurable operational problems across the physical agricultural value chain. Its proposed innovation will be validated through pilot testing.
Sustainable Change: AgriCold AI could help transform fragmented agricultural supply chains into more coordinated, data-driven and resource-efficient systems. By making demand, inventory, storage conditions and produce movements more visible, it could help farmers and small agribusinesses make better decisions, reduce avoidable losses and respond more reliably to market requirements. At the enterprise level, the solution could improve operational planning, produce quality, customer reliability and commercial performance. At the community level, it could expand market access and create income-generating opportunities for youth and women. At the environmental level, reduced food waste, better transport coordination and the use of appropriately designed solar-powered refrigeration could contribute to more sustainable food systems. The platform could subsequently be adapted to other perishable value chains, including fruits, vegetables and selected dairy products, subject to appropriate food-safety and temperature requirements. Expansion into additional districts and countries would involve local farmer and buyer partnerships, adaptation of forecasting models, data-quality validation and compliance with applicable standards. Over time, aggregated and appropriately protected operational data could help participating businesses, researchers and policymakers better understand seasonal supply patterns, food-loss hotspots and infrastructure needs. The approach could support broader adoption of affordable AI tools by agricultural MSMEs and demonstrate how industrial AI can contribute to inclusive, climate-resilient development. Systemic impact would depend on successful pilot validation, reliable data, commercial adoption, access to appropriate infrastructure and partnerships for scaling.
Funding Sources: Reality Escape Ltd has developed its existing agricultural aggregation and market-linkage activities through a combination of entrepreneurial resources, business revenue and external startup-support funding. The company has previously reported RWF 4.8 million in revenue and RWF 720,000 in net profit from produce-market activities. It has also received startup support through entrepreneurship and business-development programs. The proposed AgriCold AI system has not yet received dedicated funding for development or implementation. Future funding will be sought to develop and validate the AI platform, acquire IoT monitoring equipment, establish appropriate cold-chain infrastructure, and conduct a pilot in Rwanda.
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: AgriCold AI would add forecasting, temperature monitoring and traceability to an existing Rwandan produce aggregation business. The operating base is the strong part; the platform itself has no build, no pilot and no evidence.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems; AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry

Title: EcoTrace AI: Decentralized Industrial Circularity Platform
Subtitle: An offline-first edge-AI platform empowering informal green workers and SMEs to automate waste valorization, optimize resource efficiency, and track circular supply chains.
Problem Statement: Industrial clusters across developing economies like Bangladesh (such as peri-urban light manufacturing and textile recycling hubs in Dhaka) face severe resource inefficiencies and digital exclusion. Over 85% of local SMEs and informal green workers lack access to expensive enterprise software or high-speed internet. This results in unverified waste disposal, high water and energy waste, and the marginalization of millions of grassroots recyclers who are locked out of formal green value chains and digital economic benefits.
Solution Overview: How it works: EcoTrace AI deploys lightweight, mobile-accessible computer vision and predictive models directly at the cluster level. Workers and youth volunteers use standard smartphones to instantly grade recyclable materials and receive real-time operational prompts to reduce energy and water waste. Methodologies & Technologies: Edge AI for low-bandwidth processing, computer vision for material classification, and decentralized logging for traceable material provenance. Partnerships & Collaboration Models: Implemented through collaborative community frameworks bridging Mission Green Bangladesh volunteers, local MSME cooperative networks, and formal industrial upcyclers.
Solution Provider(s): Mission Green Bangladesh, Dhaka, Bangladesh (Grassroots environmental education, youth climate action, and campaign network; Sector: Civil Society Organization / Environmental Sustainability) Ecoversity Network, Dhaka, Bangladesh (Youth-led sustainability, green skill development, and ecological research network; Sector: Civil Society Organization / Education & Capacity Building)
Implementation location(s): Dhaka, Bangladesh (Mirpur & Mohammadpur peri-urban industrial and recycling clusters)
Implementation timeline(s): Q1 2026 – Q3 2026 (Initial prototype testing, local material dataset mapping, and baseline cluster assessment)
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 to 4 months (facilitated by an offline-first modular architecture that minimizes reliance on heavy local IT infrastructure)
Desired impact: Main Objectives: To democratize industrial AI tools for informal green workers and SMEs, achieve a 20% average reduction in industrial resource waste, and integrate 500+ grassroots recyclers into verified circular supply chains. Quantified Impact: Expected 18–25% reduction in water and energy consumption in participating pilot units; over 5,000 metric tons of industrial byproducts successfully rerouted from landfills to upcycling channels; verified digital micro-credentials provided to informal green workers.
Key technologies: Artificial Intelligence (Computer Vision and Edge Machine Learning models), IoT telemetry sensors, and lightweight mobile-based data logging frameworks.
Unique Characteristics: EcoTrace AI's primary innovation lies in its offline-first design built specifically for resource-constrained industrial workshops with limited connectivity. By combining grassroots youth mobilization (via Mission Green Bangladesh) with accessible mobile edge-AI, it bridges the gap between informal waste sorters and formal industrial buyers, ensuring fair pricing and digital inclusion.
Sustainable Change: EcoTrace AI creates a scalable, open blueprint for transitioning informal recycling and manufacturing economies into structured green digital marketplaces across developing nations. By leveraging youth leadership and low-cost AI deployment, the solution can be replicated across South Asian and LDC industrial clusters, driving sustainable industrial transformation while ensuring marginalized workers directly benefit from the digital economy.
Funding Sources: Previously funded through a combination of grassroots community crowdfunding, institutional grants from youth-led climate networks, and pro-bono technical development support from civic technology volunteers. Pilot testing and local data mapping have also benefited from resource-sharing partnerships with civil society environmental organizations and academic institutions in Bangladesh.
Testimonials and Endorsements: "EcoTrace AI bridges a critical gap in our peri-industrial clusters by putting powerful digital and circularity tools directly into the hands of youth green workers and small-scale recyclers." Youth Climate Action Network Leader, Dhaka "By decentralizing resource optimization, this platform transforms informal waste management into verified, transparent green supply chains that directly benefit marginalized workers." Ecoversity Network Stakeholder Review
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: EcoTrace AI proposes edge computer vision on ordinary smartphones so that informal recyclers can grade materials and follow circular supply chains. Prototype testing and a baseline assessment were carried out in two Dhaka clusters during 2026.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry; Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access

Title: VOX PROMEUM - Auditable Industrial Evidence Intelligence
Subtitle: A governed industrial intelligence engine that converts fragmented operational data into traceable findings while preserving provenance, conflicts and human accountability.
Problem Statement: Industrial decisions often depend on fragmented and inconsistent data held across laboratory systems, operational records, SCADA platforms, spreadsheets and supplier documentation. Conventional analytics may silently merge conflicting values, lose source provenance or generate conclusions that cannot be independently audited. This creates operational, environmental, regulatory and financial risk, particularly for organisations with limited technical resources. VOX PROMEUM addresses this evidence gap by transforming heterogeneous industrial data into structured, traceable findings while preserving disagreements, uncertainty and the original source of every observation.
Solution Overview: VOX PROMEUM is a governed industrial evidence-intelligence engine designed to support complex operational and sustainability decisions. The workflow moves through Import, Inspect, Map, Validate, Normalise, Run, Results and Evidence, Mitigation, and Export. Source records are ingested through configurable mapping profiles rather than facility-specific code. PROMEUM validates and normalises the information into a canonical evidence structure while retaining every source record, transformation and conflict. Its governed intelligence layer evaluates the evidence across multiple steps, identifies material inconsistencies or risks, and produces findings linked to their supporting observations. It does not silently choose between contradictory measurements. Instead, it preserves the conflict, identifies the affected decision and requests verification or human review where required. The current validation build has successfully processed a complete historical multi-source industrial dataset containing approximately 2.52 million provenance observations and 1,800 canonical records. It correctly preserved a significant disagreement between laboratory and SCADA measurements without merging them or selecting an unsupported winner. PROMEUM is intended to integrate with existing laboratory, SCADA, maintenance, environmental and enterprise systems. Pilot collaboration would involve the industrial operator, relevant technical specialists and Apraxys Group Limited, with the operator retaining authority over operational decisions. The current collaboration model includes independent industry review and prospective evaluation support from FWE GmbH in Germany. FWE GmbH has expressed willingness to explore a small-scale evaluation pathway involving an existing BIOGASTIGER demonstration unit in Tonga, subject to access, condition, permissions and feasibility. This is prospective evaluation interest and is not represented as an existing customer deployment or formal contracted partnership.
Solution Provider(s): FWE GmbH, Rostock, Germany — biogas-sector company represented by CEO Pierre Haider. FWE GmbH independently reviewed the VOX PROMEUM concept, intended application and Prototype A demonstration, confirmed the relevance of the problem to biogas operators, and expressed interest in possible future real-world evaluation. FWE GmbH has also indicated willingness to explore whether an existing BIOGASTIGER demonstration unit in Tonga could provide a small-scale evaluation environment, subject to equipment access, technical condition, permissions and practical feasibility. Apraxys Group Limited, Tonga — developer and owner of VOX PROMEUM, responsible for the product architecture, governed intelligence workflow, technical validation and future pilot implementation.
Implementation location(s): N/A — not yet operationally implemented. Technical validation was conducted in Tonga using complete historical multi-source industrial data from a wastewater and resource-recovery operation.
Implementation timeline(s): N/A — historical data validation was completed in October 2026; operational pilot implementation has not yet commenced.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 8–12 weeks after securing an implementation partner, data-access approval and the required operational documentation. This includes source-system assessment, mapping configuration, controlled ingestion, user validation, governance setup and pilot acceptance testing.
Desired impact: PROMEUM’s main objective is to make industrial evidence reliable, auditable and usable for operational, environmental and investment decisions. Its immediate objectives are to reduce time spent manually reconciling fragmented records; prevent unsupported conclusions caused by silently merged or conflicting data; preserve provenance from source to finding; identify missing evidence before a decision is made; and provide accountable human review and escalation. During historical real-data validation, PROMEUM processed approximately 2.52 million provenance observations into 1,800 canonical records while retaining their source lineage. It also detected and preserved a material disagreement between laboratory and SCADA measurements rather than averaging the values or choosing an unsupported result. A controlled pilot would measure reconciliation hours saved, data conflicts detected, evidence gaps identified, time to operational decision, duplicate work avoided and the reliability of environmental or resource-recovery reporting. Emissions or energy savings have not yet been claimed and would be quantified only from verified pilot evidence.
Key technologies: Governed AI and multi-step evidence reasoning; configurable mapping-driven data ingestion; schema validation and normalisation; provenance and audit-trail architecture; conflict-preserving evidence models; deterministic verification controls; human review, approval and escalation gates; structured mitigation workflows; and exportable evidence packages. The architecture is designed to connect with existing laboratory, SCADA, maintenance, environmental and enterprise data systems without replacing them.
Unique Characteristics: PROMEUM is differentiated by treating industrial AI as an accountable evidence process rather than a black-box answer generator. Every finding remains connected to its supporting source observations and transformations. Conflicting measurements remain visible and are never silently averaged, overwritten or assigned an artificial winner. The engine uses configurable mapping profiles rather than customer-specific ingestion code, making the architecture transferable across facilities and data structures. It separates generated findings from acceptance criteria so that validation data cannot influence the inference process. It also incorporates explicit uncertainty, refusal, verification and human-override pathways. This combination of reusable industrial data normalisation, provenance-preserving intelligence and governed human decision control is particularly suitable for regulated operations and resource-constrained organisations that require trustworthy AI without replacing existing systems. The solution also has a practical prospective evaluation pathway through FWE GmbH’s industry support and willingness to explore the use of an existing BIOGASTIGER demonstration unit in Tonga. This creates a potential low-cost route from validated MVP to controlled physical evaluation, subject to access, condition, permissions and feasibility.
Sustainable Change: PROMEUM can provide a reusable trust layer between fragmented industrial data and consequential decisions. Instead of requiring organisations to replace their existing laboratory, operational or enterprise systems, it can be configured to interpret and reconcile evidence across them. Once validated through controlled pilots, mapping profiles and governance templates could be adapted across wastewater treatment, waste-to-energy, renewable energy, utilities, manufacturing and other resource-intensive sectors. This would enable smaller operators and developing economies to adopt accountable industrial intelligence without the cost of rebuilding their entire digital infrastructure. At scale, PROMEUM could support comparable evidence standards across facilities, improve environmental and operational reporting, accelerate due diligence and financing decisions, and make AI-assisted industrial decisions more transparent, reviewable and transferable between countries. Beginning from Tonga also demonstrates how governed industrial intelligence can be developed and piloted in a Small Island Developing State, including environments with limited specialist capacity and fragmented digital infrastructure.
Funding Sources: Beginning from Tonga also demonstrates how governed industrial intelligence can be developed and piloted in a Small Island Developing State, including environments with limited specialist capacity and fragmented digital infrastructure.
Testimonials and Endorsements: “I consider the general problem addressed by PROMEUM to be relevant to biogas operators.” - Pierre Haider, CEO, FWE GmbH, Letter of Industry Support and Future Evaluation Interest, 26 August 2026. FWE GmbH reviewed the PROMEUM concept, intended application and Prototype A demonstration. The company also expressed interest in possible future evaluation and willingness to explore whether an existing BIOGASTIGER demonstration unit in Tonga could provide a small-scale evaluation environment, subject to access, technical condition, permissions and feasibility. FWE GmbH website: https://www.fwe.energy/
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: VOX PROMEUM assembles fragmented industrial records into an auditable evidence chain that keeps conflicts visible. The design is the most rigorous in its group; with only historical validation, no site and no media, it scores 38.

Title: SmartVision QC: AI-Powered Quality Inspection for SMEs
Subtitle: Affordable computer vision system that detects product defects in real time on production lines, helping small and medium factories reduce waste and improve quality.
Problem Statement: Many small and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises (SMEs) in developing and middle-income economies still rely on manual visual inspection. This process is slow, inconsistent, prone to human error, and costly. Defective products often reach customers or cause high scrap rates, leading to financial losses, wasted materials, and reduced competitiveness.
Solution Overview: SmartVision QC is a modular computer vision system designed specifically for SME production lines. It uses industrial cameras and edge AI devices to inspect products in real time, identifying surface defects, dimensional errors, color variations, and assembly issues. The system works as follows: Cameras capture high-resolution images of products moving on the conveyor. An on-device AI model (optimized for low-power hardware) analyzes each image within milliseconds. Defects are flagged instantly, and the system can trigger alerts, divert defective items, or stop the line if needed. A simple dashboard shows real-time statistics, defect trends, and performance reports. Methodologies and technologies used: Deep learning-based object detection and classification (YOLO and similar architectures), transfer learning for rapid adaptation to new products, edge computing for low latency, and lightweight models that run without expensive cloud infrastructure. Partnerships and collaboration models: The solution is designed for easy collaboration with local system integrators, camera suppliers, and manufacturing associations. It can be deployed through a “hardware + software subscription” model or licensed to regional partners for localization and support.
Solution Provider(s): N/A (Independent innovator / Solo developer). Open to future partnerships with local industrial associations, camera hardware suppliers, and manufacturing support organizations.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3–6 months (including local product adaptation, camera setup, and operator training)
Desired impact: Main objectives: Enable SMEs to achieve consistent, high-accuracy quality control without expensive equipment or highly skilled inspectors. Reduce product waste and rework rates. Improve overall production efficiency and customer satisfaction. Expected impact: Reduction of defect-related waste by 30–60% Decrease in customer returns and complaints Improved productivity and competitiveness of small factories Creation of new technical jobs related to system operation and maintenance Contribution to more resource-efficient manufacturing
Key technologies: Computer Vision, Deep Learning (object detection & classification models), Edge AI / Edge Computing, Industrial cameras and sensors, Transfer Learning, Lightweight neural networks optimized for low-cost hardware.
Unique Characteristics: Specifically designed for SMEs with limited budgets and technical capacity (unlike most industrial vision systems that target large factories). Runs primarily on edge devices, reducing dependence on expensive cloud services and ensuring data stays on-site. Fast adaptation to new products using transfer learning (minimal data and time required). Modular and scalable: starts with one camera and can expand to full production lines. Simple user interface that does not require AI expertise to operate.
Sustainable Change: By making advanced quality inspection accessible and affordable for SMEs, the solution can help raise overall manufacturing standards in developing and middle-income economies. Widespread adoption would reduce industrial waste at scale, improve product quality in local markets, strengthen the competitiveness of small manufacturers, and accelerate the digital transformation of traditional industries. The modular design and focus on local adaptation also support knowledge transfer and the growth of regional AI and automation ecosystems.
Funding Sources: The solution is currently at the Proof-of-Concept stage and has been self-funded by the independent innovator. No external funding has been received yet. Future development and pilot deployments are planned to seek support through grants, innovation funds, and partnerships with industrial associations and development organizations.
Testimonials and Endorsements: N/A – The solution is still at the prototype stage and has not yet been deployed with external stakeholders or beneficiaries.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: SmartVision QC proposes low-cost edge vision for defect detection on SME production lines. The market logic is sound; with no demonstration, no accuracy and no deployment, it cannot be assessed as a working system.
