Title: Arisole: Reliability Infrastructure for Physical AI
Subtitle: AI-powered evaluation, regression testing and sim-to-real validation that helps industrial robots move from laboratory performance to reliable real-world deployment.
Problem Statement: Industrial AI and robotics are advancing rapidly, but deployment remains constrained by a critical reliability gap. A robot policy that succeeds in simulation or controlled testing may fail when software, hardware, environments, payloads or operating conditions change. Industrial teams often lack standardized ways to measure repeatability, detect behavioural regressions between model releases, quantify sim-to-real performance gaps and determine whether a new AI policy is ready for production. This increases deployment risk, engineering effort, machine downtime and the need for repeated physical testing. The challenge is particularly important for manufacturers and industrial operators in emerging economies, where access to large robotics test facilities, specialized engineering teams and expensive validation infrastructure may be limited.
Solution Overview: Arisole provides a reliability engineering and continuous-evaluation layer for Physical AI and industrial robotics. The platform ingests robot and simulation evidence including ROS2/MCAP telemetry, video, sensor streams, task outcomes and model/policy versions. It evaluates repeated executions of the same industrial task and measures whether robot behaviour remains stable across software releases, environments and real-world operating conditions. Arisole combines four capabilities: Continuous evaluation and regression testing: Robot policies and software releases are tested across repeated task executions to identify deterioration in task success, trajectory consistency, timing, contact behaviour and other reliability indicators. Sim-to-real validation: Comparable simulation and physical-world runs are analysed to quantify where model behaviour diverges after deployment. Failure and variation analysis: AI-assisted analysis identifies abnormal runs, recurring failure modes and changes between reference and candidate policies. Robot CI/CD evidence: Evaluation results can become release gates, enabling industrial teams to determine whether a new robot model, policy or configuration should proceed to wider deployment. The platform is designed to work across robot embodiments and does not require customers to disclose proprietary model weights. Organizations can provide recorded execution data or connect evaluation pipelines while retaining control of underlying intellectual property. Arisole's collaboration model is designed around robot manufacturers, industrial operators, research laboratories, system integrators and simulation/platform providers. Partners can define representative tasks, reference states and acceptance criteria, then use Arisole to evaluate subsequent robot releases continuously. By detecting regressions before widespread deployment and reducing unnecessary physical retesting, the approach can improve equipment utilization, reduce failed deployments and support more efficient use of physical testing, compute and engineering resources.
Solution Provider(s): Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT), Centre for Innovation and Robotics (CIR) - applied robotics and industrial automation research; collaboration focused on Physical AI evaluation, repeated-run testing, reference-state definition and sim-to-real validation.: Suunto - wearable and sensor technology ecosystem; Arisole participates in the Suunto Partner Program, supporting multimodal movement and sensor-data applications.
Implementation location(s): Singapore
Implementation timeline(s): Since Sep 2026
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 2 months
Desired impact: The primary objective of Arisole is to make deployment of AI-powered industrial robots more reliable, measurable and scalable. The solution provides continuous evaluation, regression testing, sim-to-real validation and deployment-readiness evidence for Physical AI systems before and during production use. By identifying behavioural regressions, unstable task performance and sim-to-real divergence earlier in the development lifecycle, Arisole aims to reduce failed deployments, repeated physical testing, engineering rework and avoidable machine downtime. This can improve utilization of robotics assets and lower the cost of bringing autonomous systems into industrial environments. A second objective is to make advanced robotics validation more accessible to organizations that do not have large dedicated robotics test facilities or specialized evaluation teams. The platform can work with recorded robot runs, simulation outputs, video, telemetry and sensor data, enabling distributed evaluation across different geographies and robot platforms. Expected impact includes shorter validation cycles, fewer repeated physical test runs, earlier detection of failures, improved production reliability and more efficient use of engineering and compute resources. Arisole is currently progressing applied evaluation work around repeated runs, reference states, sim-to-real comparison and robot CI/CD workflows, with quantitative impact metrics to be established through pilot deployments.
Key technologies: Arisole combines Physical AI, robotics, machine learning, computer vision, simulation and industrial data infrastructure. Core technologies include AI-assisted analysis of robot behaviour, ROS2 and MCAP telemetry processing, video and sensor fusion, repeated-run comparison, statistical regression detection, policy and model version tracking, simulation-to-real comparison, and automated evaluation pipelines. The platform can ingest data from physical robots and simulation environments, establish reference states, compare candidate software or policy releases against previous performance, and generate reliability evidence for deployment decisions. Arisole is designed to integrate with modern robotics development environments, simulation systems and CI/CD workflows, allowing evaluation to become a continuous part of the robot software lifecycle rather than a one-time test before deployment.
Unique Characteristics: Arisole is differentiated by treating robot reliability as a continuous engineering discipline rather than a one-time benchmark or isolated simulation test. The platform evaluates how robot behaviour changes across software releases, model updates, environments and real-world operating conditions. It combines repeated-run evaluation, behavioural regression detection, sim-to-real validation and deployment-readiness evidence within one workflow. A key differentiator is that Arisole does not require access to proprietary model weights. Evaluation can be performed using execution evidence such as telemetry, video, sensor streams and task outcomes, allowing robot manufacturers and industrial operators to retain control of their intellectual property. Arisole is also designed to be embodiment-agnostic. The long-term goal is to provide a common reliability layer across different robot types, models, simulation environments and industrial applications. This creates the basis for comparable reliability evidence across heterogeneous Physical AI systems.
Sustainable Change: As industrial AI adoption expands, organizations will need a repeatable way to determine whether autonomous systems remain reliable after every software, model or environmental change. Arisole has the potential to make continuous robot evaluation and regression testing a standard part of industrial AI deployment, similar to the role that automated testing and CI/CD now play in conventional software engineering. At scale, the platform can support common evaluation practices across robot manufacturers, industrial operators, research institutions and system integrators. This can enable more consistent deployment criteria, reusable evaluation methodologies and stronger evidence for safety, quality assurance and future conformity assessment. Because the solution is designed to work across robot embodiments and commonly used robotics data formats, it can be replicated across manufacturing, logistics, inspection, warehousing and other industrial environments. The same infrastructure can also support technology transfer to developing and middle-income economies by reducing dependence on large proprietary robotics test facilities. Over time, aggregated and appropriately governed reliability evidence could create a broader industrial knowledge layer linking robot models, task conditions, software versions, failure modes and real-world performance. This could improve how Physical AI systems are designed, validated and deployed across industries globally.

Title: An AI-powered, journey-based, personalized financial health platform for migrant workers and their families.
Subtitle: Empowering migrant workers - the often-overlooked force behind the global economy.
Problem Statement: Labour migrants in essential industries face irregular income, recruitment debt, remittance obligations, language barriers, and unfamiliar financial systems. Yet existing financial education is often generic and disconnected from their migration stage and cross-border family responsibilities. General-purpose AI can improve access to information but may produce unverified guidance or opaque calculations. Migrant workers need trustworthy, context-aware support to understand trade-offs and make informed financial decisions safely.
Solution Overview: UPCorp Global is a human-governed, AI-powered financial decision-support platform for labour migrants and their families. Users ask real-life questions in their preferred language. Conversational AI interprets the question, gathers missing context, explains results in plain language and verifiable calculations, while identifying knowledge gaps to recommend relevant micro-learning modules when needed. AI does not generate material financial calculations or underlying rules. These are handled by transparent, deterministic scenario engines using human-designed, tested, and version-controlled logic. Learning content is drawn from a human-reviewed knowledge database with jurisdiction-specific sources. The platform separates verified facts, user assumptions, calculations, and AI explanations, while high-risk or regulated questions are referred to appropriate human support. The solution combines multilingual conversational AI, structured data extraction, curated knowledge retrieval, deterministic financial modelling, modular micro-learning, and privacy-by-design safeguards. It initially focuses on Thai and Vietnamese workers in Sweden and is designed to scale through reusable technology combined with corridor-specific languages, content, rules, scenarios, and referral networks. UPCorp collaborates with migrant communities to co-design and test the product. Employers, recruitment organisations, NGOs, municipalities, unions can deploy it through fixed-price pilots or annual licences, while financial educators and subject-matter experts validate content and calculations. Future partnerships may support responsible skills development, referrals, and safe financial-service onboarding without compromising user independence or data privacy.
Solution Provider(s): We're at an early, pre-revenue stage so we don't have key partners thus far.
Implementation location(s): Sweden
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3 months
Desired impact: UPCorp Global’s main objective is to improve the financial resilience and decision-making capacity of low-wage labour migrants and their cross-border families. It helps users understand financial trade-offs, prepare for income disruptions, strengthen emergency savings, and access relevant learning in their preferred language. A parallel objective is to demonstrate a safer model for financial AI in which communication is AI-powered while material calculations and knowledge are human-governed, transparent, and auditable. Expected outcomes include increased emergency-savings readiness, improved understanding of financial scenarios, fewer harmful financial choices, and greater confidence in managing irregular income and remittance obligations. Impact will be measured through changes in financial knowledge, savings goals, decision quality, repeated platform use, and users’ ability to explain calculations and trade-offs. At scale, UPCorp is designed to strengthen workforce stability, reduce vulnerability to debt and exploitation, and improve the resilience of families and communities across migration corridors. Environmental impact will be monitored through lightweight digital delivery and efficient AI use, but the primary impact is social and economic inclusion.
Key technologies: UPCorp Global combines multilingual generative AI with human-governed financial decision technology. The main technologies are: - Conversational AI and natural language processing: Interpret users’ questions, gather relevant context, support multiple languages, and explain results in accessible language. - AI-assisted knowledge-gap detection: Identify concepts users may need to understand and recommend relevant micro-learning modules. - Curated knowledge retrieval: Retrieve corridor- and jurisdiction-specific content from a human-reviewed knowledge database rather than relying on the AI model’s general knowledge. - Deterministic financial modelling: Human-designed, tested, and version-controlled algorithms calculate savings runway, income shocks, remittance affordability, and other financial scenarios, reducing the risk of AI hallucinations. - Rules-based safety architecture: Separate verified facts, user inputs, calculations, estimates, and AI explanations; restrict regulated or high-risk responses and trigger human referrals when necessary. - Privacy-by-design data infrastructure: Apply informed consent, data minimisation, controlled retention and deletion, and secure handling of sensitive financial information. The AI acts primarily as the communication, interpretation, and navigation layer; it does not independently make financial decisions, generate material calculations, or execute transactions.
Unique Characteristics: Unlike generic financial education or general-purpose AI, UPCorp connects conversation, deterministic “what-if” calculations, and just-in-time micro-learning around each user’s migration stage, employment situation, remittance obligations, and cross-border family context. The platform helps users compare consequences without prescribing decisions or executing transactions. Its modular corridor-based architecture enables scaling by adapting languages, regulations, financial scenarios, and referral networks while reusing the core technology. UPCorp combines direct community co-design with B2B/B2G deployment: NGOs, municipalities, unions, and responsible employers can purchase pilots or annual licences with privacy-preserving impact reporting. This creates scalable distribution while keeping individual financial data confidential and migrant users in control of their decisions.
Sustainable Change: UPCorp Global can drive systemic change by making trusted financial decision support part of the infrastructure surrounding labour migration, rather than a one-off training intervention. NGOs, municipalities, unions, employers, and recruitment organisations could integrate the platform into pre-departure, workplace integration, employment-transition, and reintegration programmes. Its modular architecture enables replication across migration corridors by retaining the core AI, calculation, safety, and learning systems while adapting languages, regulations, scenarios, and referral networks. Aggregated, privacy-preserving insights could help institutions identify recurring barriers and improve migrant-support programmes without exposing individual financial data. As adoption grows, UPCorp could establish shared standards for transparent, human-governed financial AI, strengthen responsible recruitment and employment practices, and improve access to relevant skills and services. The long-term effect would extend beyond individual financial knowledge: more resilient migrant households, reduced vulnerability to debt and exploitation, more stable workforces, and remittances that contribute more effectively to long-term family, community and economic development.
Funding Sources: We got small funding support from Leapfrogs Malmö program through Malmö University.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access

Title: SIGMA® – Sovereign AI Decision Governance for Sustainable Industry
Subtitle: A sovereign governance architecture that enforces human authority, risk-based compliance, and pre-execution control over AI-driven decisions in industrial environments.
Problem Statement: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into industrial operations, AI-driven systems are gaining the ability to generate decisions, coordinate processes, and initiate actions with limited human intervention. This creates a fundamental operational governance challenge: the ability of an AI system to produce or initiate a decision does not establish its authority to execute that decision. Existing governance approaches often emphasize policies, risk assessments, monitoring, and post-execution auditing without consistently enforcing governance requirements within the decision execution pathway itself. For industrial organizations, this distinction is critical. Unauthorized or insufficiently verified algorithmic decisions may affect operational safety, regulatory compliance, accountability, resource management, and trust in industrial AI adoption. The central challenge is therefore to establish an enforceable governance architecture that connects algorithmic decision-making with legitimate human authority, contextual risk assessment, regulatory requirements, verification, and traceable authorization before execution. Addressing this challenge can support safer, more accountable, and sustainable industrial AI adoption, particularly in developing and middle-income economies.
Solution Overview: SIGMA® – The Sovereign Human–AI Algorithmic Interaction System SIGMA® is an independently developed, internationally patent-published engineering invention designed to establish enforceable human authority, operational governance, and pre-execution control over artificial intelligence decisions. 1. Operational Architecture The system introduces an independent sovereign governance layer between AI-generated decisions and their operational execution. It is designed to integrate with external AI systems without requiring modification of their underlying models. Its decision governance lifecycle comprises: * Decision Identification: Capturing the algorithmic decision, its source, operational context, and associated authority. * Contextual Governance: Applying dynamically selected governance controls according to decision risk, applicable policies, regulatory requirements, and operational conditions. * Sovereign Verification: Validating decision integrity, authorization conditions, evidence, and compliance thresholds. * Human Authority: Enforcing legitimate human authorization wherever required by the governing decision policy. * Pre-Execution Gate: Preventing unauthorized or non-compliant decisions from proceeding to execution through a fail-closed control mechanism. * Decision Sealing and Traceability: Establishing verifiable decision records, digital integrity protection, and auditable execution evidence. 2. Engineering Methodologies and Technologies The architecture incorporates several distinctive engineering mechanisms: * Elite Algorithmic Spraying Method (EASM): A patented-application methodology for structuring algorithmic interaction and governance processing. * Sovereign Decision Engineering: Treating the algorithmic decision as an independently governed operational object. * Dynamic Risk-Proportionate Governance: Adapting applicable controls to decision context and risk while preserving mandatory safeguards. * Sovereign Behavioral Vector: Supporting context-sensitive human–AI interaction and decision governance. * Continuous Sovereign Verification: Maintaining verification requirements throughout relevant decision lifecycle stages. * Sovereign Decision Seal and Traceability Chain: Supporting integrity, provenance, accountability, and reconstructable audit records. The architecture separates algorithmic computational capability from the authority to authorize and execute consequential decisions. 3. Industrial Applications and Sustainability The proposed industrial application enables governance controls to be incorporated into AI-assisted manufacturing, industrial automation, resource management, infrastructure operations, and industrial decision-support systems. Its intended contribution is to support trustworthy industrial AI adoption, accountable automation, operational risk management, and regulatory compliance. For developing and middle-income economies, the architecture offers a model for strengthening institutional control over AI-enabled industrial transformation while maintaining human authority over consequential operational decisions. 4. Title: Nurabox: AI Governance and Control for Sustainable Industry
Subtitle: AI-powered governance for industrial organisations, combining regulatory change tracking, data protection, policy controls, safety checks and auditable human oversight.
Problem Statement: Industrial organisations need to adopt AI while maintaining control over the information it uses, the recommendations it produces and the actions it can take. Relevant requirements span legislation, regulatory guidance, technical standards, customer obligations, and internal policies. As these sources change, businesses must identify what affects their operations, update their controls, and demonstrate how they govern decisions. Meanwhile, employees may share sensitive information with unapproved tools, rely on outdated procedures or act on AI-generated recommendations without sufficient evidence. Smaller enterprises often lack the specialist resources to coordinate these responsibilities across engineering, operations, compliance and IT. Nurabox addresses this fragmentation by connecting regulatory developments, company policies, data controls, AI assessments and accountable decisions in one workflow. Its industrial applications include maintenance planning, quality inspection, supplier assessment, and reviewing resource-efficiency recommendations.
Solution Overview: Nurabox is an AI governance and decision-assurance platform developed by Rowvar Limited. It helps industrial organisations translate relevant requirements into practical controls over how AI uses information, supports decisions and interacts with connected systems. The platform connects six functions: Regulatory change tracking: monitors selected official regulatory, guidance and standards sources on a configured schedule. It records detected changes, source references, and retrieval status, and routes updates for relevance assessment. Policy management: helps reviewers identify candidate obligations and connect them to company requirements. Policies have defined owners, scopes, versions and review dates. Proposed changes are tested and approved before activation. Data protection controls: supports classification, sensitive-information detection, redaction and data minimisation. Organisations define who may use information, for what purpose and through which approved processing routes. AI safety and decision review: assesses proposed outputs against approved sources and configured rules. Findings identify missing evidence, outdated references, conflicting instructions and actions outside permitted boundaries. Escalates uncertain or consequential decisions to designated reviewers. Permissions and connected-action controls: apply access restrictions and approval requirements within supported integrations. Approvals are tied to a defined action, destination, and scope; changes require reassessment. Audit and continuous improvement: retains source references, assessments, policy versions, approvals and exceptions. Confirmed failures can become regression tests for subsequent rules and model changes. AI supports document analysis, retrieval and evidence-linked summaries. Deterministic rules evaluate explicit requirements and permissions, while authorised people interpret obligations and approve consequential decisions. For example, an engineer can assess an AI-generated maintenance work order against an approved equipment manual, company policy and data-handling requirements. Nurabox presents issues and supporting evidence before the engineer records a decision. Rowvar leads technical development, configuration and pilot support. The delivery approach combines software with workflow mapping, reviewer training and evaluation. Wider implementation would involve industrial organisations and appropriately qualified local or sector specialists.
Solution Provider(s): Rowvar Limited — United Kingdom-based technology company specialising in AI applications, workflow automation, systems integration and applied research; lead developer and technical delivery organisation for Nurabox.
Implementation location(s): United Kingdom
Implementation timeline(s): April 2026 – Present (ongoing pilot)
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 8–12 weeks from confirming a pilot partner and gaining access to the required documents and systems. This includes 2–4 weeks for local regulatory mapping, policy configuration and user onboarding; 4–6 weeks for a supervised pilot; and 2 weeks for evaluation and refinement. Timing depends on local requirements, language adaptation, integration complexity and the pilot organisation’s readiness.
Desired impact: Nurabox’s main objective is to help industrial organisations adopt AI while maintaining clear control over regulatory requirements, sensitive information, operational decisions, and connected actions. Its initially focuses on UK businesses, particularly SMEs with limited specialist governance resources. The solution aims to: Strengthen regulatory readiness: track selected official sources, identify relevant changes and connect reviewed requirements to company policies and controls. Protect organisational information: support data minimisation, approved processing routes and restrictions on access and use. Improve decision quality and accountability: identify missing evidence, outdated references and actions outside permitted boundaries, with designated human review. Reduce governance effort: bring monitoring, assessments, approvals and audit evidence into a consistent workflow. Support responsible production: improve oversight of maintenance, procurement and resource-efficiency recommendations that may affect equipment life, rework and material waste. Proposed evaluation targets include: Assessing at least 100 AI-assisted workflow cases against an independently reviewed reference set. Achieving a 25% reduction in median review and evidence-preparation time, without deterioration in review quality. Recording the applicable policy version, evidence status and review outcome for 100% of assessed cases. Assigning an accountable owner to 100% of detected regulatory changes assessed as relevant. Evaluation will also measure missed issues, false alerts, reviewer acceptance and exception handling. These figures are targets rather than verified outcomes. Operational and environmental benefits will be assessed against agreed baselines, including maintenance rework, unnecessary parts replacement and material waste where suitable data are available.
Key technologies: Nurabox combines AI-assisted analysis with explicit policy controls and accountable human review. Its principal technologies include: Natural-language processing and large language models: analyse regulatory publications, company policies and technical documents, identify candidate obligations and prepare evidence-linked summaries. Retrieval-augmented generation: retrieves relevant passages from approved sources to support assessments, preserving document and version references. Deterministic rules engines: evaluate defined requirements, permissions, required information and operational boundaries. Regulatory source monitoring and version comparison: detect captured changes in selected official publications on a configured schedule and route them for review. Data protection controls: support sensitive-information detection, redaction, minimisation and restrictions on permitted processing destinations. Authenticated APIs and access controls: connect supported document repositories and operational systems through scoped permissions and action-specific approvals. Structured audit records and regression testing: preserve assessment and approval histories and evaluate whether changes introduce previously identified failures. AI assists analysis; authorised people approve policy changes and consequential decisions.
Unique Characteristics: Nurabox’s distinctive approach connects regulatory developments directly to the controls applied during everyday AI-assisted work. It brings regulatory monitoring, company policies, data protection, decision assessment, and human approval into a single traceable workflow. Its principal differentiating features are: Regulation-to-action traceability: links an official source and reviewed requirement to the relevant company policy, operational control, assessment and approval record. Change-aware governance: detected source updates can trigger review of affected policies and workflows. Changes are interpreted, tested and approved before activation. Combined data and action oversight: addresses both the information AI may use and the actions it may perform through supported integrations. Evidence-led decisions: findings identify supporting sources, document versions, missing information and unresolved uncertainty, helping reviewers understand and challenge an assessment. Continuous improvement: confirmed operational failures can become regression tests for subsequent rules and model changes. Accessible adoption for SMEs: organisations can begin with one workflow and expand through configurable controls, practical onboarding and reviewer training. For example, a reviewed change to a data-handling requirement can lead to an updated company control. A maintenance work order containing restricted information can then be held for review before transmission through a supported connector. The requirement, finding and reviewer decision remain linked in the audit record. The delivery approach combines software with implementation support and domain expertise. Pilot evaluation will assess its comparative performance, usability and commercial value.
Sustainable Change: Nurabox could help make responsible AI use a routine organisational capability across industry. By connecting regulatory developments, company policies, data controls, and accountable decisions, it provides a repeatable approach that adapts as technologies, requirements, and business processes change. Starting with UK industrial SMEs, the solution could expand from individual workflows into maintenance, quality assurance, procurement and resource-efficiency planning. Reusable policy templates, control libraries and training materials could reduce repeated implementation effort. Manufacturing associations, technical institutions and implementation partners could support wider adoption through shared training and sector-specific programmes. This would help smaller enterprises develop internal governance skills and retain practical knowledge beyond an initial pilot. Across supply chains, permission-based sharing of relevant assurance evidence could help suppliers explain how they govern AI, protect information and approve consequential decisions. A consistent evidence structure could reduce duplicated assessments, support trust between smaller suppliers and larger customers, and protect confidential information. Experience from UK implementation could inform later deployment in developing and middle-income economies. Replication would require adaptation to local requirements, languages, infrastructure and available expertise, supported by local partners. The platform’s feedback and regression-testing approach could turn recurring operational failures into reusable lessons. Potential longer-term benefits include more confident AI adoption, stronger accountability and better oversight of decisions affecting equipment life, rework and material use. Scale-up would be guided by measured results, repeatable deployment methods and evidence that benefits persist across different organisations.

Name of your organization: Sustainable Progress and Equality Collective (SPEC), fiscally sponsored by the Hack Foundation (EIN / Tax ID: 81-2908499)
Title: Human in Control: AI-Assisted Skills Recognition for Inclusive Industry
Subtitle: AI suggests, people decide: an AI-assisted system that makes workers' hidden skills visible and portable, with a quality framework and integrity badge for trusted AI training tools.
Problem Statement: Industrial transformation in developing and middle-income economies depends on workers who can prove what they can do. Many workers gain skills on the job, in informal work and through life experience that no institution records, and this is especially true for women and young people. Their qualifications also rarely move across borders. Meanwhile, MSMEs, training providers and public agencies adopting AI have no shared way to judge whether an AI learning tool is fair, private and reliable. Our 13 October 2026 workshop drew participants from Germany, Switzerland, the United States, Australia, Canada, Cameroon, the Middle East, China and Africa. They named three blockers: structural disconnect between policy, training and communities; unclear compliance requirements for "responsible AI"; and burnout among the practitioners who carry the risk. A related divide is emerging in AI itself: current systems are dominated by Western culture and the English language, and new systems may not interoperate.
Solution Overview: How it works. The solution has three linked parts. First, AI-assisted skills recognition: AI suggests possible matches between a person's experience and recognized competencies, and a qualified human assessor validates every match, because identifying a match is not the same as confirming competence. Second, the Global Learner Quality Framework (GLQF): a shared framework that measures learner growth rather than pass/fail outcomes, so that a credential means the same thing in different countries. Third, the GOER AI Integrity Badge: a trust layer with four pillars (governance, outcomes, engagement and resilience) that shows which AI learning tools meet the standard, granted after sandbox testing and before scale-up. Methodology. Everything runs on a "Human in Control" rule, which gives the human reviewer four powers. They can see a plain-language trace of the evidence the AI used and why. They can shape the tool with context and goals. They can watch for known failure points such as bias, subgroup gaps and over-reliance on the tool. They can steer by approving, editing or overriding any output, and every override is logged. A checkpoint only counts if the reviewer has the authority, time and information to disagree. Before deployment, each site completes a one-page decision-rights register. For each use of AI, it records whether the tool decides, advises or never touches the matter, who is accountable, and how an override works. These rules come from GIEE's Model Policy for Human-in-the-Loop Regulatory Sandboxes (Rogers, Travers and Chowdhury, 2026), submitted for release under CC0. Technologies. The solution extends an existing, permissively licensed open-source AI agent harness that coordinates language models, task-scoped knowledge and tools. It supports open-weight models and a low-cost local configuration, so no personal data needs to leave the site. It adds connectors to skills and competency frameworks, a checkpoint and override-log module, and an evaluation suite that reports results by subgroup. Code will be released under MIT or Apache 2.0, and documentation under CC-BY-4.0. The skills-mapping tasks use the European Commission's open ESCO classification (about 13,890 skills in 28 languages, including French and Arabic, aligned with the ILO's ISCO-08), cross-walked in GIEE pilots to national frameworks referenced to the Global Learner Qualification Framework (GLQF). ESCO's downloadable local API lets mapping run offline, so workers' data never leaves the site. Partnership model. The solution comes from the Global Inclusive Education Ecosystem (GIEE), a Geneva Forum Global Impact Project co-led by SPEC and GOER. Partners run case studies inside a shared regulatory sandbox, and a tiered leadership model shares responsibility so that no single person, system or policy drives the agenda. Dialogue is multilingual, in English and French. AI engineering and evaluation are led by Dr. Swaptik Chowdhury, SPEC Fellow and co-lead of the GIEE Research & Development Team. He is a research engineer and former RAND researcher with more than 8 years of experience in quantitative risk modeling of advanced AI systems, including the use of LLMs as autograders for open-ended tasks. GOER works directly with providers on standards.

Geographic focus: Multinational (US and GIEE case study partner countries)
Implementation location(s): Not yet implemented in an industrial setting. The governance and quality model has been tested through GIEE Cohort 1 case studies in the United States (Los Angeles, CA); and our GIEE partners from nine countries and regions.
Implementation timeline(s): GIEE Cohort 1 case studies: Concept/Ideation March 2026 to Jan. 2027; Beta Testing Feb-April 2027. Industrial pilot: July-Sept 2027..
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6–9 months. The first 2–3 months cover partner agreements, data-consent and ethics approval, and adapting the tool to the local language and competency frameworks. A 4–6 month pilot with one employer or training provider follows. This matches the six-month prototype schedule in SPEC's open-source AI project plan.
Desired impact: Objectives: (1) make workers' existing skills visible, verified and portable across borders; (2) give employers, MSMEs and training providers a trusted signal for choosing AI learning tools; (3) keep humans, and the communities affected, in control of AI decisions about learning and work. Demonstrated impact so far (education setting): the GLITCH case study trained 109 young people and 10 alumni facilitators, who reached 500–600 educators through about 15 professional development sessions and 2 satellite programs. GOER reports engaging 32 organizations, from online schools to edtech and AI providers, in meeting its standards. GIEE has produced an openly licensed (CC0) model policy for human-in-the-loop AI checkpoints. The 13 October 2026 workshop, an official Road to Geneva event, drew 164 registrants. Its findings directly shaped the checkpoint, override-log and decision-rights requirements in the solution. Field outcome data are still emerging, and we report them as such. Expected impact of an industrial pilot: 300 workers assessed, the share of AI-suggested skills validated by human assessors, 25% of which will be women and youth recognized for prior learning, 2-3 AI training tools reviewed against the Integrity Badge, and the override rate and reasons logged.
Key technologies: • Large language models in an open-source agent harness: coordinates models, task-scoped knowledge and tools. It supports open-weight models and a choice of providers. • AI skills mapping: groups and maps people's descriptions of their experience to competency frameworks (SPEC AI Grouping & Learning Tool, in development). • Checkpoint and override-log module: every AI suggestion goes to a human reviewer, and approvals, edits and overrides are logged with reasons, so oversight can be audited. • Evaluation suite: checks quality against a baseline and reports results by subgroup, so gaps for women, multilingual or neurodiverse users are visible. An unexplained gap blocks release. • Privacy by design: a low-cost local configuration, data minimization, de-identification and role-based access. • Digital credentialing: the GOER AI Integrity Badge. • Open licensing: code under MIT or Apache 2.0, and data and documentation under CC-BY-4.0, using standard formats (JSON, CSV).
Unique Characteristics: • Human in Control, not just human in the loop. A checkpoint only counts if the reviewer has the authority, time and information to disagree, and every override is logged. Oversight becomes something that can be audited, not a rubber stamp. • Decision rights spelled out before deployment. A one-page register states, for every use of AI, whether the tool decides, advises or never touches the matter, and who is accountable. • Open digital public goods. The code, evaluations and model policy are openly licensed, so any country, MSME association or training body can reuse them without a vendor. • Built for low-resource settings. It can run locally on low-cost hardware with open-weight models, so it does not depend on strong connectivity or sending personal data abroad. • Quality assurance before scale. Tools are tested in a regulatory sandbox and earn an Integrity Badge before wider use. • Equity checks by default. Results are reported by subgroup, and an unexplained gap blocks release. • Users as designers. Women and youth are co-designers and trainers. In the GLITCH model, young people train educators. • Multilingual and cross-cultural by design. The solution works in English and French and is built to interoperate across regions.
Sustainable Change: Every component is designed as an open digital public good, not a proprietary product. The GLQF, the Integrity Badge criteria, the CC0 model policy, the decision-rights register and the open-source code can each be adopted by any country, training provider or MSME association. Mutual recognition of verified skills would let workers carry their qualifications across borders and sectors. The train-the-trainer model already multiplies reach: 109 trained youth reached 500–600 educators. GIEE's findings feed directly into the 18th Geneva Forum (7–11 December 2026) and the Geneva AI Summit (21–22 June 2027), giving the model a route into international policy. Through AIM Global's Centres of Excellence, a successful pilot could be replicated in other developing and middle-income economies.
Funding Sources: GIEE Cohort 1 (2026), including the 13 October 2026 workshop, an official event of the Swiss Confederation's Road to Geneva, was delivered through in-kind contributions of staff time, expertise and platforms from the co-leads SPEC and GOER and the partner institutions, with convening support from the Geneva Forum-Global Impact Project partners. To fund the open-source AI components, SPEC is seeking a $598,690, 18-month grant from the K-12 AI Infrastructure Program ("pending", not "awarded"). Selection through this UN Call would help secure partners and co-financing for a first industrial pilot.
Testimonials and Endorsements: • "What you are creating is exactly what women need around the world." – Workshop participant, Women in AI breakout room, 13 October 2026 • "Compassion must not be an afterthought in artificial intelligence frameworks; it must be their foundation." – Workshop participant, Flowwwly with GOER breakout room, 13 October 2026 • "These systems are biased…they can make things harder for us, especially when people assume AI is always right." – Madissyn Christmas, GLITCH student member, Howard University
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access
Summary: SPEC proposes AI-assisted recognition of workers' existing skills, with a human assessor confirming every match, a quality framework for credentials and a badge for trustworthy AI learning tools. The governance design is the best developed part; the industrial application does not yet exist.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems

Title: AquaGreen AI Africa
Subtitle: An AI-Powered Industrial Wastewater Recovery and Circular Water Management Platform
Problem Statement: AquaGreen AI Africa addresses the lack of affordable, integrated tools that help SMEs monitor industrial water use, identify inefficiencies and determine safe, economically viable wastewater reuse opportunities. This gap can contribute to unnecessary freshwater demand, higher operating costs and avoidable environmental impacts.
Solution Overview: AquaGreen AI Africa is a proposed AI-powered platform that will help small and medium-sized industrial enterprises in Ghana reduce freshwater consumption, recover reusable water from industrial processes, prevent water pollution, and improve resilience to climate-related water stress. Water-intensive businesses, including food and beverage processors, agro-processing enterprises, laundries and textile manufacturers, face increasing pressure to manage water efficiently while controlling operating costs and environmental impacts. Smaller enterprises may lack the monitoring technology, technical expertise and financial resources required to identify water losses and implement effective wastewater reuse systems. AquaGreen AI Africa will address this gap through affordable digital water monitoring, artificial intelligence, water-quality assessment and practical circularity recommendations. The platform will analyze water-use patterns, identify anomalies, forecast demand, estimate opportunities for water recovery and help participating enterprises prioritize cost-effective interventions. The project will initially pilot the solution with five to eight industrial enterprises in Ghana. Over six months, it will establish water-use baselines, install selected monitoring devices, develop and test the AI-enabled decision-support platform, assess suitable wastewater reuse opportunities and evaluate environmental, economic and social outcomes. The pilot will target measurable improvements in freshwater efficiency, safe wastewater reuse, water-related energy consumption and enterprise operating costs. It will also build local capacity by training workers, supporting women- and youth-led enterprises, and strengthening collaboration between industry, technology providers and water-management specialists. AquaGreen AI Africa will use a modular, affordable design that can be adapted to other industrial clusters and African countries. Its longer-term business model will combine subscription-based digital services, water-efficiency assessments, technical support and partnerships with water-treatment providers. The initiative contributes to inclusive digital transformation by making practical AI-enabled environmental management accessible to smaller businesses that are often underserved by advanced industrial technologies.
Solution Provider(s): Ghana Water Company (Winneba Water Treatment Plant), Kwanyarko Water Treatment Plant
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 6 Months
Desired impact: AquaGreen AI Africa aims to accelerate the green transition of Ghanaian and African industries by using artificial intelligence (AI) and affordable digital technologies to improve industrial water efficiency, enable safe wastewater reuse and strengthen resilience to climate-related water stress. The solution has five main objectives: Reduce freshwater consumption: Help small and medium-sized industrial enterprises identify water losses, improve operational efficiency and reduce freshwater use per unit of production. Promote industrial circularity: Identify opportunities to recover and reuse appropriately treated wastewater for suitable non-potable industrial applications, reducing wastewater discharge and demand for new freshwater supplies. Improve energy efficiency and climate performance: Identify opportunities to reduce the energy required for water pumping, heating and treatment, and quantify associated greenhouse gas emission reductions where verified. Enable data-driven industrial decisions: Apply AI to water-use monitoring, demand forecasting, anomaly detection and the prioritization of cost-effective water-saving and reuse interventions. Promote inclusive digital transformation: Make AI-enabled water management accessible to smaller enterprises, including women- and youth-led businesses, through affordable services, local capacity development and accessible digital tools. Expected impact During the proposed six-month pilot in Ghana, AquaGreen AI Africa aims to engage five to eight industrial enterprises, establish water-use and energy baselines, and deploy monitoring and AI-enabled decision support at selected sites. The provisional environmental targets are: 10–15% reduction in freshwater consumption per unit of production at participating intervention sites, subject to baseline assessments and site feasibility. Increased volumes of appropriately treated wastewater safely reused in suitable industrial processes, with site-specific targets established after water audits and technical assessments. Measurable reductions in water-related energy consumption where efficiency interventions demonstrate savings. Quantification of greenhouse gas emissions avoided using verified energy savings and applicable emissions factors. Training for at least 20 workers and enterprise representatives in water efficiency, digital monitoring and sustainable industrial practices. Participation by five to eight enterprises, with the number of women-led and youth-led businesses tracked during recruitment and implementation. The project will also assess enterprise cost savings, operational improvements and the financial viability of water reuse interventions. As the solution is currently at concept stage, these figures represent proposed targets rather than demonstrated outcomes. A baseline assessment, reliable monitoring data and post-intervention verification will be used to establish actual results. Greenhouse gas reductions will be reported only where they can be substantiated through appropriate calculations and evidence.
Key technologies: AquaGreen AI Africa will combine artificial intelligence, the Internet of Things (IoT), cloud-based data analytics and water-quality monitoring to support industrial water efficiency and circular water management. 1. Artificial intelligence and machine learning AI will be used to identify abnormal water consumption, forecast industrial water demand, detect potential leaks or process losses, and prioritize water-saving interventions. A decision-support engine will assess potential wastewater reuse opportunities using available water-quality information, process requirements, treatment needs and estimated costs. 2. Internet of Things (IoT) and smart sensors Affordable water-flow meters, tank-level sensors and selected pressure sensors will collect operational data from participating enterprises. Where appropriate, energy meters and water-quality instruments will provide additional information. Data loggers or IoT gateways will transmit readings to the platform, with local data buffering to support intermittent connectivity. 3. Data analytics and digital dashboards A mobile-friendly dashboard will integrate water consumption, production volumes, energy use and relevant water-quality results. It will provide alerts, performance indicators, water balances and recommendations to help enterprise managers make informed operational decisions. 4. Weather and climate data integration Where relevant, rainfall records, weather forecasts and seasonal information will support water-demand planning and assessments of vulnerability to water shortages. 5. Digital reporting and communication SMS notifications, digital reports and low-bandwidth interfaces will help make the service accessible to enterprises with limited connectivity or limited technical capacity. The initial implementation will use established forecasting and anomaly-detection methods alongside transparent decision rules. Models will be refined as reliable pilot data becomes available. The platform will not independently authorize wastewater reuse or replace laboratory testing, qualified engineering assessments or regulatory oversight. The proposed architecture is modular, allowing additional sensors, analytical functions and industrial applications to be introduced as the solution develops.
Unique Characteristics: AquaGreen AI Africa's principal innovation is its integration of AI-powered water monitoring with practical wastewater recovery decisions and industrial resource-efficiency planning. Rather than simply measuring water consumption or providing a conventional monitoring dashboard, the solution will help businesses determine where water is being lost, which wastewater streams may be recoverable, what treatment and infrastructure are required, and which interventions offer the greatest potential environmental and economic benefits. AI-enabled, action-oriented decision support: The platform will connect anomaly detection and water-demand forecasting with a reuse recommendation engine that considers water quality, intended use, operational constraints, treatment requirements and estimated costs. Designed for resource-constrained enterprises: The solution will use affordable sensors, modular software and low-bandwidth reporting. This approach is intended to reduce the cost and complexity of adopting digital industrial technologies, particularly for SMEs that cannot afford comprehensive proprietary water-management systems. Integration of environmental and financial performance: Recommendations will be assessed against freshwater savings, potential wastewater recovery, energy requirements, operating costs and estimated payback periods. This will help businesses evaluate the commercial feasibility of sustainable production improvements alongside their environmental benefits. Circular economy approach: The platform will support a transition from treating wastewater solely as a disposal problem toward identifying opportunities to recover water as a resource. Reuse decisions will remain subject to appropriate treatment, water-quality verification and regulatory requirements. Collaborative delivery model: The project will connect an NGO or social enterprise with industrial enterprises, AI developers, engineering specialists, research institutions and relevant public authorities. This model combines technology development with local implementation capacity and independent assessment of results. Phased and evidence-based deployment: The project will begin with a six-month Ghanaian pilot, validate the technology under actual operating conditions, and expand only after its environmental, technical and economic performance has been assessed. The solution is currently proposed at concept stage. Its differentiating features will be validated during development and pilot implementation rather than presented as already demonstrated capabilities.
Sustainable Change: AquaGreen AI Africa has the potential to contribute to systemic change by making AI-enabled industrial water efficiency and circular resource management more accessible, affordable and replicable across Ghana and other African economies. 1. Transforming industrial water management The solution will encourage participating enterprises to move from reactive water management toward continuous monitoring, predictive decision-making and measurable resource efficiency. If validated, this approach could become part of routine industrial operations and environmental performance management. 2. Accelerating adoption among SMEs By offering a modular, affordable service instead of requiring every enterprise to build its own advanced digital infrastructure, AquaGreen AI Africa could reduce barriers to technology adoption among smaller manufacturers and agro-processors. Industrial associations and cluster-based partnerships could enable several enterprises to benefit from shared technical support and knowledge. 3. Strengthening the circular economy Successful pilot interventions could demonstrate practical approaches to recovering and reusing appropriately treated wastewater. Replication could reduce pressure on freshwater resources, encourage investment in resource-efficient production and support the development of local water-treatment and environmental technology services. 4. Building African digital and technical capacity The project will create opportunities for local AI developers, water engineers, environmental specialists and technicians to work together on an applied industrial sustainability challenge. Training and collaboration will strengthen local capabilities in sensor deployment, data analysis, water auditing and circular water management. 5. Supporting climate mitigation and adaptation More efficient water use can strengthen business resilience to water shortages and climate variability. Where verified interventions also reduce pumping, heating or treatment energy, the solution can contribute to greenhouse gas mitigation. Documented results can help enterprises identify further investments and strengthen the evidence base for climate-related financing. 6. Enabling replication across industrial clusters Following evaluation in Ghana, the platform could be adapted for other African industrial clusters, subject to local water-quality conditions, regulations, infrastructure and commercial demand. Potential future users include food processors, beverage producers, laundries, textile manufacturers and other industries with suitable wastewater recovery opportunities. 7. Developing a sustainable service ecosystem A combination of enterprise subscriptions, paid water-efficiency assessments, industrial association partnerships and development funding could support continued operation beyond the initial pilot. As evidence of cost savings and environmental benefits accumulates, the model could attract additional industrial customers and investment. The project's contribution to systemic change will ultimately depend on demonstrated pilot results, sustained enterprise adoption, a viable operating model and successful partnerships. The six-month pilot will therefore establish not only whether the technology works, but also whether its environmental and economic benefits justify wider deployment.
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: AquaGreen proposes an AI and IoT platform for industrial water efficiency and wastewater reuse among Ghanaian SMEs. The problem is real and utility partners are named; without a system, a pilot or a demonstration, it cannot be assessed.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making

Title: Wieta.AI: African Industrial Intelligence for Sustainable Production
Subtitle: An African-language AI platform helping manufacturers, agro-processors and MSMEs improve productivity, reduce waste and make sustainable operational decisions through accessible, locally adaptable AI.
Problem Statement: African manufacturers, agricultural processors and small and medium-sized enterprises face barriers to adopting industrial AI, including limited access to affordable digital infrastructure, fragmented operational data, shortages of AI skills, and tools that do not adequately support African languages or local operating conditions. These barriers make it difficult to monitor production, identify inefficiencies, reduce material waste, optimize resource use and make data-driven decisions. Wieta.AI addresses this gap by developing an accessible, African-language AI platform designed to help enterprises transform operational information into practical insights for more productive, inclusive and sustainable industrial operations.
Solution Overview: Wieta.AI is an AI platform focused on African languages and locally adaptable AI applications. Its proposed industrial solution will help manufacturers, agro-processors and MSMEs analyze operational data, identify inefficiencies, forecast needs and improve resource utilization. It combines machine learning, natural language processing, large language models, analytics dashboards and optional IoT integrations. Implementation will involve collaboration with industrial enterprises, research institutions and technology partners, subject to securing partnerships and pilot sites.
Solution Provider(s): Wieta.AI — African AI research and innovation initiative. Prospective collaborators include manufacturing and agro-processing MSMEs, universities, AI research institutions and industrial technology providers. External partners will be confirmed as collaborations are established.
Implementation location(s): DRC, Rwanda and UGANDA is the intended initial pilot market, subject to securing an implementation partner.
Implementation timeline(s): N/A — No formal industrial deployment period has been established.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 3–6 months, depending on partner readiness, data availability and integration requirements.
Desired impact: Wieta.AI aims to improve industrial productivity, reduce operational waste, support resource efficiency and expand AI access for African MSMEs. Proposed pilot indicators include a 5–10% reduction in a selected waste or inefficiency metric and a 15–20% improvement in selected reporting tasks. These are targets for evaluation, not achieved results.
Key technologies: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, natural language processing, large language models, African-language datasets, predictive analytics, knowledge bases, dashboards and optional IoT integrations.
Unique Characteristics: Wieta.AI combines African-language AI, adaptable industrial analytics and sustainability-oriented decision support. Its modular approach aims to make AI more accessible to smaller enterprises while supporting local-language interaction and resource-efficient production.
Sustainable Change: Wieta.AI could help African enterprises adopt AI, strengthen local technical skills and improve sustainable production. Following a successful pilot in Rwanda, its modular approach could be adapted to other industries and African markets through partnerships, validated use cases and measurable results.
Funding Sources: Wieta.AI has been developed through founder-led research, personal contributions and independent product development. The project is pursuing partnerships, grants and investment to support further development, validation and pilot implementation. No external funding is claimed unless formally confirmed.
Testimonials and Endorsements: Formal testimonials and endorsements specifically for Wieta.AI's industrial AI solution are not yet available. Stakeholder feedback and independent validation will be collected during pilot implementation.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: Wieta.AI aims to give African manufacturers and processors a local-language analytics platform. The language focus is sensible and the targets are declared; with no deployment and no industrial component, it ranks on intent.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Embodied AI, Industrial Robotics and Smart Manufacturing; Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems
