Title: CDRScope: AI-Assisted MRV for High-Integrity Carbon Removal
Subtitle: An AI-assisted digital MRV platform that structures, checks and traces carbon-removal evidence to improve verification readiness, transparency and trust.
Problem Statement: Carbon removal projects generate large volumes of fragmented evidence across spreadsheets, laboratory reports, production records, sensor data, chain-of-custody documents and other operational systems. For emerging project developers, particularly in Africa, organising this information for monitoring, reporting and verification can be costly, slow and technically complex. Missing data, inconsistent records and weak traceability can delay verification, increase project costs and reduce confidence among buyers, investors and other carbon-market participants. CDRScope addresses this evidence-integrity gap by helping project developers structure, validate and trace MRV evidence before formal third-party verification.
Solution Overview: CDRScope is an AI-assisted digital MRV and evidence-integrity platform being developed by CarbonRem Technologies Limited, initially for durable carbon removal projects such as biochar. The platform is designed to ingest evidence from multiple sources, including laboratory reports, spreadsheets, production records, sensor data and chain-of-custody documents. AI-assisted processing extracts and structures relevant information, while methodology-aware rules check data completeness, consistency and potential anomalies. Source provenance is retained so that extracted information can be traced back to the underlying evidence. Human review remains part of the workflow, particularly where methodology interpretation or professional judgement is required. The technical approach combines artificial intelligence, document and data processing, deterministic validation rules, structured MRV data models and human-in-the-loop review. CDRScope does not replace accredited verification bodies or automatically certify carbon credits. Its role is to help project developers prepare higher-quality, traceable and verification-ready evidence. The collaboration model is designed around partnerships with carbon-removal project developers, laboratories, research organisations, methodology experts, verification stakeholders and other climate-market participants.
Solution Provider(s): N/A. No formal external implementation partners have been confirmed at this stage. CarbonRem is currently developing CDRScope and intends to engage carbon-removal project developers, laboratories, research institutions, methodology experts and verification stakeholders as pilot and technical partners.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 8 to 12 weeks, subject to partner onboarding, availability of project data, methodology configuration, technical integration requirements and access to relevant MRV evidence.
Desired impact: The primary objective of CDRScope is to improve the integrity, traceability and verification readiness of carbon-removal project evidence through responsible use of artificial intelligence and structured digital MRV. The solution aims to reduce the administrative and technical burden associated with preparing carbon-removal evidence, identify missing or inconsistent information earlier in the project lifecycle, improve traceability between reported claims and source evidence, and strengthen confidence in project-level carbon accounting. For African project developers, CDRScope also aims to reduce barriers to participation in high-integrity international carbon markets by providing digital MRV infrastructure that would otherwise require significant specialist capacity. The solution is currently at prototype stage, therefore CarbonRem is not claiming verified greenhouse-gas reductions, cost savings or commercial impact at this stage. Initial pilots will measure indicators including evidence-processing time, data completeness, traceability, number and type of anomalies identified, preparation time for verification, user efficiency and the quantity of carbon-removal evidence processed. At scale, the platform is intended to support projects responsible for measurable and independently verified tonnes of durable CO2 removal while strengthening the quality of the evidence supporting those claims.
Key technologies: CDRScope combines several digital technologies: • Artificial intelligence and machine learning for evidence extraction, classification and anomaly identification. • Natural language processing for interpreting information contained in technical documents, laboratory reports and other MRV records. • Deterministic rules engines for methodology-specific validation and compliance checks. • Structured data models for organising carbon-removal evidence and project-level MRV information. • Data provenance and traceability mechanisms linking extracted information to its original source. • Human-in-the-loop review for decisions requiring technical interpretation or professional judgement. • Cloud-based digital infrastructure for scalable data processing, storage and collaboration. The architecture is being designed to support future integration with sensors, IoT systems, laboratories, project-management systems and other external data sources.
Unique Characteristics: CDRScope combines AI-assisted evidence processing with deterministic validation, source-level traceability and human oversight. Rather than using AI as an autonomous carbon verifier, the platform applies AI to activities where it can improve efficiency, such as extracting information, structuring evidence and identifying potential inconsistencies. Checks that depend on explicit methodology requirements can be handled through deterministic rules, while human reviewers retain control over decisions requiring professional judgement. A key differentiator is the focus on evidence integrity rather than simply carbon calculation. Information generated or extracted by the platform is intended to remain linked to its underlying source, allowing reviewers to understand where a claim originated and how it was assessed. The initial focus on African carbon-removal projects also addresses an underserved market where project developers often face limited access to affordable specialist MRV infrastructure. CDRScope therefore combines AI, methodology-aware validation, provenance tracking and human review within a single verification-readiness workflow
Sustainable Change: CDRScope has the potential to address a structural bottleneck in the carbon-removal ecosystem: the difficulty of producing consistent, traceable and verification-ready evidence as projects scale. By creating reusable digital workflows for evidence collection, validation and methodology mapping, the platform could help standardise elements of MRV preparation across multiple projects rather than solving the same evidence-management problems independently for each project. The initial focus is biochar, providing a defined pathway for validating the technology against a real carbon-removal methodology. The underlying evidence-integrity architecture can subsequently be adapted to other durable carbon-removal pathways and industrial decarbonisation applications. For African climate projects, improved digital MRV infrastructure could lower technical barriers to participation in international carbon markets, increase confidence among investors and buyers, and support mobilisation of climate finance towards credible projects. As adoption grows, CDRScope could also facilitate interoperability between project developers, laboratories, carbon standards, verification organisations, buyers and financing institutions. This creates the potential for broader change from fragmented, manually intensive MRV processes towards more structured, traceable and digitally enabled carbon-market infrastructure.
Funding Sources: CDRScope is currently bootstrapped and funded through CarbonRem Technologies Limited's early-stage product development activities. The solution has not yet received external investment, grant funding, paid pilot funding or customer financing. CarbonRem is currently focused on developing and validating the prototype while pursuing relevant technical partnerships, pilot opportunities and non-dilutive funding programmes.
Testimonials and Endorsements: N/A. CDRScope is currently at the prototype stage and does not yet have formal stakeholder or beneficiary testimonials or endorsements.
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: CDRScope structures and checks carbon-removal evidence so that small developers can reach verification. The design is sound and the problem real; with no prototype performance and no project, it scores 40.

Name of your organization: Telecommunications and Digital Government Regulatory Authority (TDRA)
Title: Solar Powered AI Computing with Dielectric Immersion Cooling and Battery Storage
Subtitle: An integrated GPU AI platform combining dielectric immersion cooling, solar PV and battery storage to minimise cooling overhead and run AI workloads on 100% renewable electricity.
Problem Statement: AI and large language model (LLM) workloads run on power-dense GPU servers that consume large amounts of electricity and generate significant heat. In conventional air-cooled facilities, a substantial share of energy is spent on cooling and supporting systems rather than on computing itself, raising operating costs, emissions and the overall energy footprint of AI. Where that electricity comes from fossil sources, the expansion of AI services directly increases greenhouse gas emissions. Organisations adopting AI therefore face two linked challenges: reducing the energy overhead of cooling and supporting systems (measured as power usage effectiveness, PUE), and supplying the remaining demand from renewable electricity, including at night. There is also limited measured evidence on how immersion cooling, solar generation and battery storage perform together under demanding, real AI workloads, which makes it difficult to plan future AI infrastructure investment on a defensible basis.
Solution Overview: TDRA proposes an integrated computing solution combining GPU-based artificial intelligence, customised dielectric immersion cooling, solar photovoltaic (PV) generation and battery energy storage. It has two complementary objectives: to minimise cooling and supporting-system energy overhead, targeting PUE as close to 1.0 as practicable; and to supply 100% of the servers' and cooling system's electricity demand from solar generation and stored solar energy. The proposal builds on TDRA's operational experience with immersion-cooled servers since 2022, supporting building management (BMS), computer-aided facilities management (CAFM), computer-aided drafting, CCTV and access control systems. How the solution works: (1) AI computing – GPU servers run LLMs and related services, including reasoning, AI agents, speech-to-text, document search, embeddings and search-result ranking. TDRA's current cloud AI environment provides four NVIDIA H100 80 GB GPUs across two virtual machines (640 GB RAM), using RHEL and Docker-based model serving through an OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, with Qwen-based reasoning and fast-response models, Whisper speech-to-text, and embedding and reranking models for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). (2) Immersion cooling – compatible server hardware is immersed in an electrically non-conductive dielectric fluid; heat is removed through a circulation and heat-exchange system engineered to match the server configuration, operating environment and maintenance requirements. (3) Renewable electricity and storage – solar panels supply the servers and cooling during daylight while charging a battery bank for night-time operation, sized against measured demand, seasonal solar availability, night-time hours and conversion and storage losses. An integrated monitoring system tracks computing performance, equipment temperatures, cooling energy, solar production, battery condition and total electricity consumption. Methodology: a staged, evidence-based demonstration – Stage 1: establish a baseline of throughput, response time, concurrency, GPU utilisation and energy on agreed models and workloads; Stage 2: operate a two-H100 server in the customised immersion tank and compare sustained capacity, temperature stability, reliability and energy per completed workload; Stage 3: scale to four immersed H100 GPUs and test whether this can approach the throughput of a conventional six-H100 configuration for selected workloads (a hypothesis to be tested); Stage 4: integrate the load with solar and battery storage and verify daytime operation, battery charging, night-time autonomy and any backup electricity used. Comparisons control model version, precision, input/output lengths, concurrency, GPU power limits and software configuration. Partnerships and collaboration model: TDRA's facilities and sustainability team leads integration, cooling and energy requirements, monitoring and sustainability assessment; TDRA's ICT and AI/LLM development team defines workloads, GPU requirements, software architecture, security and acceptance criteria; a GPU server supplier/integrator, an immersion cooling specialist and a solar and battery specialist deliver their respective systems; and a research or independent testing partner, where appointed, validates performance and energy results. Parties work through a jointly agreed specification, staged commissioning, shared test procedures and documented acceptance criteria.
Solution Provider(s): TDRA Facilities and Sustainability Team (public sector; facilities and sustainability – project lead for integration, cooling, energy and sustainability assessment), TDRA ICT and AI/LLM Development Team (public sector; ICT and AI – workloads, software architecture, security and performance criteria), GPU server supplier/integrator (private sector; ICT hardware – to be appointed), Immersion cooling specialist (private sector; data-centre cooling – to be appointed), Solar and battery specialist (private sector; renewable energy – to be appointed), Research or independent testing partner (academia/testing body; independent validation – where appointed). Specific external partners will be identified during project development.
Implementation location(s): United Arab Emirates – Dubai –TDRA facilities (immersion-cooled servers in operation since 2022 for BMS, CAFM, computer-aided drafting, CCTV and access control). The AI, solar and battery demonstration will be carried out at TDRA.
Implementation timeline(s): 2022 – present: immersion-cooled server operations at TDRA. AI immersion and solar/battery demonstration: staged implementation (Stages 1–4) planned.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Installation & commissioning: 2-3 weeks if all items procured and shipped to location
Desired impact: Main objectives: (1) minimise cooling and supporting-system energy overhead for AI computing, targeting PUE as close to 1.0 as practicable; (2) supply 100% of the servers' and cooling system's electricity from solar generation and stored solar energy; and (3) deliver reliable, high-performance AI services (LLM reasoning, AI agents, speech-to-text and RAG) on this sustainable platform, providing a measured basis for future AI infrastructure investment. Expected impact and success measures: AI throughput and response time at defined service levels; total energy consumed per completed AI workload; cooling and supporting-system energy consumption; sustained equipment temperatures and service availability; renewable electricity share against the 100% target, night-time battery autonomy and any backup electricity use; and operating cost and emissions reductions against the agreed baseline. Energy efficiency and renewable supply are assessed separately. PUE equals total facility energy divided by IT equipment energy over the same period and boundary – for example, 100 kWh of IT load plus 10 kWh for cooling and supporting systems gives a PUE of 1.10, even if all 110 kWh is solar. Cooling, conversion and battery losses within the boundary are included. The demonstration will quantify the achieved PUE, renewable electricity share, computing performance, energy savings and emissions reductions before wider deployment. A further research objective is to test whether four immersed H100 GPUs can approach the throughput of a conventional six-H100 configuration for selected workloads.
Key technologies: Artificial intelligence: GPU-accelerated computing (NVIDIA H100 GPUs, with a proposed cloud expansion of two NVIDIA H200 GPUs and 512 GB RAM); containerised AI model serving (RHEL, Docker, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway); LLM inference with Qwen-based reasoning and fast-response models, AI agents, Whisper speech recognition, and embedding and reranking models for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Cooling: customised dielectric immersion cooling – tank, electrically non-conductive dielectric fluid, circulation, heat exchange and external heat rejection – with hardware and fluid compatibility confirmed with suppliers before deployment. Energy: solar photovoltaic generation, battery energy storage and energy management, sized against measured demand and seasonal solar availability. Monitoring and validation: instrumented benchmarking, thermal monitoring and energy metering through an integrated monitoring system, with progressive commissioning, compatibility checks and operational validation.
Unique Characteristics: Integrated design: the solution combines AI computing, immersion cooling and solar-plus-battery supply in one engineered system, addressing both energy efficiency (PUE close to 1.0) and energy source (100% renewable, including night-time operation) rather than only one of them. Built on operating experience: TDRA has run immersion-cooled servers in production since 2022 for building and facilities systems; the project extends this proven base to demanding AI and LLM workloads. Rigorous, transparent measurement: a staged, controlled methodology with a defined baseline, controlled test variables, and separate reporting of PUE and renewable share, so that renewable supply is never used to mask energy overhead. Backup electricity use, cooling, conversion and battery losses are all included in reporting. Performance hypothesis: the project explicitly tests whether immersion cooling allows fewer GPUs (four immersed H100s) to approach the throughput of a larger conventional configuration (six H100s) for selected workloads – a potential hardware and cost saving that is treated as a hypothesis to be validated, not an assumed benefit. Collaborative delivery: a clear multi-party model (facilities, ICT/AI, hardware, cooling, energy and independent testing partners) working to a joint specification and documented acceptance criteria.
Sustainable Change: The demonstration is designed to produce measured, independently verifiable evidence on the energy, performance and operational benefits of solar-powered, immersion-cooled AI computing. This evidence provides a replicable blueprint and a defensible basis for future AI infrastructure investment, first within TDRA and then for other government entities and organisations planning AI deployments. Because the system is modular – GPU servers, immersion tanks, solar generation and battery storage sized to measured demand – it can be scaled from a two-GPU demonstration to larger configurations and replicated in other locations, including sun-rich, hot-climate regions where conventional air cooling is especially energy-intensive. The documented methodology, test procedures and acceptance criteria can be shared to help others design, size and validate similar systems, supporting a broader shift towards AI computing with minimal cooling overhead and fully renewable supply.
Funding Sources: TDRA Budget
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: TDRA proposes an immersion-cooled, solar-powered inference facility and, unusually, a measurement design that would separate efficiency from renewable supply. It is a public-sector demonstration with a real budget and no results yet, which places it in the middle of the field.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry

Title: HydroQ Studio: Local AI for wastewater treatment decisions
Subtitle: Talk to your plant in plain language. HydroQ Studio combines plant records, cited engineering guidance and process simulation to help operators investigate wastewater quality changes.
Problem Statement: Municipal and industrial wastewater teams often have lab results, operating logs and engineering guidance in separate places. When effluent quality changes, operators may have limited access to specialist process-modelling expertise and unreliable connectivity. South Africa’s 2025 Green Drop assessment rated 396 of 848 audited municipal wastewater systems critical, illustrating the need for better evidence and support for plant teams.
Solution Overview: HydroDrip is developing Water Intelligence, an AI decision-support platform for wastewater design and operations. HydroQ Studio, its first product, lets plant teams ask plain-language questions using existing lab results and operating records. It retrieves cited engineering guidance and can run process simulations to test plausible explanations. The working prototype builds treatment flowsheets and runs simulations through a locally hosted language-model interface. Proposed on-site deployment is designed to keep approved plant records on site and support limited connectivity. Operators retain decision authority. HydroDrip proposes to validate the first ammonia investigation workflow with a South African municipal plant, subject to site and data permissions. A BORDA memorandum of understanding provides a separate pathway to decentralised wastewater systems.
Solution Provider(s): Bremen Overseas Research and Development Association (BORDA) — international non-profit active in decentralised sanitation. HydroDrip has an MOU for a deployment pathway on BORDA’s decentralised wastewater systems. Site and data arrangements are subject to agreement.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Indicative: up to six months for site scoping, data preparation and a supervised pilot, subject to local approvals, data availability and site readiness.
Desired impact: The first objective is to help wastewater operators investigate rising effluent ammonia faster and with evidence they can check. In a proposed South African municipal pilot, plant experts will assess historical cases against the existing workflow. Measures will include time to investigate, agreement with expert findings and the quality of cited evidence. Criteria will be agreed before testing. Better investigations can support reliable treatment, pollution prevention and safe reuse. Field impact has yet to be measured. The work primarily supports SDG 6.3 and contributes to more capable water infrastructure under SDG 9.
Key technologies: Locally hosted language models, retrieval-augmented generation over approved engineering references, mechanistic wastewater process simulation and a flowsheet interface. HydroDrip plans to compare open models using Aqua AI, an expert-scored benchmark for calculations, qualitative plant scenarios and uncertainty. Selected models will be fine-tuned where benchmarking shows a benefit. Engineering solvers calculate numerical results.
Unique Characteristics: HydroQ Studio connects a plain-language plant question to cited engineering guidance and process simulations. It shows sources, assumptions and data gaps so operators can decide what to verify. Local deployment is designed to help facilities work with limited connectivity and keep records on site. A first use case based on existing records gives plants a practical way to test usefulness before widening deployment.
Sustainable Change: A reusable evaluation protocol and a common workflow for lab and operating records could help smaller municipal teams and industrial treatment operators access specialist process knowledge. After the first pilot, HydroDrip would assess transfer to decentralised and industrial sites, with local configuration, separate data permissions and operator training. Shared benchmark methods and approved engineering references could support knowledge transfer across sites and regions.
Funding Sources: Grant funding
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: HydroQ Studio lets a wastewater plant team ask a plain-language question, retrieves cited engineering guidance and can run the process simulation to test an explanation. A South African municipal pilot is proposed and a memorandum with BORDA is in place.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems; AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry

Title: ClimaSense Africa: AI for Climate-Smart Farming & Early Warning
Subtitle: AI-powered climate forecasts, drought/flood alerts, and adaptive farming advice delivered via WhatsApp to help African communities build climate resilience.
Problem Statement: Climate change is causing unpredictable rainfall, droughts, and floods across Africa. 70% of smallholder farmers rely on rain-fed agriculture but lack access to timely, localized climate data. This leads to crop failure, food insecurity, and displacement. Existing weather services are not hyper-local, not in local languages, and not linked to action.
Solution Overview: ClimaSense Africa combines satellite data, IoT weather sensors, and AI to deliver 14-day hyper-local climate forecasts and early warnings via WhatsApp and SMS. How it works: AI models predict rainfall, heatwaves, and flood risk at village level. Farmers then receive adaptive advice: "Plant maize in 3 days" or "Risk of flood - move livestock". Methodology: Climate data + ML models + farmer feedback loops. Partnerships: We collaborate with meteorological agencies, NGOs, and community leaders for data, validation, and distribution to rural communities.
Solution Provider(s): Ghana Meteorological Agency - Public Sector, Climate data and validation, Ghana. Local NGOs and Farmer Groups - Civil Society, Community outreach and feedback collection, Ghana.
Implementation location(s): Kumasi, Ashanti region, Tamale, Northern region
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 4-6 months. Includes deploying local weather sensors and training community focal points.
Desired impact: Objective: Help 100,000 farmers and communities adapt to climate change by 2028 with actionable forecasts. Impact: 1. Reduce climate-related crop losses by 30%. 2. Cut disaster response time by 50% through early flood/drought alerts. 3. Improve water use efficiency by 20% through climate-smart planting advice. Expected: Prevent $5M in annual losses across 10 pilot districts.
Key technologies: Artificial Intelligence - ML for climate prediction and risk modeling. IoT - Low-cost weather sensors for hyper-local data. Cloud Computing - Data processing and forecasting. Mobile Technology - WhatsApp/SMS delivery for offline access.
Unique Characteristics: 1. Hyper-local + Actionable: Not just weather, but "what to do" advice in Twi/Hausa 2. Low-cost: Uses WhatsApp and $20 weather sensors instead of expensive infrastructure. 3. Community-owned: Trains local youth as "Climate Champions" to maintain sensors and explain alerts. 4. Finance link: Climate data can trigger index-based insurance payouts automatically.`
Sustainable Change: By creating an open, Africa-specific climate AI platform, we enable governments and NGOs to replace outdated national forecasts with village-level resilience tools. This can be replicated across 20 African countries, shifting disaster response from reactive to predictive and making agriculture climate-resilient at scale.
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: ClimaSense Africa would send village-level forecasts and farming advice by WhatsApp and SMS in Ghana. The channel choice and the met agency link are sound; with no validation and no deployment, it is a proposal.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems; Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry

Title: Digital Solar Cold-Chain Infrastructure & Dual-Licensing IP Model to Secure Africa's Food Future
Subtitle: Reforming Intellectual Property & Technology Transfer Frameworks for Agritech Innovation in Africa
Problem Statement: Sub-Saharan African agricultural systems, particularly in Nigeria and Kenya, forfeit over $4 billion worth of fresh produce annually due to an acute 95% deficit in localized cold-chain storage. In Nigeria, 45% of horticultural harvests rot prior to reaching urban markets, forcing 93 million resource-poor smallholders to forfeit roughly 25% of their annual income. Similarly, Kenya’s high-value horticultural sector experiences post-harvest losses exceeding 40%. While African universities and public research consortiums generate viable technological innovations in solar thermodynamics and IoT telemetry, rigid colonial-era Intellectual Property (IP) policies and underfunded Technology Transfer Offices (TTOs) trap these innovations in the academic "valley of death", demanding prohibitive upfront royalties that local agritech startups and smallholders cannot afford.
Solution Overview: The Century 21 Foundation deploys off-grid modular 20-foot solar cold storage hubs (comprising 30kW solar PV arrays and lithium battery storage) in high-density horticultural aggregation markets—such as Muthurwa Market in Nairobi—to eliminate post-harvest losses and drive circular economy solutions. Farmers and market vendors utilize these physical walk-in cold rooms on an affordable pay-as-you-store Cooling-as-a-Service (CaaS) model, removing the high upfront capital expenditure of cooling infrastructure. Physical storage is seamlessly integrated with organic waste bioconversion loops using Black Soldier Fly (BSF) or vermicomposting systems to process unrecoverable food waste. Within 12 months, the primary pilot aims to deploy one solar container in Muthurwa Market to mitigate 4,000 tonnes of annual produce loss, redirect 6,000 tonnes of edible produce to community kitchens and orphanages, and process 2,000 tonnes of organic waste into 200 tonnes of protein meal and 80 tonnes of organic fertilizer, effectively mitigating ~400 tonnes of methane emissions. The infrastructure operates on an advanced digital servitization layer driven by an AI-backed IoT backend Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and mobile application (incorporating systems like Coldtivate/Your VCCA developed with BASE and Empa). Embedded IoT sensors capture real-time ambient microclimate metrics (temperature and humidity), while physics-based "Digital Fruit Twin" algorithms process telemetry data to continuously model crop decay. Two days prior to anticipated spoilage, the platform automatically sends SMS advisories to vendors’ feature phones, prompting them to retrieve, discount, or redistribute produce before loss occurs. By Month 6, this digital backbone secures active B2B market linkages, optimizes inventory routing, and enhances supply chain transparency across urban food supply chains. Sustainability and long-term ecosystem growth are maintained through a CSO-managed Dual-Licensing Framework that bridges public research outputs and commercialization. A non-profit Civil Society Organization (CSO) custodian accepts public university and research IP, managing a two-tiered distribution system. Tier 1 (Public Open-Access Core) provides core sensor schemas, baseline fruit twin algorithms, and multilingual crop advisories under open-source licenses to smallholders, micro-vendors, and grassroots agritech ventures at zero cost. Tier 2 (Enterprise Commercial SaaS) monetizes advanced software modules—such as predictive fleet management routing, automated ERP integration, and alternative credit-scoring algorithms—via annual SaaS subscriptions to corporate supermarket chains, logistics fleets, and financial institutions. Net revenues generated from Tier 2 commercial licensing flow directly back to the non-profit custodian to cross-subsidize Tier 1 open-access maintenance and fund future rural cold-hub capital expansions. Targeted capacity building ensures socio-economic equity and community ownership across the value chain. By Month 24, the initiative will train and certify 100 smallholder farmers, traders, women, and youth in digital inventory tools, cold chain handling, and sustainable waste management. To directly address gender inequalities in agricultural commerce, 40% of all physical cold storage capacity is strictly reserved for female-led traders, driving a projected household income increase of over 10% for participating women. Partnerships and Collaboration Models 1-Non-Profit NGO (e.g., Century 21 Foundation): Serves as the institutional IP trustee and ecosystem steward. 2-Academic & Public Research Institutions (University TTOs, Science Granting Councils, CGIAR Centers) 3-Cold-Chain Infrastructure Operators & Technology Developers (Coldtivate, BASE Foundation, Empa): 4-Private Engineering & Enterprise SaaS Clients: 5- Multilateral & Continental Coalitions e (UN FAO, Smart Africa) 6-National Governments & Regulatory Authorities (Ministries of Finance)
Solution Provider(s): BASE Foundation, Empa): Hardware partners manage site acquisition, off-grid hardware installation, and day-to-day CaaS hub operations. BASE and Empa co-develop and maintain the digital stack (Your VCCA / Coldtivate), Digital Fruit Twin algorithms, and impact analytics dashboards. Smart Africa Alliance, AEDIB, AU/AfCFTA Secretariat, FAO
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 18 months
Desired impact: Overall Project Goal: Establish a self-sustaining circular economy framework pairing decentralised solar cold-chains with a zero-waste marketplace to aggregate, divert, process, and eliminate organic food waste at farm-gates and market hubs, diverting >4,000 tonnes of produce annually and preventing ~400 tonnes of direct atmospheric methane emissions per hub. 1.Infrastructure Deployment & Food Redistribution: Deploy 1 solar-powered 20ft cold storage container in Muthurwa market, Nairobi within 12 months to mitigate 4,000 tonnes of fresh produce lossed annually and process 6,000 tonnes annually in partnership with community kitchens/orphanages. 2. Digital Circular Economy Platform: Launch an AI-driven IoT backend DIP system and mobile app by Month 6 to track real-time inventory, monitor temperature/humidity, and secure active B2B market linkages. 3. Capacity Building & Gender Inclusion: Train and certify 100 smallholder farmers/traders, women, and youth by Month 24; reserve 40% of cold storage capacity for female-led traders to boost household incomes by >10%. 4. Methane Mitigation via BSF System: Operationalise a Black Soldier Fly facility by Month 12 to process 2,000 tonnes of organic waste into 200 tonnes of protein meal and 80 tonnes of organic fertiliser, mitigating ~400 tonnes of methane. TARGET BENEFICIARIES" •Primary Beneficiaries:Vulnerable and food-insecure urban residents in Nairobi (~6,000 tonnes processed annually); 40% reserved hub capacity for female farmers/traders; 100+ smallholder farmers/sellers onboarded for digital waste payouts and green- tech training. • Secondary Beneficiaries: Local agribusinesses and livestock farmers (gaining low-cost BSF protein feed and frass fertiliser); municipal market communities and waste management authorities (reduced drainage blockage and landfill pressure). • Estimated Total Reach:~10,000+ people reached directly and indirectly by Year 2. EXPECTED RESULTS: • Outputs: 1 operational solar cold hub; 1 live AI-powered DIP mobile app; BSF facility processing 2,000t waste into 200t protein meal & 80t fertiliser; 100+ certified trained stakeholders. • Outcomes: Drastic reduction in post-harvest agricultural spoilage; stabilised daily incomes for female traders (+10%); 6,000 tonnes processed annually; 15 Green Jobs- 5 direct jobs (Hub Managers, Inventory Clerk, Security) and sustains an additional 10 indirect jobs (Labour workers) • Long-Term Impact: Mitigation of 400 tonnes of direct atmospheric methane emissions per hub; establishment of a regional circular-bioeconomy blueprint integrated across AfCFTA trade and East-African corridors.
Key technologies: AI, IoT, Digital Twins The infrastructure operates on an advanced digital servitization layer driven by an AI-backed IoT backend Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) and mobile application (incorporating systems like Coldtivate/Your VCCA developed with BASE and Empa). Embedded IoT sensors capture real-time ambient microclimate metrics (temperature and humidity), while physics-based "Digital Fruit Twin" algorithms process telemetry data to continuously model crop decay. Two days prior to anticipated spoilage, the platform automatically sends SMS advisories to vendors’ feature phones, prompting them to retrieve, discount, or redistribute produce before loss occurs. By Month 6, this digital backbone secures active B2B market linkages, optimizes inventory routing, and enhances supply chain transparency across urban food supply chains.
Unique Characteristics: The Century 21 Foundation’s solution introduces a distinct circular bioeconomy model by integrating two previously isolated value-chain interventions, decentralized solar cold storage and Black Soldier Fly (BSF) Larvae bioconversion, directly at the municipal market level. Traditional post-harvest interventions focus solely on thermal preservation, treating inevitably spoiled organic matter as an external waste liability. In contrast, this end-to-end framework creates a closed-loop system: off-grid solar cold rooms extend produce shelf life to prevent initial spoilage, while adjacent modular BSF bioconversion units instantly process unmarketable, wet market waste into high-protein animal feed and nutrient-dense organic frass fertilizer. By capturing organic waste at the precise point of generation, the model eliminates landfill transportation costs and prevents direct landfill methane emissions, transforming a municipal waste crisis into a localized supply of affordable agricultural inputs. Technologically, the solution achieves physical digital synergy through off-grid thermal storage engineering and predictive digital telemetry. By utilizing phase-change material (PCM) thermal energy storage instead of short-lived chemical batteries, the solar cold rooms will maintain stable 2–8°C cooling for up to 72 hours during low-solar periods, significantly reducing long-term operational maintenance. On the software side, the physical infrastructure is integrated with predictive decision-support applications like Coldtivate, which employ physics-based "Digital Fruit Twin" algorithms to process microclimate sensor data. These algorithms model crop decay in real time and send automated, multilingual SMS alerts to farmers' feature phones days prior to spoilage, enabling proactive inventory management and targeted waste diversion into the BSF conversion stream. The model’s business architecture is anchored in a novel Non-Profit Organization (NGO) managed dual-licensing Intellectual Property (IP) blueprint designed to overcome traditional university Technology Transfer Office (TTO) bottlenecks. Publicly funded agritech research and software algorithms are transferred to the non-profit custodian, which partitions them into two distinct tiers: a Tier 1 Open-Access Core provided at zero royalty to smallholders, micro-vendors, and local startups, and a Tier 2 Enterprise Commercial SaaS platform licensed to corporate supermarkets, logistics fleets, and financial institutions. Net revenues generated from Tier 2 corporate licensing, combined with commercial sales of BSF protein and organic fertilizer, create a permanent cross-subsidization mechanism that funds rural hub construction, maintains open-access tools, and keeps daily pay-as-you-store cooling rates accessible for low-income market vendors. From a delivery and partnership perspective, the solution replaces high CapEx equipment purchasing with an inclusive "Cooling-as-a-Service" (CaaS) micro-rental model, effectively removing the multi-thousand-dollar financial entry barrier for women market vendors and smallholders. Execution is supported by a multi-stakeholder coalition that aligns local municipal market authorities for site access with private technical partners, academic TTOs, and regional bodies like the Smart Africa Alliance, UN FAO and the AfCFTA Secretariat. By embedding cross-border telemetry protocols and Productive Uses of Energy (PUE) policy waivers into regional trade frameworks, the model creates a scalable, financially self-sustaining blueprint for climate resilience, food security, and waste-to-value transformation across Sub-Saharan Africa.
Sustainable Change: Theory of change If decentralised solar cold storage hubs, AI tracking apps and BSF upcycling systems are implemented, then farmers and traders will stop food spoilage and divert organic waste from landfills, leading to community food security and lower methane emissions. This is expected because physical preservation extends shelf life from 2 days to over 21 days directly bypasses regional infrastructure bottlenecks, community kitchens repurpose surplus, and bioconversion upcycles organic waste. SUSTAINABILITY PLAN •Community Ownership: Training local graduates and women to operate hubs (15 green jobs); transferring operational capacity to female-led trading cooperatives (40% storage allocation); localizing digital app units (e.g., "baskets") to build long- term trust. • Income Generation & Hybrid-Revenue Model: Self-sustaining hybrid model through Pay-As-You-Go (PAYG) micro-leasing fees extending produce shelf-life from 2 to 21 days, marketplace transaction fees, and commercial sales of upcycled BSF protein meal and frass fertiliser. • Partnerships & Institutional Support: Municipal PPPs securing free market land; technical alliances with cold chain partners for remote monitoring; solar panels donated; verified emission reductions positioning the project for carbon credit financing and ESG grants. • Data Monetisation & Market Intelligence APIs: Monetising real-time agricultural supply chain data from the Digital Intelligence Platform (DIP) • Specialised Advisory & Circular Economy Consulting: Leveraging operational expertise to offer paid technical consulting, to governments, private agribusinesses, and institutionalising a regional circular bioeconomy blueprint within and East-African corridors Kenya is selected as the primary pilot expansion based on: -High Perishable Exposure: Horticulture accounts for 33% of agricultural GDP, suffering 40%$ post-harvest losses. -FinTech Readiness: High M-Pesa adoption minimizes end-user onboarding friction for PAYG storage payments. -Off-Grid Solar Market: Mature regulatory frameworks for productive use off-grid energy. -Policy Alignment: Aligns with Kenya-Japan TICAD9 commitments and Smart Africa's Continental Agritech Blueprint. Institutional Sustainability: Long-term operational continuity is anchored by aligning the technology with national energy and rural development policy frameworks across West and East Africa. Incorporating these solar cold storage hubs into the Rural Electrification Agency (REA) Productive Use of Energy (PUE) programs ensures integration into broader off-grid electrification rollouts. Furthermore, backing from multilateral organizations such as the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) provides the institutional scaffolding, policy backing, and public sector alignment necessary to scale and replicate these decentralized assets across broader regional markets This approach is consistent with research highlighting the potential of productive uses of electricity in African agriculture and the importance of addressing rural access to sustainable cooling. Social Sustainability: Local adoption and long-term community stewardship are driven through inclusive design and targeted socio-economic empowerment. Utilizing participatory community co-design processes ensures the hubs directly address local supply chain dynamics, while deploying multilingual user interfaces in major regional languages, like Swahili- could make digital services more accessible to farmers and vendors. Such inclusive, context sensitive design is supported by research on agricultural technology development in Africa. Prioritizing the recruitment of local women as hub managers is also proposed as a way to advance gender inclusion and create supervisory employment opportunities for women in rural agricultural value chains.
Funding Sources: This is a new business concept adapted from Cooling-as-a-service solar cold chain hubs. From using Coldhubs as my case study reference in my research policy paper, we can see that it was a culmination of: Constructing off-grid solar cold hubs required high upfront capital (~$40,000 per 3-ton hub in 2020), creating a barrier to rapid commercial expansion. Nnaemeka Ikegwuonu initiated ColdHubs in 2014 by building the initial walk-in prototype from scrap metal and basic materials to prove that decentralized cooling could serve local farmers (Food Planet Prize, n.d.). He then secured vital catalytic development funding in 2015, including an $80,000 seed grant from the German development agency GIZ to engineer proper modular units with ILK Dresden and an $18,000 grant from the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition (GAIN) for a refrigerated van. In 2016, ColdHubs obtained a $270,000 equity investment from Factore Ventures to expand early operations. This financial foundation culminated in a 2024 strategic partnership with Heifer International to finance major hub construction, including 10 MT and 100 MT regional facilities at the Farin-Gada Fresh Fruits and Vegetables Market in Jos, Plateau State (ColdHubs, 2024).
