Title: AfriQA: Building Trust and Capability for Industrial AI
Subtitle: An inclusive AI assurance and workforce development model helping organisations evaluate AI systems, demonstrate reliability and build locally sourced quality engineering capability.
Problem Statement: As more organisations across Africa and other developing economies begin using AI, an important question is emerging: how do they know these systems are reliable, safe and working as intended? For many businesses, particularly smaller ones, access to people with the skills to test and evaluate AI systems is limited. They may be able to adopt AI technologies but lack the expertise to identify problems, assess risks or check whether the systems continue to perform as expected. At the same time, universities across Africa are producing talented graduates who often struggle to find opportunities to gain practical industry experience. Many have the knowledge and potential but have not had the chance to apply their skills to real-world projects. AfriQA is working to bring these two needs together. By connecting emerging African talent with practical quality engineering and AI assurance work, we aim to help organisations build confidence in the technology they use while creating meaningful opportunities for young people to develop their skills and careers.
Solution Overview: AfriQA is working to address two challenges we see across Africa: businesses need people who can test and evaluate the technology they use, while many talented graduates struggle to get the practical experience employers are looking for. Our approach is to bring the two together. We work with emerging African technology professionals, giving them opportunities to develop their skills through real industry projects. This includes software testing, test automation, API testing and monitoring. Rather than focusing only on qualifications, we want people to be able to demonstrate what they can actually do. We have already seen this approach work. In one engagement, we placed an emerging professional with an industry client for what was initially a three-month assignment. The placement eventually ran for twelve months, during which they developed an API testing framework, automated quality metrics and monitoring capabilities. The work was delivered remotely, showing us that this model can work across borders. We now want to build on that experience by extending our work into AI assurance. As more organisations adopt AI, they need ways to check whether these systems are doing what they are supposed to do. That means looking beyond whether an application works and asking questions about reliability, accuracy, unexpected behaviour and the risks that arise when AI is used in real business processes. Our proposed approach is to use practical testing scenarios to evaluate AI systems, identify weaknesses and document the results so organisations have evidence to support their decisions. We currently use tools such as Cypress and Jira in our quality engineering work. As we develop our AI assurance capabilities, we intend to introduce more structured AI evaluations, automated testing and performance monitoring. Partnerships are central to how we work. We want to bring universities, employers and technology organisations together so that students and early-career professionals can gain experience while businesses benefit from the work they deliver. Our longer-term goal is to build a network of African quality engineering and AI assurance professionals who can support organisations locally and internationally. We believe Africa should not only be adopting AI technologies but also developing the skills and expertise needed to test them, challenge them and make sure they can be trusted.
Solution Provider(s): AfriQA Ltd – UK-based quality engineering and emerging AI assurance company, working at the intersection of industry, education and digital workforce development. AfriQA has experience collaborating with industry clients and emerging African technology professionals to deliver practical software testing and quality engineering activities. Additional academic, research and industrial collaborations are being explored to support the development and validation of AI assurance methodologies.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3-6months
Desired impact: Our goal at AfriQA is to help organisations adopt AI with greater confidence while creating opportunities for African talent to take part in the growing digital economy. As more businesses begin using AI, they need people who can test these systems, identify problems and assess whether they are reliable and fit for purpose. Not every organisation, particularly smaller businesses, can afford to build this expertise in-house. We want to help close that gap by developing practical AI assurance capabilities and connecting businesses with emerging African professionals who can do this work. An important part of our approach is working with universities and employers to give students and graduates experience on real projects. We believe people should have opportunities to demonstrate their abilities through the work they do, not just the qualifications they hold. We have already seen what this can achieve. One of our industry placements was originally planned for three months but continued for twelve months. During that time, the participant developed an API testing framework, automated quality metrics and monitoring capabilities for the client. It showed us that emerging talent, given the right opportunity and support, can make a meaningful contribution to real business needs. Through our schools activities, we have also reached more than 500 students, introducing them to technology and giving them opportunities to develop practical digital skills. As we expand into AI assurance, we want to build on these experiences. We plan to measure our progress through the number of organisations supported, AI systems evaluated, problems identified, people gaining practical experience and participants progressing into employment. We are still developing this part of our work, so we do not yet have measured outcomes specifically for AI assurance. Our aim is to demonstrate those results through future pilots and use what we learn to improve and expand the model. Ultimately, we want to see more African professionals contributing to the development and assurance of AI systems, and more businesses having access to the expertise they need to use these technologies responsibly.
Key technologies: At AfriQA, we use a range of software testing and quality engineering tools to help organisations check that their systems work as expected. Our work includes automated testing, regression testing, API testing and monitoring. We have used tools such as Cypress to automate tests and Jira to manage defects and track progress. We have also developed automated quality metrics and monitoring capabilities through our industry projects. We are now looking to build on this experience by applying similar approaches to AI systems. Unlike traditional software, AI does not always produce the same result for every input, which means testing it requires different methods. Our approach will involve creating realistic test scenarios, evaluating how AI systems respond, identifying weaknesses and measuring how reliably they perform. We also want to explore how AI itself can help automate parts of the testing process, including generating test cases, analysing results and monitoring system behaviour. This is an area we are actively developing. Our existing experience is in software quality engineering, and our next step is to build and test these AI assurance capabilities through practical projects with industry and research partners.
Unique Characteristics: What makes AfriQA different is that we are not just looking at how to test technology. We are also looking at who gets the opportunity to develop the skills to do that work. Across Africa, there are talented graduates who struggle to gain practical experience, while businesses need people who can test their systems and help them adopt new technologies with confidence. We want to bring these two groups together. Our approach focuses on giving emerging professionals real industry assignments where they can demonstrate what they are capable of, rather than relying solely on qualifications or certificates. We have already shown that this can work through a remote industry placement that grew from three months to twelve months and delivered practical testing and monitoring capabilities for a client. We now want to take this approach into AI assurance, developing ways for emerging professionals to evaluate AI systems, identify weaknesses and provide businesses with evidence of how well those systems perform. We believe this combination of practical experience, industry delivery and AI assurance could make specialist expertise more accessible to businesses while opening up new career opportunities across Africa.
Sustainable Change: We believe Africa should not only be adopting AI technologies developed elsewhere, but also building the skills and expertise needed to test, evaluate and improve them. At AfriQA, our ambition is to help make that possible by bringing universities, businesses and emerging technology professionals closer together. One of the challenges we see is that many graduates struggle to find opportunities to gain practical experience, while businesses often struggle to find people with the skills they need. By connecting students and early-career professionals with real industry projects, we hope to help close that gap and create more pathways into technology careers. As AI becomes more widely used, we also see an opportunity to make testing and assurance services more accessible to smaller businesses. Not every organisation can afford its own team of AI specialists, but they still need to understand whether the systems they use are reliable, safe and performing as expected. Our approach is designed to grow beyond one organisation or country. By working with universities, employers and local partners, we hope to develop a model that can be adapted and replicated across different African markets and industries. Over time, this could create more employment opportunities, strengthen local technology businesses and reduce dependence on expertise from outside the continent. Ultimately, we want to help build an African workforce that does more than use AI. We want African professionals to have the skills, experience and opportunities to question it, test it and help shape how it is used. We believe that is an important part of ensuring Africa benefits from the growth of AI rather than simply becoming a market for it.
Funding Sources: AfriQA has so far been funded through contributions from its founders and income generated from its early commercial activities. We have not received external investment. We have used these resources to support our quality engineering activities, practical industry placements and engagement with students and emerging technology professionals. Our AI assurance capabilities are still being developed, and we are exploring partnerships and funding opportunities to support further development, testing and pilot implementation.
Testimonials and Endorsements: AfriQA has successfully supported an industry placement that was initially planned for three months and extended to twelve months. During this engagement, the participant developed an API testing framework, automated quality metrics and monitoring capabilities. We are seeking permission to share feedback from the industry client and participant as evidence of the value of this approach.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access
Summary: AfriQA offers AI assurance and quality-engineering skills development for African organisations. The two-sided model is sensible; with no assessment delivered and no AI-specific method, it remains a concept with one placement behind it.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access; Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems
Media links (as submitted): AfriQA website: https://afriqa.co.uk Our website provides further information about our work in quality engineering, practical skills development and creating pathways for emerging African technology professionals.

Title: GreenVera: Transforming Waste into Value Through Circular Innovation
Subtitle: A women-led, technology-enabled circular economy solution integrating waste recovery, smart collection, river restoration and resource regeneration to create cleaner, healthier communities in Africa.
Problem Statement: Rapid urbanization in Kenya has intensified waste management challenges, including inadequate waste segregation, inefficient collection systems, illegal dumping, polluted waterways and limited recycling infrastructure. Valuable recyclable materials are routinely lost to landfills or the environment, while communities face flooding, public health risks and environmental degradation. Existing waste management systems are often fragmented, with limited digital traceability, insufficient material recovery facilities and weak integration between community collection, recycling and environmental restoration. These challenges disproportionately affect underserved communities and informal waste workers, while limiting opportunities for green employment and circular economic growth. GreenVera addresses these interconnected challenges through an integrated, technology-enabled circular economy model that combines decentralized material recovery, digital waste tracking, river restoration, drainage waste interception and resource recovery.
Solution Overview: GreenVera Environmental Solutions Ltd is a women-led Kenyan circular economy enterprise developing an integrated, technology-enabled waste management and environmental restoration solution. Our innovation combines digital waste management infrastructure, decentralized material recovery facilities (MRFs), river restoration, drainage waste interception and organic waste valorization into one scalable ecosystem. This is how our Solution Works: 1. Digital Waste Management:GreenVera OS™, our operational digital platform, supports waste collection management, collector coordination, material recovery operations, recycler engagement, client management, compliance and environmental reporting. The platform provides a foundation for improving traceability, operational efficiency and data-driven decision-making. 2. Decentralized Material Recovery: Our proposed Maji Mazuri Micro-MRF in Nairobi will serve as a demonstration facility for sorting, weighing, recovering and aggregating recyclable materials, including plastics, paper, cardboard, glass and metals. Recovered materials will be directed to recycling and manufacturing value chains. 3. River Restoration: Through RiverRestore™, GreenVera is developing community-based river waste interception and recovery solutions designed to prevent solid waste from moving downstream while supporting riverbank restoration 4. Drainage Protection: GreenDrain™ proposes modular waste interception traps for drainage channels to reduce solid waste accumulation, drainage blockages and pollution. 5. Organic Waste Solutions: Our VeraCycle™ initiative promotes decentralized organic waste processing and resource recovery to reduce biodegradable waste disposal. Our approach integrates digital waste tracking, material flow monitoring, decentralized recovery infrastructure, circular economy principles, community engagement and environmental impact measurement. GreenVera OS provides the digital foundation, with opportunities to introduce AI-assisted waste classification, predictive collection planning and operational optimization as the platform develops. GreenVera has already partnered with some UN Agencies such as UN Global Compact and UN Women under WEPs. We are also seeking collaboration with counties, manufacturers, recyclers, residential communities, technology providers, research institutions and international development organizations. Our model combines service agreements, recycling value-chain partnerships, community-based implementation and public-private collaboration. The solution is designed for phased implementation, beginning with Nairobi and expanding to other Kenyan and African urban centres. By connecting digital infrastructure with physical waste recovery and environmental restoration, GreenVera aims to transform waste into economic value, create inclusive green employment and support cleaner, more resilient cities.
Solution Provider(s): GreenVera Environmental Solutions Ltd (Kenya) – Private sector; solution developer, technology platform owner and implementation lead. Green Legacy Initiative Network (GLIN) (Kenya) – Community and environmental initiative; potential community mobilization, environmental awareness and youth engagement collaborator. Additional partnerships are being explored with recycling companies, residential communities, local authorities, environmental organizations and international development institutions to support pilot implementation, technical development and scaling. These prospective collaborations are not yet represented as formal implementation partnerships.
Implementation location(s): Nairobi, Kenya. GreenVera OS has been developed and deployed as a digital platform. The initial physical demonstration site is planned for Maji Mazuri Estate, Mwiki, Kasarani, Nairobi County, where a decentralized material recovery facility is being established. Proposed river restoration and drainage waste interception pilots will also target Nairobi, subject to relevant approvals and implementation partnerships.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: An estimated 3–6 months is required to establish an integrated pilot in a new geography, depending on regulatory approvals, local partnerships and infrastructure readiness. Month 1: Stakeholder engagement, baseline assessment, site identification and regulatory planning. Months 2–3: Digital platform configuration, community mobilization, equipment procurement and operational setup. Months 4–6: Pilot deployment, staff training, waste recovery operations, environmental monitoring and performance evaluation. Digital-only deployment could be completed faster, while physical infrastructure and river interception components may require additional time.
Desired impact: GreenVera Environmental Solutions Ltd aims to transform urban waste management in Africa through an integrated, technology-enabled circular economy model that combines digital waste management, decentralized material recovery, environmental restoration and inclusive green entrepreneurship. The solution has five primary objectives: 1. Increase Waste Recovery and Circularity: Establish decentralized material recovery facilities that divert recyclable materials from landfills, illegal dumping sites and waterways into productive recycling and manufacturing value chains. 2. Accelerate Digital Transformation: Deploy GreenVera OS to improve waste collection coordination, material traceability, recycler engagement, operational efficiency and environmental performance reporting. 3. Restore Urban Ecosystems: Implement RiverRestore™ and GreenDrain™ solutions to intercept solid waste, reduce drainage blockages and support cleaner rivers and healthier communities. 4. Promote Inclusive Green Employment: Create employment and income-generating opportunities for women, young people, waste collectors and small recycling enterprises. 5. Support Climate Action and Sustainable Industrialization: Reduce waste leakage, encourage resource efficiency and facilitate the substitution of virgin raw materials with recovered recyclable materials. GreenVera's initial Nairobi pilot will target the following outcomes: Waste Recovery: An initial target of approximately 6 tonnes of recyclable materials per week through the proposed Maji Mazuri Micro-MRF, equivalent to approximately 144 tonnes annually at sustained operating capacity. Employment Creation: Four direct operational positions during the initial MRF phase, with opportunities for additional employment as operations expand. Digital Transformation: Deployment and progressive validation of GreenVera OS across waste collection, material recovery, recycling coordination and environmental reporting activities. Environmental Restoration: Pilot implementation of river and drainage waste interception technologies, with quantities of intercepted waste measured during implementation. Climate Impact: Establishment of a monitoring framework to estimate greenhouse gas emissions avoided through recycling, waste diversion and resource recovery using appropriate emission factors. Community Participation: Engagement of residential communities, waste collectors, recyclers and local stakeholders in improved waste segregation and recovery practices. Following successful pilot validation, GreenVera intends to replicate its integrated digital and physical circular economy model across Kenyan cities and subsequently other African markets. The anticipated systemic benefits include reduced environmental pollution, improved urban resilience, increased availability of secondary raw materials, stronger recycling value chains, expanded green employment and improved environmental data for decision-making. GreenVera OS has been developed and deployed as a digital platform. The Maji Mazuri Micro-MRF and associated river restoration and drainage interception initiatives are being prepared for phased pilot implementation. The quantified figures above represent initial operational targets rather than independently verified outcomes. GreenVera's long-term vision is to demonstrate that digitally enabled circular economy infrastructure can deliver commercially viable waste recovery while generating measurable environmental and social benefits.
Key technologies: GreenVera integrates digital technologies with decentralized circular economy infrastructure to modernize waste management and environmental restoration. 1. Cloud-Based Digital Platform: GreenVera OS is a live, web-based platform designed to support waste collection, collector coordination, material recovery operations, recycler management, client contracts, compliance and environmental reporting. 2. Digital Waste Traceability: The platform provides a foundation for recording waste collection, material recovery and recycling activities, improving accountability and visibility across the waste value chain. 3. Environmental Data Analytics: GreenVera OS incorporates reporting modules for tracking waste recovery, river waste removal and estimated carbon emissions avoided, supporting evidence-based environmental performance assessment. 4. AI Integration Roadmap: Planned capabilities include AI-assisted waste classification, predictive collection scheduling, recycling demand forecasting and data-driven operational optimization. These enhancements are proposed for future development rather than represented as currently deployed. 5. Decentralized Material Recovery Technologies: The proposed Maji Mazuri Micro-MRF will incorporate material segregation, weighing, sorting and aggregation technologies, with opportunities for future mechanization. 6. Environmental Interception Technologies: RiverRestore™ and GreenDrain™ are developing physical waste interception approaches for rivers and urban drainage systems. The solution combines digital infrastructure, circular economy methodologies and adaptable environmental technologies into an integrated platform designed for replication across African cities.
Unique Characteristics: GreenVera's innovation lies in integrating digital waste management, decentralized recycling infrastructure and environmental restoration into a unified circular economy model. 1. Integrated Digital-Physical Ecosystem:Unlike fragmented waste collection approaches, GreenVera combines GreenVera OS™ with planned material recovery facilities, river waste interception and drainage protection systems. 2. Locally Developed Digital Innovation: GreenVera OS™ is designed around the operational realities of African waste management, including fragmented collection networks, informal waste recovery activities and limited environmental data infrastructure. 3. Modular and Scalable Infrastructure: The proposed Micro-MRF model is designed to operate with relatively modest infrastructure and can be adapted for residential estates, communities and municipalities. 4. Circular Economy Value Creation: Rather than treating waste solely as a disposal problem, GreenVera seeks to recover commercially valuable materials and connect them to recycling and manufacturing markets. 5. Environmental Restoration Integration: RiverRestore™ and GreenDrain™ extend waste management beyond collection by targeting waste leakage into waterways and drainage systems. 6. Digital Environmental Accountability: GreenVera OS™ is designed to support measurable reporting of material recovery, environmental outcomes and sustainability indicators. 7. Inclusive, Women-Led Innovation: GreenVera promotes women's leadership, community participation and green employment opportunities within the circular economy. 8. Future AI-Enabled Optimization: The platform offers a foundation for introducing AI-assisted material identification, predictive waste management and intelligent resource allocation. Our competitive differentiation is the integration of digital infrastructure, physical waste recovery, environmental restoration and inclusive economic participation within one adaptable business model.
Sustainable Change: GreenVera has the potential to catalyze systemic transformation by shifting urban waste management from fragmented collection and disposal practices toward digitally connected, resource-efficient circular economy systems. 1. Transforming Waste into Economic Resources: By connecting decentralized material recovery facilities with recycling and manufacturing value chains, GreenVera aims to increase material recovery, reduce landfill dependence and strengthen secondary raw material markets. 2. Creating Replicable Urban Infrastructure: The proposed Maji Mazuri Micro-MRF will serve as an initial demonstration model that can be adapted and replicated across residential estates, municipalities and underserved urban communities. 3. Accelerating Digital Transformation: GreenVera OS provides a foundation for digitizing waste collection, material recovery, recycler coordination and environmental reporting. Its modular architecture creates opportunities for replication across different geographic and operational contexts. 4. Strengthening Environmental Resilience: RiverRestore™ and GreenDrain™ seek to prevent waste leakage into waterways, reduce drainage blockages and contribute to cleaner urban environments. 5. Promoting Inclusive Green Industrialization: The model creates opportunities for women, young people, informal waste workers and small recycling enterprises to participate in more structured circular economy value chains. 6. Enabling Evidence-Based Decision-Making: Improved waste traceability and environmental data could support municipal planning, extended producer responsibility initiatives, sustainability reporting and investment decisions. 7. Supporting Regional Replication: Following validation in Nairobi, GreenVera intends to establish partnerships with municipalities, recyclers, manufacturers and development institutions to adapt the model across Kenya and other African countries. 8. Catalyzing Industrial Innovation: Future integration of AI-assisted waste classification, predictive analytics and automated sorting technologies could improve resource recovery efficiency and strengthen local recycling industries. Our long-term vision is to contribute to an African circular economy in which waste is recognized as an economic resource, communities participate in sustainable value chains, environmental restoration becomes measurable and digital innovation enables more efficient and inclusive urban services. By combining technology, infrastructure, entrepreneurship and environmental stewardship, GreenVera aims to demonstrate a commercially sustainable model capable of generating lasting environmental, social and economic benefits beyond individual pilot locations.
Funding Sources: GreenVera Environmental Solutions Ltd is currently self-funded through personal investments by its founder, supporting technology development, operational setup and pilot preparation. No external grants or institutional investment have been received to date. The company is actively pursuing grants, strategic partnerships and impact investment to accelerate pilot implementation and scale its circular economy solutions across Africa.
Testimonials and Endorsements: GreenVera is an early-stage enterprise currently developing its pilot initiatives. Formal beneficiary testimonials and independent impact endorsements are not yet available. The company has established a relationship with the United Nations Global Compact and is pursuing additional institutional collaborations. Stakeholder feedback and verified impact testimonials will be documented as pilot implementation progresses.
Primary thematic focus area: AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry
Summary: GreenVera has built a waste operations platform in Nairobi and proposes to add a micro recovery facility, river interception and drainage traps around it. The software exists and the model is coherent; the physical infrastructure, the tonnage and the AI are all still to come.
Thematic focus areas (as submitted): AI for Green, Resilient and Sustainable Industry; Industrial Ecosystem Enablers: Finance, Skills and Market Access; Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems

Title: Annita: AI-Powered Digital Trade Infrastructure for Sustainable Industrial Growth
Subtitle: Connecting African MSMEs to commerce, payments, logistics, and intelligent trade infrastructure through one integrated, AI-powered digital ecosystem.
Problem Statement: African MSMEs face significant barriers to participating in regional and global industrial value chains. Fragmented digital infrastructure, limited market access, inefficient logistics, disconnected payment systems, inadequate business intelligence, and complex cross-border trade procedures prevent businesses from scaling sustainably. These challenges are particularly pronounced in developing economies, where many businesses operate through informal processes and lack access to integrated digital tools, reliable trade information, and intelligent decision-making capabilities. The absence of interconnected digital trade infrastructure increases operational costs, limits productivity, restricts market participation, and weakens the competitiveness of local enterprises. Annita addresses these structural challenges by connecting commerce, payments, logistics, and AI-powered business intelligence within a unified digital ecosystem.
Solution Overview: Annita is an AI-powered digital trade ecosystem designed to strengthen Africa's participation in regional and global commerce by connecting MSMEs, buyers, logistics providers, and payment infrastructure through one integrated environment. Developed by Annita LLC in Liberia, the solution addresses the fragmentation of digital trade infrastructure by bringing together three interconnected pillars: commerce, payments, and logistics, supported by an AI-driven intelligence and orchestration layer. How the Solution Works: 1. Digital Commerce Infrastructure: MSMEs can establish digital business presence, create product listings, manage inventory, connect with buyers, and access broader markets without requiring advanced technical expertise. 2. Integrated Payment Infrastructure: AnnitaPay facilitates digital transactions within the ecosystem, supporting more transparent payment processes, transaction records, and business settlements. 3. Connected Logistics Infrastructure: The ecosystem connects businesses with logistics providers to facilitate delivery coordination, order fulfilment, and trade-related operations. 4. AI-Powered Business Intelligence: Annita's AI orchestration architecture is designed to support MSMEs with product listing generation, pricing assistance, business insights, customer interactions, operational recommendations, and trade-related decision support. 5. Intelligent Trade Enablement: The Trade Engine is designed to assist with cross-border trade processes, including HS code guidance, tariff information, rules of origin, customs documentation, landed-cost estimation, and logistics coordination, using clearly identified official, third-party, and estimated data sources. Methodologies and Technologies: The solution follows an integrated, API-driven architecture supported by artificial intelligence, modular services, digital payment infrastructure, and interconnected commerce and logistics workflows. Its AI execution framework follows a PLAN–VALIDATE–CONFIRM–EXECUTE methodology, introducing human confirmation and safeguards before consequential transactions or business operations are executed. The architecture also prioritizes mobile-first accessibility, low-bandwidth environments, offline-resilient workflows, multilingual interaction, and simplified user experiences to accommodate MSMEs with different levels of digital literacy. Partnership and Collaboration Model: Annita operates through a collaborative ecosystem model involving MSMEs, buyers, logistics providers, technology partners, financial service providers, and relevant public institutions. The model is designed to enable partnerships with government agencies, industrial development institutions, financial institutions, logistics networks, research organizations, and regional trade organizations to support interoperability, technology transfer, and cross-border expansion.
Solution Provider(s): Annita LLC – Lead solution developer and implementing organization. A Liberian technology company responsible for developing, operating, and expanding the Annita Digital Ecosystem, with a focus on AI-powered commerce, payments, logistics, and digital trade infrastructure. Annita Group – Parent and strategic governance structure supporting the long-term development and expansion of the Annita ecosystem. External implementation partners: Strategic collaborations with financial service providers, logistics operators, technology providers, MSME associations, and public-sector institutions are being pursued to strengthen interoperability and regional deployment. No additional external implementation partners are being presented as formally confirmed at this stage.
Implementation location(s): Annita is developed and operated in Liberia, with implementation activities focused on serving MSMEs and connecting businesses, buyers, and logistics providers within its digital ecosystem across Africa starting with west Africa.
Implementation timeline(s): 2021–Present. Annita was founded on 24 August 2021. Product development and ecosystem implementation have progressed through successive development and deployment phases, with the company formally registered in 2023.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 3–6 months, depending on the next local market readiness, regulatory requirements, payment infrastructure integration, logistics partnerships, and MSME onboarding requirements. The deployment process would include market assessment, localization, partner integration, MSME onboarding, technical configuration, and controlled pilot testing before broader implementation.
Desired impact: Main Objectives: Annita's primary objective is to build accessible, AI-powered digital trade infrastructure that enables African MSMEs to participate more efficiently in local, regional, and international markets. The solution aims to: 1. Reduce fragmentation across commerce, payment, and logistics operations. 2. Improve MSME productivity through AI-assisted business management and intelligent decision-making. 3. Expand access to buyers, markets, and cross-border trade opportunities. 4. Strengthen digital infrastructure supporting regional supply chains and trade. 5. Improve financial and operational transparency through integrated digital transaction and business management processes. 6. Support inclusive industrial development by making advanced digital capabilities accessible to underserved businesses. Demonstrated Progress and Expected Impact: Annita has developed its digital ecosystem in Liberia and has reached more than 3,000 MSMEs through its ecosystem development and market engagement activities. The company currently operates with a seven-person full-time team. Its expected impact includes: - Increased digital participation and market access for MSMEs. - Reduced operational fragmentation through connected commerce, payments, and logistics workflows. - Improved business decision-making through AI-assisted intelligence. - Increased opportunities for women-led and underserved enterprises to participate in digital markets. - Improved coordination between businesses, buyers, and logistics providers. - Greater capacity for African MSMEs to participate in regional and international value chains. Additional impact indicators will include the number of active MSMEs onboarded, transactions facilitated, businesses accessing new markets, logistics fulfilment efficiency, operational cost savings, and employment opportunities created. Annita's longer-term objective is to establish scalable digital infrastructure that strengthens economic productivity and supports sustainable industrial development across Africa.
Key technologies: 1. Artificial Intelligence (AI): AI-powered business assistance, intelligent recommendations, product listing support, pricing assistance, and trade-related decision support. 2. AI Orchestration: A modular orchestration architecture that coordinates multiple AI capabilities and external model providers through structured workflows and controlled execution. 3. API-Driven Digital Infrastructure: Interconnected services linking commerce, payments, logistics, and business operations. 4. Digital Payment Infrastructure: Integrated digital transaction processing, payment records, and ecosystem settlement workflows. 5. Data Analytics and Business Intelligence: Structured business and transaction data supporting operational insights and informed decision-making. 6. Mobile-First Technology: Accessible mobile experiences designed for MSMEs operating in bandwidth-constrained environments. 7. Offline-Resilient Architecture: Workflows designed to accommodate intermittent internet connectivity and improve accessibility. 8. Trade Intelligence Technologies: Tools designed to support trade classification, tariff guidance, origin requirements, customs documentation, and landed-cost estimation.
Unique Characteristics: Annita's primary innovation is its approach to treating digital trade as interconnected infrastructure rather than isolated digital services. While many existing solutions address individual aspects of commerce, payments, or logistics, Annita integrates these capabilities into one connected digital ecosystem supported by artificial intelligence. Key Differentiating Features: 1. Unified Digital Trade Infrastructure: Connects commerce, payments, and logistics instead of requiring MSMEs to navigate disconnected services. 2. AI-Powered MSME Intelligence: Uses AI orchestration to help businesses perform operational tasks, access business intelligence, and make informed decisions without requiring advanced technical knowledge. 3. Intelligent Trade Engine: Designed to simplify complex cross-border trade processes, including customs information, trade classification, tariff guidance, documentation, and landed-cost estimation. 4. Human-Controlled AI Execution: Its PLAN–VALIDATE–CONFIRM–EXECUTE architecture introduces safeguards and user confirmation before consequential actions. 5. Inclusive and Accessible Design: Prioritizes mobile accessibility, offline-resilient workflows, multilingual capabilities, and simplified interactions for businesses with limited digital literacy. 6. Ecosystem-Based Business Model: Connects multiple economic participants, including MSMEs, buyers, logistics providers, and payment service providers, creating network effects as participation grows. 7. Designed for Emerging Markets: Developed in Liberia to address infrastructure and market-access challenges common across developing economies, with potential for adaptation across different African markets. Annita's differentiation is not simply the use of AI. It is the integration of AI into practical economic infrastructure that enables businesses to participate in connected digital trade.
Sustainable Change: Annita has the potential to contribute to systemic change by addressing one of Africa's fundamental development challenges: the fragmentation of digital infrastructure supporting commerce, payments, logistics, and industrial value chains. Rather than developing a solution for individual businesses in isolation, Annita is designed to establish an interconnected ecosystem through which MSMEs, buyers, logistics providers, and other economic participants can collaborate and conduct business more efficiently. 1. Strengthening African Industrial and Trade Infrastructure: By connecting fragmented digital services, Annita can help establish more accessible and interoperable infrastructure for MSMEs participating in domestic, regional, and international trade. 2. Accelerating MSME Formalization and Digital Transformation: The ecosystem can encourage businesses to adopt digital operations, maintain structured transaction records, improve business visibility, and strengthen their readiness to participate in formal supply chains. 3. Expanding Regional and Cross-Border Trade: Through its commerce, payment, logistics, and trade intelligence capabilities, Annita can help reduce barriers that prevent African MSMEs from accessing opportunities across regional markets, particularly under the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). 4. Democratizing Access to Artificial Intelligence: Annita makes AI-assisted business capabilities accessible to enterprises that may not have the financial resources, technical expertise, or infrastructure to independently adopt advanced AI technologies. 5. Supporting Inclusive and Sustainable Industrial Development: By improving coordination, reducing operational inefficiencies, and expanding market access, Annita can contribute to more productive, inclusive, and resilient business ecosystems. 6. Replication and Regional Scale-Up: The solution is designed around modular infrastructure that can be adapted to different country contexts through localized payment integrations, logistics partnerships, regulatory configurations, and trade requirements. Starting in Liberia, Annita aims to establish a replicable model that can expand across African markets and eventually support broader international trade networks. Problem Statement: Across Egypt and comparable MENA contexts, waste collection for residential communities, industrial facilities and rural areas remains largely informal and unmeasured. Title: Smart Incubator with Local-Language GSM Alerts for Smallholder Poultry Farmers
Subtitle: A low-cost ESP32-GSM intelligent incubator that uses AI to regulate temperature and humidity and sends voice alerts in the farmer's mother tongue for low-connectivity rural poultry farming
Problem Statement: Smallholder poultry farmers in Kenya and similar developing economies lose income and protein supply because day-old chicks are scarce and expensive: hatchery capacity is concentrated in a few large firms, and most rural farmers rely on natural brooding, which typically yields only 50–60% hatchability with high chick mortality. Imported incubators cost USD 500–3,000, assume stable grid power and internet, and are hard to repair locally. Rural farms face intermittent electricity, no Wi-Fi, low literacy, and interfaces available only in English or Swahili — excluding mother-tongue users. The result is recurring losses, weak food security, and limited youth and women's participation in a viable agribusiness value chain. There is a clear need for an affordable, repairable, offline-capable incubator whose alerts a farmer can actually understand.
Solution Overview: The solution is a low-cost intelligent egg incubator built around an ESP32 microcontroller. Temperature and humidity sensors feed a control loop that switches heating elements, fans and an automatic egg-turning motor via relays; an on-board AI model (edge/TinyML inference on the ESP32) learns normal operating behaviour and flags anomalies — heater failure, door left open, power loss, overheating — before eggs are lost. Readings are mirrored to a local display and relayed wirelessly (ESP-NOW/LoRa) to a second unit several meters away, so the farmer or a nearby attendant can monitor without a smartphone. A GSM module sends SMS and automated voice calls in the user's mother tongue — recorded local-dialect prompts such as “temperature too high, open the vent” — which works on any basic phone with no internet or app. A battery/solar backup keeps the unit alive during outages. Methodologies/technologies: embedded systems design, IoT sensing and control, edge AI/TinyML, GSM voice and SMS telephony, human-centred design, iterative prototyping and field testing with farmers. Collaboration model: developed at Rift Valley National Polytechnic with students as co-designers, tested with local poultry farmer groups and county extension officers, with a local assembly and repair model so units are built and serviced by trained TVET graduates.
Solution Provider(s): Geothermal Development Company (GDC) — Menengai Geothermal Project, Nakuru — Public sector; Kenyan state corporation developing the Menengai geothermal field, including direct-use applications of geothermal heat for agro-processing. Partner for direct-use geothermal heat supply, heat-exchanger design input, and siting of pilot incubator units within the Menengai direct-use/agro-industrial framework. Kenya Power and Lighting Company PLC (KPLC) — Public sector; national electricity transmission, distribution and retail utility. Partner for power-reliability assessment and grid-outage data used to size the incubator's backup and control strategy. Rift Valley National Polytechnic — Academia; host institution providing research, prototyping, testing facilities and student training.
Implementation location(s): Kenya — Nakuru County, Nakuru (Rift Valley National Polytechnic); Menengai geothermal direct-use site, Nakuru County (pilot heat-source testing).
Implementation timeline(s): Prototype development: 2025 – ongoing. Incubation trials at Rift Valley National Polytechnic: 2026 – ongoing. Pilot heat-source testing at Menengai geothermal direct-use site: ongoing]

This period will cover local needs assessment, adaptation to local poultry breeds and climatic conditions, hardware assembly, GSM network configuration, translation and recording of local-language alerts, installation, user training and controlled field testing. The modular design allows deployment in different rural environments with limited internet connectivity and varying electricity supply.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Edge Intelligence: Lightweight AI models are proposed for identifying abnormal temperature and humidity patterns, detecting equipment faults and supporting intelligent incubation decisions directly on the ESP32 microcontroller. 2. Internet of Things (IoT): ESP32-based embedded monitoring and control architecture for collecting, processing and managing real-time environmental data. 3. Title: Optimization Intelligence™ for Adaptive Industrial Decision-Making
Subtitle: A governed system-level optimization capability that improves interconnected industrial decisions across objectives, constraints, resources, and changing conditions.
Problem Statement: Industrial organizations increasingly use AI, analytics, automation, digital twins, and operational software, yet these systems often optimize individual tasks or domains independently. Local improvements do not necessarily produce the best overall system outcome. Changing demand, resource availability, operating constraints, supply disruptions, energy conditions, production priorities, and human decisions can create trade-offs across the broader operation. Organizations need a governed way to continuously evaluate these interacting factors, identify better feasible actions, reassess decisions as conditions change, and preserve human authority, traceability, and operational constraints.
Solution Overview: VEQSA Technologies develops Optimization Intelligence™ (OI), a modular system-level optimization capability designed to continuously pursue improved overall outcomes across interconnected decisions, objectives, constraints, resources, and changing operating conditions. OI operates as a decision and optimization layer that can work with existing enterprise systems rather than requiring organizations to replace their current infrastructure. Within a defined Decision Environment, relevant operational state, objectives, constraints, available resources, feasible actions, and approved data are evaluated together. OI can generate governed recommendations, compare feasible alternatives, reassess decisions as conditions change, incorporate authorized outcome evidence, and maintain traceability around recommendations and authority boundaries. The technology combines AI-assisted decision processes, optimization methods, governed adaptation, evidence tracking, APIs, and enterprise data integration. Initial deployments are designed as bounded validation environments before progressing to licensed Decision Environments. VEQSA’s collaboration model is enterprise-led: the industrial partner defines operational objectives, constraints, approved data, authority boundaries, and success measures, while VEQSA configures and validates the OI environment. Operational control remains with the partner during initial validation.
Solution Provider(s): N/A — VEQSA Technologies, Inc. currently owns and leads development of Optimization Intelligence™. External enterprise validation and implementation partnerships are being developed.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Approximately 6–8 weeks for a bounded pilot or validation environment, depending on data availability, integration requirements, security review, decision scope, and partner readiness.
Desired impact: The primary objective of Optimization Intelligence™ is to improve system-level industrial outcomes by evaluating interconnected decisions, objectives, constraints, resources, and changing conditions together rather than optimizing isolated tasks independently. Potential applications include production planning, material allocation, inventory and replenishment decisions, energy and resource coordination, infrastructure operations, supply-chain resilience, and coordination across AI-enabled or automated systems. VEQSA has completed controlled integrated acceptance of its current OI implementation. In a fixed synthetic comparison against a no-learning control, OI recorded 2 wins, 4 ties, and 0 losses, with 22 modeled cost units lower across the six-case comparison. These are controlled engineering results, not customer savings or demonstrated field ROI. External pilots will establish partner-specific measures such as reduced disruption, lower resource consumption, improved utilization, reduced emergency procurement, improved service levels, reduced operating cost, or other agreed operational and sustainability outcomes. VEQSA does not currently claim quantified field-level emissions, energy, or financial impact prior to external validation.
Key technologies: Optimization Intelligence™ combines artificial intelligence, optimization and decision methods, governed adaptation, enterprise data integration, APIs, evidence and outcome tracking, constraint-aware decision logic, and controlled authority mechanisms. OI can integrate with operational technologies such as enterprise applications, digital twins, planning systems, AI models, autonomous agents, industrial data platforms, IoT environments, and robotics without requiring those systems to be replaced. The specific technology configuration depends on the Decision Environment and the industrial partner’s approved systems, data, security requirements, and operational constraints.
Unique Characteristics: Most enterprise AI systems optimize a model, task, workflow, asset, or local objective. Optimization Intelligence™ is designed around a different responsibility: continuously pursuing improved overall outcomes across interacting decisions, objectives, constraints, resources, and changing conditions. Key differentiators include: - system-level rather than isolated task optimization; - compatibility with heterogeneous existing AI, software, planning, and automation systems; - explicit operational constraints and authority boundaries; - governed recommendation and decision processes; - continuous reassessment as conditions and outcomes change; - evidence and outcome traceability; - the ability to operate initially in recommendation or approval-gated modes before higher levels of bounded autonomy; - a modular commercial model in which one underlying OI capability can support multiple industry-specific Decision Environments. This allows organizations to add a persistent optimization responsibility across existing intelligent systems without replacing their entire technology stack.

Once validated within one Decision Environment, the same underlying capability can be configured for additional decisions, facilities, operating units, industries, and geographies while preserving local objectives, constraints, data requirements, and authority structures. This creates potential for broader industrial impact as organizations adopt increasing numbers of AI models, agents, digital twins, planning systems, connected assets, and autonomous technologies. Title: aikonOS: Governed AI Agents for Industry
Subtitle: An open-source, self-hosted control plane that decides, action by action, what an AI agent may do, and records every decision in a tamper-evident audit trail.
Problem Statement: Industrial organisations want to put AI agents to work on real systems and documents, but cannot safely let a model act on its own. Prompt injection is unsolved, so a compromised agent can leak data, call unapproved tools or run up unbounded costs. Auditors and regulators also expect proof of who authorised what. Without governance, SMEs and organisations in developing and middle-income economies either avoid agent-based AI or adopt it without controls, which widens the digital divide.
Solution Overview: An agent only proposes actions; the aikonOS broker decides. Every tool call crosses four independent, fail-closed gates: (1) identity via OIDC and SPIFFE mTLS, (2) access via OpenFGA relationship-based checks on every call, (3) routing via OPA policy that sends a call to auto-execute, human approval, step-up or deny, and (4) a single-use Biscuit capability token that can only be narrowed, never widened. High-risk steps pause for human approval (n-of-m, with separation of duty). Every decision is written to a hash-chained, signed audit trail in a WORM store and can be re-run offline against the policy revision that produced it. Provider credentials never enter the agent loop, each user's agent runs in its own process, and documents are handled by a service with no network egress and no credentials. Users get a web console and a native Windows app for chat, files, schedules, skills and delegating tasks to colleagues. Technologies: Go, Node/TypeScript, Vue 3, Rust, Postgres with row-level security, NATS, Vault, MinIO, OpenFGA, OPA, Biscuit, Keycloak or any OIDC provider. It is model-agnostic (any OpenAI-compatible provider) and deploys with Docker Compose. Released under Apache-2.0 with signed images, SBOMs and build provenance. Collaboration model: open source, community contributions, and operators or integrators deploying it in their own environment.
Solution Provider(s): No formal partners at present (open-source project, Apache-2.0); open to deployment, integration and pilot partners.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: About 2 to 4 weeks, including identity provider integration and policy setup. The base stack starts with four commands on a single host with Docker Compose.
Desired impact: Objectives: let organisations adopt AI agents safely by bounding what an agent can do to what policy already allows; make every AI action attributable and auditable; cap spend per user and per task; and keep control in the operator's hands through self-hosting and open source. Impact: not yet quantified. aikonOS is pre-1.0 and no deployment results are claimed. Expected impact is lower risk and cost of adopting AI agents, faster compliance evidence, and a free, auditable governance layer that SMEs and organisations in developing and middle-income economies can run on their own infrastructure.
Key technologies: AI agents and LLMs (model-agnostic, OpenAI-compatible APIs), policy engines (OPA, OpenFGA), capability tokens (Biscuit), zero-trust identity (OIDC, SPIFFE), tamper-evident audit logging (hash chain, WORM storage), Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool servers, and containerised deployment (Docker Compose).
Unique Characteristics: Governance is enforced at the unbypassable boundary instead of trusting the model: aikonOS contains prompt injection rather than claiming to prevent it. Distinctive features: four independent fail-closed gates; per-call access re-checks; single-use capability tokens that can only be narrowed along a delegation chain; routing by effect class that decides how a step is gated but never whether it is allowed; replayable decisions that can be re-run offline with the stock OPA binary; per-user and per-task spend caps; and a self-hosted, open-source delivery model with no vendor lock-in and signed releases.
Sustainable Change: Open, auditable governance lowers the barrier for organisations to adopt AI agents responsibly, and for regulators and auditors to verify them. Because it is Apache-2.0, self-hosted and model-agnostic, it can be replicated across countries and sectors without licensing cost or dependence on a vendor. Policy and audit conventions can become a shared reference for trustworthy industrial AI. Planned scale-up includes a Kubernetes (Helm) deployment, an independent security audit, and a sovereign profile with a locally hosted model and no external network egress.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial AI Models and Intelligent Decision-Making
Summary: aikonOS is an open-source control plane that decides, call by call, what an AI agent may do and records the decision in a tamper-evident log. The design is the most carefully reasoned piece of AI governance in the field; the evidence that it has been used anywhere is, on the applicant's own account, still to come.

Title: ENGAGE WATCH: Persistent AI Intelligence for Africa’s Critical Infrastructure
Subtitle: An on-premise AI platform that combines drone, sensor and geospatial data to spot threats to pipelines and energy assets in real time, without sensitive data leaving the operator’s site.
Problem Statement: Africa’s energy, utility and industrial assets are spread across large, hard-to-reach areas: swamps, creeks, forests and insecure corridors. Pipelines, wellheads and flow stations face theft, vandalism, sabotage, leaks and intrusion. Nigeria’s regulator, NUPRC, reported about $3.3 billion of crude lost to theft over 14 months. Losses have dropped sharply since 2024, but daily losses are still large, and new methods such as barge-based theft keep appearing. Operators have three main problems: Data that isn’t connected. Drone footage, CCTV, sensors, field reports and maps sit in separate systems. Nobody gets one clear picture. Slow, manual monitoring. Ground patrols and helicopter surveillance are expensive, dangerous and occasional. Incidents are often found days later, after the environmental and financial damage is done. Data that can’t leave the site. Most AI tools are hosted in foreign clouds. National-security, regulatory and commercial rules often require critical-infrastructure data to stay on site, so operators can’t use these tools. The result is lost revenue, lost government income, oil spills that damage farmland and waterways, and danger to the people who protect these assets.
Solution Overview: How it works. ENGAGE WATCH is a decision-intelligence platform for operators of critical assets. It works in four steps: Sense: It collects data from long-endurance fixed-wing VTOL drones (JOUAV CW-25 class), fixed cameras, IoT and pipeline sensors, satellite and geospatial layers, and field-team reports. It works with drones and sensors from other makers too. Fuse: It puts all these sources onto one live, location-based map of the asset. Detect: AI models find and flag unusual activity, such as unauthorized people or vehicles, illegal tapping points, barge movement, leaks, fire and right-of-way encroachment. Each alert is ranked by risk. Respond: It sends alerts with evidence to the right security, operations or HSE team. It supports dispatch and drone follow-up, and keeps a full audit trail.
Solution Provider(s): JOUAV (Chengdu JOUAV Automation Tech Co., Ltd.) – unmanned aerial systems maker of industrial fixed-wing VTOL drones; drone supplier and partner for local assembly in Nigeria; Aerospace/UAV & Industrial Technology, Milsat Africa – Nigerian geospatial and location-data company; data partner for maps, geodata and ground data collection; Geospatial/Data Services, ARCO Worldwide Services – Nigerian operations and services firm; local deployment and field-operations partner; Energy Services/Operations
Implementation location(s): nigeria
Duration to pilot in a new geography: 12 weeks
Desired impact: Find threats to critical assets in minutes instead of days. Cut production losses, theft and environmental damage. Lower the cost and danger of monitoring remote assets. Build African capacity in AI, drone operations and drone assembly. Expected impact (pilot targets, to be checked against each site’s baseline): At least 70% faster detection-to-response time compared with patrol-based monitoring 30–50% fewer ground and air patrol hours, with fewer staff exposed to dangerous areas Ongoing coverage of hundreds of pipeline kilometres per drone unit Earlier leak and tamper detection, so fewer and smaller spills, less cleanup cost and less damage to farmland and waterways Recovered revenue for operators and government. Even a small cut in the remaining theft is worth millions of dollars a year at national scale. Skilled local jobs: drone pilots, data analysts, field technicians, and later drone assembly roles
Key technologies: AI and computer vision: object detection, tracking, change and anomaly detection on aerial and fixed video Data fusion engine that combines drone, sensor, geospatial and human reports into one picture of the site Long-endurance fixed-wing VTOL drones, compatible with any maker’s hardware IoT and edge computing: pipeline and site sensors, AI processing on the drone or on site GIS and remote sensing: satellite and geospatial layers, mapping, digital models of pipeline routes On-premise, offline-capable AI setup with role-based access and audit logs Alerting and response workflows that connect to security and HSE teams
Unique Characteristics: Sells outcomes, not drones. Customers pay for measurable results: faster detection, fewer losses, safer operations. Many operators have tried drone programs that didn’t change much. ENGAGE WATCH is the intelligence layer that turns raw footage into action. Keeps data on site. Full offline deployment means security-sensitive operators can use advanced AI without sending data to foreign clouds. Works with any hardware. It combines existing cameras, sensors and any maker’s drones, so operators keep what they’ve already invested in. Built for Africa. It’s designed for swamps, creeks, poor connectivity and local threats such as barge-based theft, and it uses local geospatial data. Local value chain. Drone assembly in Nigeria and local operations partners keep skills, jobs and maintenance in the country. Dual-use and cross-sector. The same platform works for oil and gas, power lines, mining, ports, rail and public safety.
Sustainable Change: Replication: The same setup applies to pipelines, power transmission lines, mines, ports and rail across Africa. Shared data: Combined, anonymized data on incidents and threat patterns can help operators, regulators and security agencies coordinate, moving the sector from reacting to incidents to preventing them. Local industry: Local drone assembly, data partnerships and operator training build lasting supply chains, skills and a pool of AI and drone talent. Policy and trust: The on-premise model shows that data sovereignty and advanced AI can work together, which can inform national AI and data-protection frameworks. Environment and communities: Fewer spills protect farmland, fisheries and the health of host communities, and support better accountability in energy regions.
Funding Sources: ENGAGE WATCH has been funded to date through founder capital, including proceeds reinvested from the founder’s previous venture, Blueroomcare (a health-tech company acquired by EHA Group). This has funded platform development, partnership building with JOUAV, and preparation for pilot demonstrations with energy-sector operators. No previous implementation has been funded by grants or external investors. For pilots, we plan a mix of operator-funded pilots (paid proof-of-value engagements), strategic grants, and seed investment to support local drone assembly and expansion across Africa.
Primary thematic focus area: Industrial Digital Infrastructure and Data Ecosystems

Title: HINGA by Adroan: Connecting farm reports to actionable agricultural data
Subtitle: An AI-enabled advisory and data layer connecting farmers, extension workers and agricultural organisations, with SMS access under development.
Problem Statement: Agricultural organisations need timely, usable information from farmers, while many farmers have limited smartphone access and face language barriers. HINGA is investigating how farmer reports can support better advisory and more useful information across agricultural value chains. The team is testing specific organisational workflows and willingness to pay. No paying customer, verified cost saving or validated EUDR-compliance outcome is claimed.
Solution Overview: HINGA is an early-stage product by Adroan, developed in Uganda. Its current V1 provides farmer advisory scoped by weather and location. It uses GPT OSS 20B as the primary language model and GPT OSS 120B as a fallback through Groq, with Whisper for audio and the Sunbird API for local-language support. An SMS pipeline is being built to allow farmers with basic phones to interact with the service. The longer-term direction is a data layer connecting farmers, extension workers, exporters, processors and other agricultural organisations. Organisation-facing workflows and the use of farmer reports for traceability or insurance are proposals for validation, not deployed or certified capabilities. Farmer reports alone do not establish plot geolocation, deforestation-free status or verified insurance losses. No formal pilot or partner commitment is represented in this application.
Solution Provider(s): No formal solution partners are confirmed. Validation conversations do not constitute partnerships or commitments.
Implementation location(s): N/A. The prototype is being developed in Uganda; no implemented organisational pilot is claimed.
Duration to pilot in a new geography: Deployment time in a new geography has not yet been validated. It would depend on agreeing a bounded workflow, local-language and SMS integration, data protection requirements, and a host organisation. A pilot schedule would be agreed with that organisation.
Desired impact: The objectives are to improve access to weather-scoped agricultural advisory and develop a useful cross-organisation farm-data layer. Expected benefits include more accessible interaction for basic-phone users and better-informed organisational decisions. These are intended benefits, not demonstrated impact. No measured reduction in losses, compliance costs, emissions or claims-verification costs is asserted. A future pilot would establish a baseline and test a specific workflow before making quantified impact claims.

An SMS pipeline and a small text classifier are under development. Organisation dashboards, evidence validation and delivery-to-plot traceability are not represented as live features.
Unique Characteristics: The proposed distinction is a data layer connecting multiple agricultural organisations and farmers, rather than only a single organisation's internal workflow. HINGA combines its current advisory, audio and local-language components with planned basic-phone SMS access.
